blocks: Chapter 1
Meldan, Veridia·3724 Snowmoon 3

Gladias was walking along a foot path, with tall trees towering on both sides. A series of houses made out of large stone bricks lay behind the trees on both sides, medieval in style but without any of the junk, dust on the ground, or other imperfections that a real medieval structure would have had a thousand years earlier. A few of the houses featured small signs advertising clothing, flowers or food available for sale. Each house seemed to meld seamlessly into the scattered leaves, plants and trees that surrounded it.

He looked around, breathed in and briefly stopped to enjoy the nature, dense enough and quiet enough that he almost forgot that he was in the middle of the Kalimar district of Meldan, the capital city of Veridia.

Suddenly, a small drone flew over his head. Gladias instinctively checked his watch. Almost immediately, a green checkmark lit up. Even before he could fully process what had happened, his watch had engaged in a zero-knowledge authentication protocol, and received a cryptographic attestation verifying that the drone was a toy, and its navigation algorithm had a safety override that would prevent it from coming within five decimeters of a human without permission. His watch had learned that the drone was not a threat - and nothing else.

The drone flew off, and continued above a sidewalk branching off to the left. For a moment, Gladias could briefly see its shape: a small ball, with feather-like rotors on three sides. And the very next moment, a young boy jumped up, and grabbed it with his hand while it was still in the sky.
"Five points for me!", the boy shouted excitedly.
Gladias let his attention wander back to peacefully observing his surroundings. The boy who had just caught the ball was part of a family with four children, the younger two each riding a tricycle.

On another sidewalk branching off to the right, Gladias could see a grandmother with a small child. As they approached a bench and seemed to stop, a couple that was already sitting on the bench pre-emptively stood up to offer their seats. The grandmother thanked them, and sat down with her child.

And playing into Gladias's ear this whole time, there was an audio program from Emerald, the local AI running from Gladias's hand device, explaining the nuances of airborne virus transmission and how to calculate how much a given change to a building's ventilation or density might affect total city-wide cases in an epidemic.

As Gladias walked forward, the houses soon gave way to thick green shrubbery. As soon as the shrubbery cleared, the foot path started gently curving upward. Smoothly, and suddenly, the path transitioned into a sky bridge above a busy road, with many cars and autobuses and a few autonomous delivery vehicles passing beneath him. A chilly breeze blew into his face.

"Pause, I want to enjoy the view", Gladias said to Emerald, out of habit whispering the sentence so softly that only his throat muscles moved and no sound at all left his lips. The silken cloth band tightly covering Gladias's neck picked it up perfectly.

He stopped in the middle of the sky bridge, turned to his left side, and looked forward. The busy road beneath him continued for about two kilometers, and then turned rightward. Beyond that point, he could see a mountain covered with trees. A few apartment buildings about fifteen storeys tall, decorated and shaped like over-sized medieval castle towers though with far more windows on the sides, poked up high above the trees in several places on the lower half of the mountain slope.

Gladias turned his face left once again, and took one last look at the natural world. The nature in Veridia is beautiful, he thought. He then turned his face to the right, where the road continued past the sky bridge with a much higher density of buildings. Today, his job was to offer opinions on the human world.

Gladias began to walk forward once more, and stepped off the sky bridge. On the left side, there was now a row of five-storey apartment buildings, interspersed with walking paths and small shops selling various kinds of goods. Both the walking paths and the sidewalk were protected from the sun by tall green trees.
On the right side, there was now a tall soundproof barrier, painted with green and blue colors, barely visible behind another even thicker row of tall trees.
Shortly after he began walking beside the soundproof barrier, his hand device buzzed.
Gladias immediately knew what he was being asked to do. As a citizen of Veridia, he had been randomly selected by cryptographic sortition to vote on how much he liked the building.

The goal of the voting, Gladias remembered from the Veridian civics lessons of his youth, was to determine the public aesthetics tax - a major component of the composite land tax - that each building would have to pay. Developers paid a lot of attention to this. In Veridia, making buildings that the public found appealing was not just a chance to show off their craft - it was profitable.

Gladias looked at the building, the blue-grey colored Badra St #1103. The structure seemed in-character, not too different from the other buildings on the same street. The style was modern, but tasteful, nothing like the soulless rectangular concrete buildings that he was accustomed to seeing in pictures of places like Freetown. It had footpaths on both sides, and both footpaths were covered by trees - just like the other buildings nearby.

This was hard, Gladias realized. To get some inspiration, he waved his hand device, and took a look at the land tax rates that some of the other nearby buildings were paying. First, the building that he was supposed to vote on.

He then turned to his left, and zoomed his hand device in to point at the first few genuinely different buildings he could find: one building made with an architectural style mixing wood and stone, another with a garden on the roof, and a third, smaller but more luxurious looking, that was shaped like an octahedron, and had a beautifully arranged square garden along the perimeter of the territory with a maple tree brimming with red leaves at each corner. All three paid aesthetics taxes significantly lower than Badra St #1103, and one was even slightly negative.

He then zoomed in to another building that he could barely make out in the distance. At this distance, the trees thickly lining the streets cleverly covered it up, but his hand device easily locked on to it and downloaded both a close-up image and the tax percentages.

The building itself was a corporate headquarters for an aviation company. The company had had the bright idea to make their office look like an aeroplane. It was impressive architecture, he thought, but he would certainly demand some compensation if he had to walk by it every morning.
He checked its taxes.
Well deserved, Gladias thought. Though he was glad that Veridia's institutions let people with tastes that were so different from his express themselves, even if they had to pay for the privilege.
Gladias's mind snapped back to his task. He was voting on the blue and grey building right in front of him. He took a look at the interface again.

This was quadratic voting, he remembered. All his votes would be automatically shifted, stretched or squeezed so that the total average of the votes becomes zero, and the average of the squares of the votes becomes one. So there was no point in voting up on everything, down on everything, or overly extreme on everything. It was best, mathematically provably best, to vote not just the direction you felt right, but also with the strength you felt right - not more, not less.

Gladias's mind struggled. The aesthetics taxes given to each building seemed ... already fair? Maybe the aeroplane building was perhaps being treated a little too harshly. Allowing such a building to stand is not just a concession to people's freedom to do their own thing on their own land, it also brought genuine variety to Meldan. Maybe it's okay to have in what was already a corporate district.
Then he reminded himself that he was not voting on the aeroplane building, he was voting on Badra St #1103.
Right, he thought. What decision to make? Support or oppose?
After thinking for a moment, he finally decided by raw instinct, and pushed the slider only a slight amount toward the right.
He hit "Select".

That was just a warmup, he thought - a random fluke that he had been assigned an aesthetics vote as a Veridian citizen right before one of his more consequential votes as an Acolyte in the Order of Steering. That vote had been hard. The vote that he was about to do would be far more challenging - and there, the system would be keeping score.
He continued walking, and after a minute he arrived at an opening in the soundproof barrier: the entrance to the concert that he was attending.

Gladias held his hand device near a circle with a glowing green outline on the entrance gate. He waited briefly as his hand device produced a cryptographic proof, and then a machine embedded in the entrance gate verified it.
"Verified, welcome", the machine said.
The gate learned that someone holding a valid and unused credential had arrived - and nothing else.
Gladias passed through the gate, and headed toward the main concert area.

He could see a few of the attendees wearing the same signature Veridian Privacy Robe that he was wearing. This was a loose-fitting dark purple dress that covered the full body from the hood covering the wearer's head down to the ankles. Below the ankles, privacy robe wearers all wore shoes of the same dark purple color.
The other attendees were mostly wearing simple shirts, either plain colored or featuring slogans of their favorite bands.

Some were moving forward with clear intent and efficiency, just like Gladias. Others were dancing. Others were chatting with each other. And still others were walking forward calmly, simply trying to passively enjoy the show.
Gladias emerged into a large open field surrounded by a high soundproof barrier - the same barrier that Gladias saw before, but from the inside.

Gladias pushed through the crowd, as the noise became louder. He pulled on a strap on his privacy robe's front face cover, tightening a belt that separated the area below his nose from the area above his nose. The program on airborne virus transmission that he had been listening to only minutes earlier had primed him to take care to not get sick.
He soon got to the concert stage area, and was able to clearly hear the gnarly voice of Dreadknot's lead singer.
WE MEET THEM WITH OUR FURY IN OUR HEARTS
AND FLAY THEIR FLESH WITH SHINING STEEL AND DARTS
Gladias took out his hand device again.

Most people attending the concert were there to enjoy the music and hang out with their friends. For Gladias, this was certainly not his ideal entertainment - his preferred music was of a much softer and gentler variety - but he did not dislike it either. More than anything else, he found the concert interesting in an anthropological way, exploring the interests and emotions of people he would otherwise have little interaction with.
But ultimately, Gladias was at the concert for quite a different purpose. Gladias checked the rubric on his hand device:

In Veridia, very few things are strictly banned. If Dreadknot wanted to, they could have all their songs repeatedly shouting "Hail the Arctic Emperor" and "we hope all government officials get painfully murdered" over and over again, and they would never be shut down or go to jail. But what Veridia does have is intricate systems of taxes and subsidies, maintained by a government-linked but decentralized collective called the Order of Steering.

One part of this collective, the Keepers, voted on tax rubrics that determined what the taxes are. Another part, the Sentinels, audited individual businesses, each audit assigning a particular business a position on a particular rubric. Gladias was an Acolyte: an Order member in training.
And today, Gladias's task was to evaluate Dreadknot's position on the tax rubric for social impact of public performances.
THE SMOKE OF CITIES BURNING IN THE NIGHT
WE LEAVE NO PLACE TO HIDE FOR ALL IN SIGHT

Gladias clicked "View relevant precedents", and scrolled through them. He pressed a side button. A small popup appeared on the top right: "Emerald listening mode active". He did not speak; instead, he simply let Emerald listen to Dreadknot sing. But even after five minutes of listening, only a few relevant precedents showed up.

Gladias switched the mode to "analysis" and kept it listening for another five minutes. Emerald listed some conclusions that sounded reasonable, but Gladias could tell it was unreliable. There was just not enough source data on this kind of music for the Emerald AI to give good answers, and ultimately, it was Gladias's job to figure out when to defer to Emerald and when to let his own instinct have more of a say. Here, instinct it was.
Well, the song was definitely violent.

But on the other hand, over a century of Veridian civics lore made a distinction between advocating violence, and merely showcasing it for entertainment value. Gladias could see and hear the audience dancing, cheering and enjoying the music. They seemed to be having fun, not rising up in hatred against anyone.

But on the other other hand, Gladias knew that Sentinels in recent times paid less attention to that distinction than before, and seemed to value a softer and gentler society almost as an end in itself.

Gladias was not quite sure if this was what the Keepers who created that rubric intended, or if it was the right call for society. In a few months, he would be a Sentinel in full standing, and would have more leeway to decide. But for now, his freedom to decide was limited: the system was keeping score.
Gladias looked down at his hand device.

Ten percent of the time, any audit made by Acolytes would be repeated by Sentinels. An Acolyte's score reflected how well that portion of their votes predicted the Sentinels' judgements. Today, Gladias's score was ninety two. If it stayed above ninety, he would get in and become a Sentinel - or, if he changed his mind, a Keeper. But if his score dropped by even three points, his career would be on hold for at least another year.

The rest of the screen was filled with chat messages. There were nine Acolytes assigned to this audit, split into three groups of three. The other two members of his group could not agree. One was insisting on Tier 3 - a sort of neutral judgement - and the other was harsher, demanding Tier 4.

Gladias sighed. The other two groups were probably thinking the same way. If we simplify and say every other Acolyte was a coin-flip between Tier 3 and Tier 4, then by the binomial formula, the probability the other six would also be evenly split was six choose three - 20 - divided by 64, or about thirty-one percent. Now if the other Acolytes' votes were not coin-flips ... eh, calculating that exactly is too hard, but it's definitely lower, let's just say twenty percent. A twenty or thirty percent chance his vote would significantly affect Dreadknot's tax rate for the next year. Oh great. Actual responsibility.

Gladias looked around once more at the crowd. The first song finished, and he heard them cheering. He felt a burst of courage. He would take the ten percent chance of a hit to his prediction score. Without thinking further, he pressed Tier 3.
For a brief moment, he felt proud of his decision.
"HEY EVERYONE, IT'S AN ORDER MEMBER!", someone behind him yelled.
Gladias's body froze in shock for a moment. Before his mind could catch up, his eyes had already scanned the venue, and discovered the nearest exit.

He immediately understood what had happened. The security of the Order, particularly preventing influence and bribery, rests on the privacy of its members. Order members are strictly forbidden to reveal their assigned task. To make sure that Order members take their privacy seriously, they were kept on their toes by a sort of deliberately engineered game. Anyone can connect to the decentralized cryptographic network that manages the Order's operations, and send in a guess about what a particular Order member's assigned task is, along with a small deposit. If their guess is correct, the Order member's salary is docked, and the discoverer gets half as a reward.

Before he could react any further, another man nearby, also wearing a privacy robe, broke and ran toward the fire exit on the right. Everyone within ten meters took out their hand devices and pointed them at him, recording video. Gladias immediately understood what had happened here too: a decoy. Some member of the public altruistically diverting attention to himself, to give Gladias a chance to escape.
Gladias turned around, intending to run. But before he could take a step, he saw right in front of him a large burly man, pointing a hand device straight at his face.

Gladias froze. At first, he thought that he was done for. His mind raced through the possibilities, looking for any possible way out. Finally, Gladias the thoughtful philosopher gave way to a different Gladias, more imaginative and mischievous - a Gladias that had not been awake since recess in middle school.
Gladias looked toward the right.
"Wait, is that a new screed from the Arctic Emperor?", he asked.
The man, confused, looked to where Gladias was looking. At that moment, Gladias snatched the man's hand device from his arm, and suddenly turned around.
"Delete all audio, images and video from the last longhour. Reboot."

He began to run. A few ticks later, the device responded, "4 files deleted", and briefly showed screenshots of some photos and videos. The one on the bottom right was of Gladias's face. The screen turned black.
Gladias threw the hand device up into the air, hoping that his pursuer would choose not losing his device over chasing him. He continued running.

Despite being slowed down by his shoes, which had high heels to raise his height to the same level as other robe wearers and deliberately uneven soles to randomize his gait, Gladias managed to quickly reach the exit. Distracted by the rest of the commotion, the crowd seemed not to notice.
He exited the concert venue, and hopped onto a local autobus.

The autobus was nearly empty. To his left, Gladias saw two other people, both wearing privacy robes. Were they male, female, young or old, he could not tell. To his right, he saw a teenager wearing ordinary clothes and a backpack, who seemed to be coming home from school.
His eyes wandered to the advertisements on the inside walls of the autobus.

The first advertisement was a poster reminding Veridians of the importance of lifelong learning. On the left side of the poster was a picture of a classroom with a child, a middle-aged woman, and a much older man, all reading textbooks together. On the right side of the poster was the text:
School lasts until age 20. Education is every Veridian's responsibility and duty for a lifetime.
Learn about Veridian Graph Funding-subsidized education programs for all ages today.

The second advertisement was for Hydrafill, a brand selling water and various kinds of drinks. Nudged gently by Veridian Steering taxes, they had over the last twenty years become almost completely sugar free.
On the left side of the advertisement, was the classic yellow and green colored Hydrafill bottle. On the right side of the advertisement was the text:
Hydrafill
Our drinks are proudly free of over 2,000 known poisons and anti-recommended substances.
Gladias smiled.

He wished that it had been the Hydrafill advertisement that he had been selected to vote on, and not the blue and grey building. He would have slid the slider almost all the way to the right for this one, he knew.
We need more fun in the world.
Fifteen minutes later, Gladias stepped off the autobus. After a short walk along a street, he arrived at his house. He opened the door.
"Are you home, Seila?", he shouted.
"Was just writing up my blog post", she replied, and came out of her room to greet Gladias.
"So, what do we want for dinner?"
"Well, the Dzego food truck is coming in seven minutes, how about we have that again?"
"Sure! I assume the number ten for you again?"
"Yep!"
"Okay, I'll have the number thirteen this time."
Seila took out her hand device, and began to place the order.
They heard loud footsteps coming down the stairs.
"Dad is home!", the younger boy, Zven, shouted. Zven jumped down the stairs three steps at a time, and ran up to hug Gladias, who obliged.
The older teenage boy, Febric, walked down more slowly, carrying his hand device in one hand, attached by a cable to a larger compute box in the other.
"We're ordering from the Dzego food truck. What do you guys want?", Gladias asked.
"Number four!", Febric answered.
"Number five, I win!", Zven shouted.
"What about Lily and Hreda?"
"Lily's in the bathroom. Hreda will be back from after-school number theory in a longhour. Come on, you know she always gets the number nine."
The bathroom door opened, and Lily slowly walked out, her eyes looking to the ground.
Seila sighed. "What happened?"
"Sixty percent on the history exam. Whatever..."
Seila turned, and put her arms around Lily. "It's okay to not be good at everything", she said softly.
Lily turned her face further away from Seila and the family. She ran forward, and sat down on the couch.
Seila sighed, and ordered Lily the number eight.
Seila clicked order. Gladias, Seila, Zven and Febric sat at the table and waited.
On the couch, Lily took out her hand device, and began intently watching and quickly tapping on the screen, devoting all her attention to some game that Gladias and Seila could never make out.

This was Gladias and Seila's fourth last dinner with the kids - of whom Zven and Lily were theirs, and Febric and Hreda were from their co-family, Uncle Vil and Aunt Daia. In four days, Uncle Vil and Aunt Daia were going to come and pick all four kids up, and take care of them for the next half of the year.
Gladias sighed. He would miss the kids. But at the same time, he was looking forward to the six months of freedom.
"Are we still going to stay with Uncle Vil for six months?", Zven asked.
"Of course!", Seila replied.
"Yay, I love Uncle Vil!"
"For me Vil is Dad!", Febric made a point of reminding. He thought for a moment longer. "Uncle Glad and Aunt Seila, I love you both too!"
"And I love you."

A doorbell rang. Gladias walked to the door, opened the door, and got a bag full of food boxes. He set the bag on the table, and took out and gave each person the food box with their number on it. Gladias, Seila, Febric and Zven all started eating.
"Any plans once Vil is here?", Gladias asked.

"I'm going to visit Freetown for a month or two, see Jahn, maybe figure out some blog post to write on the United Cities. I've spent so much time reading about their co-governance, actually looking forward to seeing more how it all connects to what's on the ground."
"Nice! I'm going to go on some long walks in the forest and take a deep dive with the bot on the environment and biology rubrics. Still have four more audits to do before I can become a Sentinel!"
Gladias and Seila both resumed eating. Quietly, Lily walked up to the table, and began to open her food box as well.
At that moment, Gladias's hand device buzzed. He took it out. A single notification popped up.
And a few ticks later, another:

isDarkMode = !isDarkMode;
localStorage.setItem('darkMode', isDarkMode);
var html = document.documentElement;
var btn = document.querySelector('.dark-toggle');
if (isDarkMode) { html.classList.add('dark'); btn.textContent = '\uD83C\uDF19'; }
else { html.classList.remove('dark'); btn.textContent = '\u2600\uFE0F'; }

document.documentElement.classList.add('dark');
document.querySelector('.dark-toggle').textContent = '\uD83C\uDF19';
Chapter 2
Pafogai Du, Dzego·3724 Snowmoon 5
Fin and Zei got off the autobus and walked down Hun Min street.

Hun Min street was one of the more lively commercial and industrial streets in Pafogai Du. On both sides of the street, they could see signs with colored blinking lights advertising all kinds of electronics: hand devices, watches, compute boxes, lighting, batteries, sensors and more. Among the stores were miniature factories, building various sophisticated devices and in a few places even computer chips. The buildings were all one or two storeys tall, and many signs were on top of stairways leading underground.

On the left, there were two adjacent stores. One was selling sensors of all kinds - cameras, microphones, biological and chemical sensors, air quality monitors, and of course, sensors designed to detect sensors. The other was selling anti-transmission foil - a common material used by default in many kinds of rooms, to block wireless signals. Privacy and transparency, monitoring and anti-monitoring - the duality of keeping the Dzegojan safe.
Between the two stores, a sign read in large letters:
"Underground safe place".
"gie fe kiu kai ci bin hu", Zei thought to himself. "Grow roots, no head". The strategy that Dzego had been employing for half a century to grow and stay protected.
Fin and Zei both kept walking, enjoying the shade under the trees between the road and the sidewalk.

A drone buzzed as it flew overhead. A moment later, their watches buzzed softly once their software had run the authentication protocol and confirmed that it was a friendly security drone that came from a batch that had passed all inspections and was running friendly algorithms. The whole chain of events - the flyby, the authentication, the confirmation - finished within hundreds of milli-ticks, and Fin and Zei both barely noticed that any of it had even happened.
"How was the Minpentai game last night?", Fin asked.
"I got third place! Finally figured out a wall structure that reflected their gliders right back at them, completely wreaked havoc on their territory."
"How about you?"
"Studying for the geography exam in boring school."
"Boring, I take it?"

"Yeah, we're covering the United Cities, and they're just making us memorize all the co-governance percentages. Freetown gets five percent votes in Devanvil, Devanvil gets fifteen percent votes in Redshire, Redshire gets..."
"Do you have any new opinions on how effective that whole system is?"
"Oh no, critical governance studies only becomes a topic in university."
"The same way that chemistry is a topic in high school?"
Fin laughed. "Are they gonna cover an entire year of critical governance studies in ten days in DU now?"
DU - "Decentralized University", or dzu hu sun du in Dzegoban - the place they were going. Zei remembered that they needed to make sure they got there on time, and checked his watch.
"Time just hit sixty-nine thousand. The exact location of the classroom should be getting decrypted and broadcasted any moment now."
The watch buzzed. Zei got a notification.
Zei stopped, and showed his watch to Fin.
"Huh, yellow checkmark. Looks like they've upgraded to a new cryptographic proof system, gotta make sure we sync our codes when we get to the lesson today."
"Again?"
"Guess so. I hear the Arctic Empire is getting more aggressive, so we're stepping up security."
"Okay, anyway, it says Mun Gui 1842. We... just passed 1990 Hun Min. So it's behind us."
"Let's just turn left here on 20th, and then left again on Mun Gui?"

Zei checked over the math in his mind. Named streets were spaced two hundred meters apart, H to M was four streets. House numbers were just meters, so to get from 2000 to 1842 they had to walk one hundred fifty eight meters. Eight hundred and one hundred fifty eight together is ... nine hundred fifty eight meters to walk. The lesson starts at seventy thousand, so they had a little under a thousand ticks, or more colloquially, ten minutes. A slow walking pace is one meter per tick, and Fin and Zei were fast. So they were fine.
"Sounds good!"
They began to walk briskly, to make sure they could get there with time to spare.
A few minutes later, they arrived. "Oh Fin, there you are!", a young woman shouted. Fin and Zei were led down two flights of somewhat dusty stairs.
When they got to the bottom, another man was waiting, and stopped them. "Change of plans, it's in the opposite room on floor -1 now."
Zei sighed.
The four of them walked back up a flight of stairs, entered a large room, and sat down beside each other on one of the rows of chairs.

The walls were covered with a thick, hastily organized layer of anti-transmission foil. Coated on top of the foil was a classic aesthetic of Dzego: pictures of cute cartoon animals playing with electronic gadgets and chemistry lab equipment, with a backdrop of green trees and blue skies. At the front of the room, there was an inflated cartoon-style pig on the left and a hamster on the right. The pig, in its left hand, was holding a calculator. The hamster, in its right hand, was holding a vial of some green liquid. With their other two hands, the two together held up a poster with DU's motto:
"One man learning will set one man free. A nation learning will make the nation great."
Behind them, the instructor walked in, and closed the door. Zei checked his watch. 70,001.
"Welcome to physics class", the instructor said.
"Today, I'm going to try to introduce an important topic that I think almost everyone gets confused about: thermodynamics."
The more attentive students put away their hand devices, stopped talking, and got ready to listen. The others kept talking at first, but then quickly quieted down.

A girl beside Zei reached under the table edge and ran a finger along it without looking - a habit, not a serious search. Another student habitually waved her hand device around the room, trying to pick up on any unknown electronic devices. Nobody commented. Nobody ever did.
"Who here has heard of the word 'entropy', in the context of information theory or cryptography?"
About three quarters of the students raised their hands.

"And who here has heard of the word 'entropy', in the context of the second law of thermodynamics - that it always goes up, and one way that happens is that heat always flows from hot to cold, never the reverse?"
Almost every student raised their hands. Entropy was a favorite topic of science fiction.
"Now who here thinks they can explain the connection between the two?"
No one raised their hand.
"Alright. Let's begin."
The instructor pressed a button on his watch, and a slide showed up on the front wall:

"Imagine that we have two jars of gas. Each jar has a million molecules. But in the jar on the left, the molecules are moving much faster. Suppose, in the jar on the left, you can represent the velocities with six-digit numbers, from zero to 999,999. And in the jar on the right, the molecules are moving slowly, so you can represent the velocities with six-digit numbers, from zero to 99."

"Can someone tell me, how many digits do you need to fully represent everything going on in the jar on the left? Assume that they already know it's gas and there's a million molecules, the only free variable is the velocities."
"Six million!", about ten students shouted in unison.
"Good. Now, what about the jar on the right?"
"Two million!"

"So let's recap. From your point of view, as the observer, you know that these are both jars of gas, you know what kind of gas, and that there are a million molecules. But you don't know the velocities of each individual molecule. So for the jar on the left, the amount of information that you do not know is...?"
"Six million digits!"
"And for the right?"
"Two million digits!"
"So eight million digits in total, information that you do not know. Now, what happens if we put the two jars together and let the gas mix? What will we know about the velocities there?"
Zei raised his hand.
"Yes, you there?"
"The molecules will bounce off each other randomly. When they settle down, because of conservation of energy, the velocities end up somewhere in the middle, between zero and five hundred thousand."

"Yes, excellent! Now technically, energy is proportional to velocity squared, and we can argue about how these velocities are represented, and by the way we're also completely ignoring positions, but let's just keep it simple and say zero to five hundred thousand."
The instructor tapped his watch again. Next slide.
"Now, how many digits do we need to represent the information we don't know about this new system?"
Another student raised his hand.
"Go ahead."
"From zero to five hundred thousand is more than five digits but not quite six digits, if we go by logarithm, it should be about five point seven for each molecule."
"So what's the total?"
"Eleven point four million digits."

"Very good! So the conclusion is: by mixing the two jars, we have lost knowledge. We know less about the gas than we did before. And we can quantify how much knowledge we lost: it's three point four million digits."

"This is what we mean, when we say that entropy goes up, when heat flows from hot to cold. For each tiny increment of heat, heating up a cold thing adds more unknown digits than cooling down a hot thing by that same increment takes away, and so the total unknown goes up. Every possible action that you can do to these bottles will, on average, make the total unknown either stay the same or go up - and if you're doing anything useful or making any mistakes, it will go up. This is the second law of thermodynamics."
The instructor paused.
"Now, how do we prove this?"
None of the students answered, but many of them seemed to lean forward with curiosity.

"Let's prove by contradiction. Suppose we did have a magic procedure that could go in reverse: start with the merged jars with eleven point four million digits of unknown, and bring us to the separate jars with eight million digits of unknown."
Zei raised his hand once again.
"Can I try this?"
"Go ahead."
"I remember the laws of physics of our universe are fully time-reversible, right? So if you can do something in one direction, you can always run the same steps in reverse."
"Exactly. Now why does that time reversibility, at that level of atom-by-atom physics, imply that temperature equalization is something you cannot reverse? Isn't that a paradox?"
"Well, if we could separate medium temperature into hot and cold, then we would be able to do unlimited data compression."

"Like, imagine you had a file with eleven point four million digits of data. You would make a really perfect double-jar, and have a gun that shoots out the gas molecules with exactly the right velocities. Then, you would use your process to un-mix the gas, then split the jar, and measure the velocities at the end. You would get eight million digits out."

"And because our universe's physics is time-reversible, you would be able to do the same thing in reverse: take those eight million digits, put them into the gun to shoot out gas molecules at the right velocities, apply the exact same un-mixing procedure backwards, measure it, and you would get out whatever your original eleven point four million digits were. The output of the time-reversed process has to equal the input of the original process. And so we get a fully general-purpose way to represent any eleven point four million digits inside of eight million digits. And if we could do that, we could do it again and again, and represent the whole planet in eight million digits, or even make it smaller and do it in eight digits. And that's impossible!"

"Exactly. Or in other words, you can't go from not knowing more things to not knowing fewer things in a universe with time-reversible physics. In a universe with time-irreversible physics, you could, because you can just destroy all the things you don't know."

"Just like the Arctic Emperor!", Zei wanted to shout. But he kept quiet. It's bad form to openly explain a joke that is so obvious, that half the students probably already have on their minds. The instructor and the students briefly paused to appreciate the joke and smirk and enjoy a few moments of mental communion. The instructor then moved on.

"But in a universe with time-reversible physics, there's always things you don't know, and that lack of knowledge can only be shuffled around, and inevitably increased. The best we can do, is go from not knowing things we care about, to not knowing things we don't care about. Like going from not understanding thermodynamics, to not knowing the velocities of the molecules that are coming out of the projector showing these slides as waste heat."
"That was an amazing job, kid. What was your name?"
"Zei."
"Well, Zei, you got it per-"
A loud noise erupted from a nearby room. The whole room shook.
A fraction of a tick later, part of the wall and the floor came crashing down.
The next thing Zei knew, a fragment of stone hit him in the arm.
Zei found himself on the ground, his knocked-over chair beside him.
His mind flashed back to the man who had redirected them last minute to a different room, one floor above where they had been supposed to go.

He understood immediately. All of the extra precautions that DU had been taking - the cryptography, the sudden changes in location, the anti-transmission foil - they were not just a game. And the Arctic Empire was not just a unit in geography class. This stuff was real.
"Is everyone okay? Anyone injured?", the instructor yelled.
Zei thought for a moment, trying to figure out if his arm was injured enough to be worth complaining. He tried raising and lowering his arm. It did not respond.
The next thing he felt was two arms grabbing on to him, and pulling him up off the ground and onto a chair. Zei turned his head. It was Fin - to Zei's relief, completely uninjured.

Smoke filled the room. Every student's watch, among its many features including an air quality monitor, started beeping loudly. The students tapped their watches, and soon the beeping died down. Slowly, the students helped each other get back up, as the instructor walked around to check if there was anyone who seriously needed help.
The instructor got to Zei, and Zei silently pointed to his left arm. The instructor took out his hand device, and scanned it. AI-generated output filled the bottom of the screen.
"Are you in pain?", the instructor asked.
"Some, but I can handle it."
"It looks like a broken bone. Get it checked out at the hospital today. The sooner you go, the sooner you will get better."
"I'll take you", Fin added. "Gotta be sure you'll be good for your game at the end of the month."

The instructor kept walking. The room was filled with smoke. The air quality alarms were still blaring, but Fin and Zei could make out the instructor asking different students "are you okay?" and a student responding "I'm fine".
The air filters activated to full power, and soon the smoke cleared. Fin and Zei looked at each other. For a few moments, the students and the instructor sat in an awkward silence.
Zei pushed off the table with his uninjured arm, and stood up. "I think we know much less about this wall than we knew two minutes ago", he joked.
A few students smiled or gently laughed. He had judged the audience's mood well.
"No one else hurt, are you all sure?"
"I'm fine", about ten people replied.
"Alright, I think we've had enough entropy for one day. Let's go home."
Fin and Zei stayed in the classroom longer than the others. Zei sat back down on his chair. Fin grabbed a broom, and pushed all the debris to one side. Soon, only they and the instructor were left.
"Wow, the Arctics are getting aggressive. They didn't use to go after physics education."
"Whoever moved our room last-minute was a genius. Just saved our lives there."
"Unfortunately I expect it will only get worse from here."
Fin and Zei looked at the instructor in shock.
"Remember, their game is to permanently keep down our level of heavy industry and technology. Let us live, but only at the level of civilization where we can never be a threat."

"And our counter-game is 'gie fe kiu kai ci bin hu': grow roots, no head. Use distributed manufacturing to build all our tools. Let the official government keep going, slow and corrupt just like it was when we lost the war a hundred years ago, but use cryptography to coordinate the decisions that matter anonymously, without needing any exposed individual leaders at the helm. All of DU already runs this way. Soon big parts of our power generation, agriculture and medicine will."

"It's been effective. After the last few years, we're finally almost at the level where we can stand up for ourselves without needing any centralized heavy industry at all. The problem is, it looks like they're catching on."
"Dze go ba fau gie", Fin and Zei said in unison, calmly but defiantly.
"Dzego will rise again."

Meldan, Veridia·3724 Snowmoon 8

Gladias was walking forward along a sidewalk. On each side of the road, there were small shops one after the other, selling various goods from flowers to clothing to electronic equipment. He crossed a street.
On the other side of the street, the road sloped down, and transitioned seamlessly into a tunnel, lit just enough that it was possible to comfortably see and read, but not more.
Gladias got to a Y-shaped intersection. Pasted on the wall, there was a poster, attached at the corners with four pieces of tape. He stopped right in front of the poster to take a look.

"Yay, more Arctic propaganda", Gladias thought. Of course, the Arctic Empire is free to speak just like everyone else, but he wondered what kind of Veridian would feel inclined to vandalize the public environment and put up a printout of their message in the Veridian tunnels. He started mulling over ways to rip the poster down.
Suddenly, Gladias felt a tap on his shoulder.
Gladias turned his head.
"Oh, is it you, Mov?"
"No, it's the Arctic Emperor. I'm here to literally suck out your soul."
"Okay fine... Wait, I'm like one of a hundred people walking toward the Greater Plum Harbor wearing a privacy robe, how did you figure out where I am?"

"You put me on your trust list a year ago and never took me off, so our local AIs had permission to enable location sharing. Your AI knew that we were supposed to meet before I shadow you when you go see the mysterious gentleman, so it unlocked location sharing with me for today."
"Aaaah, I see ... something something contextual intimacy or whatever the new buzzword is."
"Yep, probably didn't even need the two-party garbled circuit feature to do that."
"So what's been on your mind?"

"Well, I'm assigned to one of the openness rubrics on internet media this year. We've been talking a lot in our Keeper group about bumping up the taxes on API restrictions. I talked to a citizens' assembly about the topic a month ago, and they're really unhappy about how things are going."
"Why is it such a big issue now?"

"Bluewhale announced a month ago that they're cutting their API and are only letting verified hardware interface with the platform. They say it's to prevent automated spam, but basically everyone in the assembly thought they just want to block alternative interfaces so they can control people's attention more and extract more money."
"Do we know exactly what kinds of things they are doing? Are any of their algorithms public?"
"Nah, their algorithms are totally opaque, and they're already paying the max tax bracket for that."
"I see..."

"So yeah, many of the Keepers think we should bump up more taxes on that kind of behavior. So either they stop, or, well, they keep going and the internet sucks more, but the gov gets enough money that we can pay for everyone to get better healthcare. The problem is, Bluewhale has been driving a hard campaign against it. One Keeper was not careful about their privacy, she and her views got found out recently, it went public, and her husband lost his job only a few days later. No idea if it's connected, but, well, this is why we gotta run this whole tax system with all these cryptographic networks randomly selecting Keepers, anonymous discussion and voting, and privacy robes."

The mention of Bluewhale brought Gladias back to his younger days, when he had learned programming by writing an alternative client for the other major social platform, Silverchat. That had only been possible, he knew, because the API was open, and the platform allowed developers to make alternative clients and users to export and migrate their data - all decisions that had undoubtedly been motivated, or at least justified to the bean counters, by trying to lower their tax rate on the hardware and software openness rubric. That experience had been what motivated Gladias to contribute back, and get involved in Steering himself.
"Anyway, speaking of privacy, what's the plan with your 200 rep anon friend?"

"Well, he told me that he thinks the whole Steering mechanism is fundamentally broken. I figured I would hear him out. Often even people who are crazy are at least ten percent right in some way that's interesting. And hopefully figure out some clue about how he found me?"
"And... what if this is a trap, to get even more compromising info on you?"

"Well, if he really wanted to hurt me, he could have just submitted my identity and task into the network and pulled me out of the running for Sentinel status for this whole year. But anyway, figuring out this kind of thing is what you're here for."
Mov then opened up his privacy robe, and took out a large package from an inside pocket.

"Here, before we get into the rest of the business, put on a fresh privacy robe. Just in case there's some piece of dirt that makes yours trackable. The Arctics are getting better at smuggling their surveillance devices in here, faster than we're getting better at detecting them. We gotta step up our paranoia."
"Surely if it's at this level we should have just not met in person at all."
"Come on Glad, you're not just someone about to join me as a Sentinel, you're a friend. I enjoy it when we see each other - while we still can."
The tunnel sloped up, and the outdoor light once again shone into Gladias's eyes. Both sides of the path were covered by trees.

He passed by two children standing beside a water fountain and talking. He could make out one of them saying something about a recent visit to Northglade with his family, and the other mentioning that he liked their Helisport team.
Soon after he had walked far enough that he could no longer hear their conversation, his watch buzzed.
He took a look.

Seila was sending some photos from Freetown. The first was of the downtown of the city. The second was of a major park, taken from in front of an entrance gate. On the left, he could see a poster with some writing. Bringing his watch closer to his eyes, he could make out a price list.
Gladias pressed a button, responding back with a heart symbol.
Turning his attention away from his watch screen back to the street, he noticed that he had now entered a more urban and more commercial part of Meldan.

To his right, he saw a series of office buildings. The ones further away shone with a clear glass and steel construction, though at that distance they were only partially visible behind the tree cover. The ones close by were under construction, all covered with large tall barriers shielding the construction site from public view.
On the first barrier, he saw a poster reminding Veridians to be kind toward their families and their community.
On the second barrier, he saw another Hydrafill advertisement. On the left side, the advertisement showed the classic Hydrafill water bottle, covered with yellow and green colors.
And on the right side, it showed the text:
Hydrogen hydroxide is:
A commonly found substance in toxic sewage waterDeadly in large dosesFrequently administered to prisoners undergoing tortureA source of skin damage if held for a prolonged time in its solid form
But did you know that you can buy YOUR OWN BOTTLE of fresh drinkable hydrogen hydroxide today?
Hydrafill, buy it now.

Gladias smiled again. The construction had been going on for a long time, and he was grateful for both posters that were covering up the construction sites. He vastly preferred looking at Hydrafill advertisements or Veridian virtue posters to construction cranes and half-built concrete buildings.
He then turned his attention to the long castle-like wall, mixing grey and purple colors, that was on his left.
In front of the wall, there were two rows of trees, with a sidewalk in between them.
Behind them, a large poster mounted on the wall:
"Learn about what Greater Plum Harbor is doing for your community!"

The text was in front of a background that featured robots picking up garbage, drawn in a child-friendly cartoon aesthetic. On the bottom right corner there was a two-dimensional barcode. Gladias scanned it out of curiosity.
Gladias saw two people sitting on a bench, each drinking a tea and looking at the billboard, one with a hand device on his lap.
"Have you ever been in there?", the first man asked.
"No I haven't, never managed to get a visa", the second replied.
"It's a fascinating place, it looks totally different inside than the rest of Veridia, it's almost like a country inside a country."

Gladias stopped, and faced the billboard to avoid arousing suspicion. Overhearing a conversation was slightly impolite, but understanding public sentiment was part of his duty as a future Sentinel. Citizens' advisory assemblies helped, but they were never quite as good as an authentic conversation by people who did not realize that anyone was listening.
The second man looked down at the hand device that the two were sharing. "Oof, check what taxes they pay."
"What taxes do they pay?", Gladias asked Emerald, whispering silently so only his neck band could make out what he was saying.
Emerald immediately replied.

"Sales tax, averaging 5.2%, half of the city average. Total land tax is 1.48%, slightly greater than the city average. Graph Funding and especially Quadratic Funding revenue recovers roughly half of this."
Gladias turned his attention back to the conversation.

"I don't get it. These guys are just peacefully off in a corner, by themselves. I've never been there, and they've never bothered me. And they even do all this work on the environment, education, healthcare, their museums. They can't even just work on the science they're actually good at, they have to do all these populistic things to push their taxes down and get some of the money back from Quadratic Funding, things that they're not even good at. And even after all this? So many people hate them, and pretend their wall is ugly just to push their land taxes up. What's the point of worrying so much about the Arctics when we're so good at being our own worst enemy?"
"At least here that's the worst we can do to them. If this was Devanvil or Inglewore, GPH would be fighting to not get shut down entirely."
Gladias had not been inside Greater Plum Harbor for nearly a decade, so this made him all the more curious to see it again. He kept walking.
Gladias held his watch near the green circle on the entrance gate, and waited for about one tick.
"Proof verified, welcome", the machine answered in a robotic but approving tone.
He walked through the gate.
He could immediately see why the two people on the bench had described Greater Plum Harbor as being so different from the rest of Veridia.

The buildings inside Greater Plum Harbor were more uniform than those outside, all with similar circular and rectangular shapes, a mixture of white, grey and purple colors, and roughly five to ten meters in height. The trees were all of a few types, and carefully planted an equal distance apart on the sidewalk. Beyond having distinct names and distinct quarter-meter-wide logos, the stores and restaurants were not trying at all to distinguish themselves, instead accepting their visual role as small elements of the Greater Plum Harbor's whole. The buildings were noticeably more futuristic, more glass-and-steel, and with more sharp edges than the usual structures in Veridia.

Gladias kept walking forward, following the directions on his watch. After five minutes, he arrived at a tunnel entrance, and went down, briefly passing through a space where there were a large number of people walking.
Just after he passed through the crowd, his watch buzzed.
Two problems, Gladias thought.
First, too many people, not enough ventilation or filtration. Gladias pulled on the strap on his privacy robe's front face cover, separating the areas above and below his nose.

Second, no idea what those unattested devices are. These days, almost every device was attested with a zero-knowledge proof verifying that it was produced in a particular batch by a particular manufacturer. Six out of fifty five was an unusually high number unattested. Unfortunately, there was no time to figure things out. It could be a kid's science project, Gladias thought, it could be that it was simply normal in Greater Plum Harbor to have devices without attestation - after all, from Veridia's perspective, the land was all just one giant business's private property - or it could be a hidden spy camera, or worse. He increased his speed slightly, and kept walking.

After taking several more turns through the maze, he was once again outside, this time in the middle of a hidden courtyard. There were several tables and chairs, with people eating and drinking water. Gladias found a table in a booth that had a cloth curtain protecting it. He went in and sat down.

There was a decorated lamp in the middle of the far end of the table, with one large flower on each side. On the floor, pressed against the corner of the booth, Gladias noticed a white box. He leaned in to look more closely, and his watch buzzed. PM2.5 readings were below 1. Must be an air filter, he thought. He took the hood off his privacy robe.
He tapped his watch against a green circle in the middle of a table, and a moment later heard a confirmation sound.
Two minutes later, a robot with a smiley face slid up to the table, carrying water and a salad. Gladias took both and put them on the table, and the robot slid away.
Five minutes later, another man wearing a privacy robe stepped in.
"So, we meet at last."

"You track me down, you tell me you know things I need to hear but only want to tell me in person, and you bring me to a far corner of GPH that I did not even know existed. And so far I don't even know your name."
"Ah, my name is Delwart. Pleased to meet you."
"And I'm Gladias."
"I knew that. And your wife is Seila, your children's names are-"
"Are you trying to intimidate me?"
"Actually no, I guess now that I think about it, that was more showing off than anything else. I do apologize."

The two went quiet for a couple minutes. Both took off the face covers and hoods from their privacy robes. Gladias started to drink his water and eat his salad. Delwart tapped his own watch against the green circle on the table, and a minute later his own tea, and some kind of rectangular nutrition bar along with a fork, arrived.
Gladias leaned forward again.
"So what do you want?"
"Do you feel happy with the Steering system lately?"
"It has its flaws like any system, but in general it feels fine?"
"I see, I haven't broken your wall yet. Okay, let's take the Dreadknot concert for example. They're a nice band, they're great fun, right?"
"Yeah, I like them."
"But a bunch of the Sentinels are trying to push them up into Tier 4, because their lyrics are not gentle enough."
Gladias nodded in agreement.
"You were brave, voting Tier 3. Most Acolytes would cave to what they think the Sentinels want. You didn't. That's rare."
"But let's take another example. What do you think about GPH?"
"It's clearly a nice place. Not like Veridia, but beautiful and impressive in its own way. It's not for everyone, but I can see why a lot of people like coming here."
"Well, do you know what their Steering taxes are?"
"The Steering taxes are okay, but they really get dinged on the land tax."
"Exactly. A well-considered argument about how much this place benefits Veridia is worth less than a barely thought-through 'I don't like you'."
"So what do you propose?"
"Freedom. Actual freedom. Stop trying to nudge everyone, and let people's true selves come out."
"And how can I help?"
"Are you planning to be a Sentinel or a Keeper if you get accepted in two months?"
"Was thinking Sentinel so far."
"Be a Keeper. And just vote to delete every rubric you see."
"That's it? That's your plan?"

"See, there's a lot more Sentinels these days than Keepers. And Sentinels are the people everyone is trying to influence. Why? Because Sentinels get direct connections to specific things in the world. Keepers adjust the global rules. But there's a limit to how much any single rule can affect any single business, and there's like twenty Keepers deciding each on each rule. Being a Sentinel, you have a much more tangible impact. And it's more fun."

"My program is different. I'm trying to round up as many Keepers as I can, because what I want is systemic change. It's not about one concert or one enclave that has too much purple in it. It's about releasing Veridians from this tyranny of people's prejudices and letting them be themselves."
"Do you want to remove Graph Funding too?"
"I think Graph Funding definitely overreaches in a bunch of ways too, but my focus is Steering."
"A lot of the open tech Graph Funding supports has been pretty key to helping Dzego modernize to defend itself, do you not think that's important?"
"Look, I like their people, but really we're playing a dangerous game cutting so close to funding a potential war. We should focus on our own problems first."
Delwart stopped speaking, and began to drink his own tea and eat his nutrition bar. Gladias took the moment to ponder Delwart's words, while continuing to drink his water and finishing his salad.

"It's an interesting thought, that the Steering is just manipulating people too much. I don't know if I fully agree with just dropping it all to zero, and especially killing the Graph Funding - which we would have to do, if the Steering taxes went to zero."
Gladias paused for a few ticks, and looked at Delwart. Delwart looked back. They each took another sip of their respective drinks.
"But okay, even if I might agree on some parts, why should I listen to you?"

"Well, I know you, I know where you live, I know how you think. And if I can find out all that, imagine what kinds of things Bluewhale might be able to do. Or, for that matter, the Arctics. I can help protect you. But I will need your help too."
"Anyway, the deadline for you to submit your final track decision is in about a month. Don't go for being a Sentinel, be a Keeper. Let's just start with that."
Delwart stood up, and exited the booth.

Gladias kept the crack in the middle of the curtain slightly open, and watched Delwart go. Just before Delwart disappeared from view, another person wearing a privacy robe exited the adjacent booth, and followed Delwart.
Gladias checked his watch.
