Jahn's taxi pulled up at the Freetown Economics Institute, where he worked as a researcher, and he got out of the car. He entered the building, and tapped his hand device to pay to get through the turnstile.
Out of the corner of his eye, he noticed that the entrance price was ten percent higher than before.
He walked to the restaurant section, and saw most tables full. Only one table had empty space, and there was already a woman sitting there.
"Can I sit down here?", Jahn asked.
"Of course."
Jahn sat down.
"I'm Jahn", he offered.
"I'm Utaku. I'm from Belpaki, I'm doing my doctorate program here at the Institute."

Jahn quickly scanned through, and ordered a dish with vegetables and fish, and a glass of water.

"Wow, the prices are all up now."
"Haven't you been following the news?"
"Not since I got back from a meeting in Hapton."
"Huh, well it should be news in Hapton too. Everyone's been talking about raising their defense budgets."
"Arctic scare?"

"Yeah, their drone activity has been going up. Though there's surprisingly many politicians who seem totally nonchalant about it. Only Redshire and its neighbors seem to be really taking it seriously."
"Well, somehow, also Freetown."
"Why us? I'm glad we are, but like half the United Cities are closer to Redshire than we are, they should be worrying more!"
"Well, Devanvil is taking it seriously - after all, Redshire chooses twelve percent of the seats in Devanvil's parliament. But yeah, Deplexi, Ondak, Imber, not at all."

"It is weird. Remember, the government here is constitutionally banned from collecting more than the basic land tax and some rent from its natural resource holdings. So it's not even the government that's taking the problem seriously, it's the megacorps."
The robot came back, carrying Jahn's food and water. Jahn picked up the plate of food and put it onto the table. He then picked up the glass of water, and immediately took a sip.

"They're now donating three percent of their revenues to defense, and even colluding to punish companies that don't. "Normally yes. But hey, times are different now."

"You off to your first Keeper meeting?", Seila asked Gladias.
"My first two Keeper meetings, back to back. First one is on cultural values in public events and performances - actually the exact one that I judged Dreadknot on way back then."
"Oh, what's the topic for cultural values in events going to be?"
"In the chat I mentioned how I thought the rubric was encouraging people to be too bland to not offend anyone. Surprisingly, a couple others agreed. I think I'll try to make a big push to fix that."
"Veridia ba 'fun' gie!", Seila joked.
"Isn't it the 'gie' that you're supposed to replace? 'fau' just means 'again'."
"Aaah right."
"But yes. Veridia will be fun again."
"What about the second one?"
"The hardware openness rubric. The topic is whether or not to modify it to exempt military and surveillance products."
"Huh, what are the tradeoffs of that?"
Gladias thought carefully about how to phrase this. He thought for a moment about whether or not he should mention Delwart, but then decided against it.

"Well", he began, "some of the Keepers think we should be staying out of funding war - it's a negative-sum game, if both sides have better bombs and battle drones, the result is the same, just more things get blown up and more people get hurt."

He was pleased with himself. He had a feeling that Seila might be sensitive about anything that could hurt Dzego, and would plead for him to take whatever position benefited Dzego the most. He braced himself, preparing for Seila's next question.
"But, funding ... isn't that more of an issue on the Graph Funding side?"
Gladias internally sighed with relief.
"Well remember, we make some weapons too. Also surveillance products. And the rubrics influence how much of the secret sauce we keep to ourselves."
"I see..."
"Well, tell me how the meetings go!"
Gladias walked down a hallway, and entered a courtyard. He found a series of booths with thick sliding doors. He went to the rightmost one, as he had been instructed.

He slid the barrier open. It took a significant effort for him to do so. He could tell immediately that this was a much more proper booth than the cloth-covered booths from the Greater Plum Harbor. As the barrier was opening, he could see its internal structure: a layer of anti-transmission foil on the inside, followed by layers of soundproofing, and other layers he could not recognize.

At that moment, he also noticed a constant humming sound that was being emitted from the outside of the booth on all sides. White noise to further mask anything that makes it through the soundproof walls, he realized. If the noise is at forty decibels and the walls are good enough to attenuate sound by fifty, then it can mask up to ninety decibels coming from the inside - perhaps seventy if you want a safety margin. That's enough to completely mask any conversation.
After fully opening the barrier, Gladias looked inside the booth. There was a table stretching from near the entrance to the opposite wall, and a long bench on each side.
There were five others already sitting down, all wearing privacy robes.
"Welcome! You must be number Four", one of them exclaimed.
"Indeed I am."
"I'm number Twenty in this circle, a third-year. We have two second-years - though Eleven has not arrived yet - two third-years, two other first-years, and now also you."
"Glad to meet you all."

Gladias sat down on the bench beside Twenty. Twenty had his hand device open, and Gladias could see him scrolling through recent audits measuring various businesses' statuses on the cultural values rubric, and the resulting decisions.
A few moments later, another Keeper walked in. He slid the barrier shut behind him, and sat down.
"So, cultural values rubric", the other third-year began.

"Cultural values in events and performances rubric", the first-year, One, corrected. "We're not doing social media or other online things, that's a different rubric. And we're not doing architecture and public billboards, that goes into the aesthetics taxes."
"We all know that, you don't have to show off here", the third-year replied, with a joking tone calibrated to try to make the point without offending One.
"How do we want to do this? Maybe we should first come to a common understanding of what the problems we're trying to solve are?"
"Let's go through some examples", a second year who had not yet spoken up replied.
Gladias saw his chance to intervene.
"How do you guys feel about Dreadknot?"
"What do you mean?"
"Their taxes got bumped up to tier 4 in the last audit."
Gladias began to read from the rubric.

"Content weakly promotes one or more of the following: violence, lawless behavior, use of anti-recommended substances, gambling or risky investment, excessive display of wealth, poor conflict resolution practices, religious or ethnic hatred."
"Do we think Dreadknot is guilty of promoting violence, lawless behavior or hatred?"
"Their last song was about destroying cities and flaying people's flesh. Why not?"

"Do we really think that those words are going to make anyone want to flay anyone's flesh in real life? It's a song. I remember we went through this with games a few years ago, and the science ended up saying that they can slightly increase a few aggressive behaviors but there's no evidence that they actually lead to violence."
"I remember that too. And my read was that the conclusion of the evidence was harsher than that."
"Do we want to dig up and go through those studies together?"
A few other Keepers nodded. They started whispering instructions at their hand devices.
Gladias took the opportunity to continue.

"But even aside from all that, do we really want Veridia to be a society where the artists have to constantly worry about this and all the songs, and the games, and the movies, become boring and pale?"

"They don't have to constantly worry. That's the whole point of Veridia's system of regulation. We're not banning them. We're just setting their taxes slightly higher instead of slightly lower. So along with the ten things that they have to worry about a medium amount already, like what their fans will like, what might or might not offend their corporate sponsors, and so on - things that won't break them, but still make a difference - we ask them to think about one extra concern: the public interest."
Gladias decided to pursue another line of argument.

"I actually like this rubric in general. I think it's great that the Northglade Science Center is getting rewarded for being such a wonderful place for kids to learn about chemistry and biology and rockets."

"But violence is part of life. The human race started out as monkeys fighting over bananas. When we were still living in forests and caves, a quarter of our men died because someone else killed them. I don't think we should be discouraging Veridians completely from engaging with such a central part of our human nature. "I'm not even that convinced the Arctics are that big a threat. Sure, they're waving more drones around the northern United Cities now, but I don't think the intention is to attack, I think they're just trying to impress us with their power so we become attracted to their ideology."
"Do you think we should be more receptive to their ideology?"
"I think we should keep an open mind. Just remember, the Dzegojan are definitely trying to manipulate us too."
For a few moments, the discussion went quiet. Gladias let it rest. He was still trying to understand how everyone else was thinking before forming his own views.
"Let's all think about this more on our own. We'll keep talking about this, we still have a few more discussions, the last one is in four months. And then the actual vote is only in six months."
Pafogai Du, Dzego
Bai and Zei sat together at a courtyard table, both staring at their hand devices.
"Fin not joining us this time?", Bai asked.
"No", Zei replied with a strong hint of disappointment. "He's busy with the Bansunpei."
The hand devices buzzed. It was their intervention turn. Zei arranged a few gliders and symbol-carrying spaceships. A few hundred turns passed.
Suddenly, as the spaceship hit a rock formation and was in the process of reflecting, gliders from Bai hit it. The spaceship exploded into a storm of gliders.
"What?", Zei shouted.
"Caught you, I had a symbol along the path, right in the position where you could not see it. So I could see the edge of your spaceship coming."
Zei groaned. That had been his last-ditch attempt to rescue the game. More gliders from Bai came in, and shredded through both of his remaining symbols in the southwest corner.
Zei clicked a button to resign.
"Good game", Zei said, not yet with total sincerity, but with more sincerity than he had in any game where he had lost to Bai before.
"You know, I am going to need your help in the nationals."
"Happy to. As long as..."
"Yes, I know, you want to visit Veridia now."
"Anyway, thanks for explaining your thought process in that championship game. Really made me think."
"Of course."
"Of course you enjoy reliving the moment you defeated me, just like I enjoyed beating you right now."
Zei sighed.
"Anyway, I have to go. The Kungaupei councilor, Den, is asking to see me again."
Zei entered the long room, and immediately saw Den and Mu sitting on the other side.
"Thank you for coming."
"Of course. I went through the hash-based signatures you recommended. It's a really fun set of constructions, especially the stateless tree-of-tree-based ones."
"Do you see why, when I looked at your style of Minpentai, I knew that you would do well in this?"
"I think so!"

"You are truly amazing. You've rushed through a third of the cryptography lectures in less than a month, and got a perfect score on both of the first two tests. I can't think of anyone who did better."
Zei's eyes gleamed with satisfaction at receiving the compliment.
"Zei, do you know why I called you in?"
At this point, Zei realized one possible implication of Den's words, and his cheerful facial expression suddenly dropped into a fearful one.
"Are you going to convince me to go into this full-time? Like, abandon the Minpentai nationals?"
Mu laughed. "So I guess my hunch was wrong - this part, you still don't get."
"Huh?"
"Have you ever thought about why the Minpentai game is so serious, so much ceremony, the priests going into the dungeon for days, and so well-funded?"
"It's a sport. Sports are taken seriously and well-funded in many countries."
"Not sports of the mind. Their audience isn't large enough to fund it just based on advertising and national prestige and all those other reasons."
"So why then?"
Mu leaned forward.
"It's because Minpentai isn't just a sport."
Zei stared.
"It's military training."
"The whole point of the sport, and why we support it so much, is to raise the next generation of defenders."
"We need people who can think quickly, and think strategically under pressure."
"People who can compete with their foes, but also cooperate with their allies, even allies that they do not personally get along with."

"People who can understand a battlefield, including the battle itself, all the way up to grand strategy and resources and logistics, and all the way down to the level of surveillance and secrecy and trickery, and ultimately entropy itself."
"People who can deal with suddenly changing rules."
"People who are able to micromanage, but are also able to set a plan in motion and watch it unfold."
"And people who can work with the latest technology - including AI - but also understand and work around its limits."

The realizations hit Zei all at once. At first, he had wanted to ask a basic question: why pretend it's a game, why not just have a regular military with regular recruitment? But as soon as he put together the question, he already knew the answer: the Arctics would put all their energy into targeting anything like that. Minpentai was only safe because it pretended to be just a game. But even then, Zei knew, the ruse could not be safe forever.
"Why are you telling me this now?"

"Because we have to give you some reason why we're now telling you to work hard on cryptography and continue to the nationals. If we didn't tell you, you might get suspicious, eventually figure it out for yourself, and then do something stupid, like excitedly blurting out your discovery to a dozen other people."
Zei nodded.
"I won't tell anyone. Not even Fin."
Den and Mu nodded.
"And when the nationals come, you'll want a sparring partner who knows your style."
No one said a name. No one had to.
"We appreciate your support", Den replied.
"Dze go ba fau gie", Mu added.
"Dze go ba fau gie."

Meldan, Veridia·3724 Bloomtime 15
Seila, Daia and Vil were standing together in a large grass field, with many other families nearby.
From a distance, Daia caught sight of Gladias approaching. She waved at him. Gladias noticed, and with a smile on his face walked toward them more quickly.
"Happy to see you here!", Daia exclaimed.
"Well I can't miss my son's first real Helisport game", Gladias answered.
"So how have you been?"
"Well, lots of Order business. Can't talk about it publicly, you know. Going well though!"
"How about you?"
Vil started to speak.
"Well, lots of documents for the lawsuit against Divergent. It's been taking up a big part of my time for the last two months."
"Remind me, what happened there?"
"Ah sorry, I've been trying not to burden you guys with the details, I know you have so much on your plate already."
"Come on, Vil, your life is important to us."

"Well, remember about half a year ago I lost my job at Jump because they went bankrupt. A month later, another one of the employees reached out to me, and I learned from him what really happened. See, the official story had been-"

"I remember this in the news. Jump was struggling, and as a last-ditch effort to save themselves, they made a risky bet on the financial markets, buying a derivative on property prices in a region that they were about to announce they would start serving. But it didn't work - not enough people cared, then they got unlucky and prices went down, so the whole thing collapsed."

"Exactly. But here's what I learned. The only reason why Jump was able to make such a large bet on a niche market without insane slippage is that a hedge fund - Divergent - had taken the other side of the bet. And the primary owners of Divergent had quietly bought a majority share in Jump for very cheap."

"If housing prices in that region had gone up, Jump would have gained, Divergent would have lost, for them it would have been a net zero. And if housing prices went down - which they did - Jump loses, and Divergent gains, also a net zero. But here's the asymmetry: if Jump loses - which they did - then Jump declares bankruptcy, and so they get out of paying end-of-year bonuses plus a year of severance for their employees. So they gave themselves a free option on our backs."

"When we found out about this, we sued - all the employees together sued, as a class action. It's been tough; Divergent even managed to intimidate some media sites into not covering it. But I feel like so far the judges are seeing through their tricks. So I'm optimistic."
They heard a loud whistle, and turned to face the direction that the sound came from.
It was the instructor. A large truck had been moved into the center of the grass field.
"Helisport game starting in five minutes!", the instructor yelled.
The instructor pressed a button, and the back door of the truck began to open gently, tilting backward on its bottom hinge. After a few ticks, it had turned into a ramp.
Some personal copters, simple chairs with rotor blades on top surrounded by shielding, automatically rolled out of the truck.

Some children, around ten to twelve years old, ran toward the truck, half wearing yellow shirts and the other half wearing purple shirts. Among those wearing yellow shirts was Zven. They grabbed their copters and began strapping into them.

The instructor walked into the truck, and soon came out with a much smaller box. He opened the box, and four bright red drones, shaped like balls a few centimeters wide with soft feather-like rotors on top, sprang out and flew into the sky.

"Welcome to today's Helisport game", the instructor said. "Today we're going to do a limited game, playing only with redballs. If you catch a redball, bring it back to me, and your team gets one point. First team to get to six points wins."

By this point all ten children had strapped into their personal copters, and the rotor blades were beginning to spin - just enough to overcome about three quarters of the earth's gravity. The kids ran around excitedly, and some jumped, reaching about two meters off the ground before gently gliding back down.
"Everyone know what to do?", the instructor asked.
"Yes!", many kids shouted in unison.
"Then we will begin the game in five ... four ... three ... two ... one ... blast off!"
The personal copters flew into the air.
"You know, I'm surprised they still do this in schools", Gladias said to Seila. "If this were invented today, they would definitely say it's too dangerous."
"It was only invented less than ten years ago."
"In Dzego."
Zven caught sight of a redball, and began flying toward it. A few moments after, two kids wearing purple shirts also saw the redball, and began to chase it right behind him.
The redball suddenly shifted direction to the left.
Zven and the other kids also turned left. Zven's copter's rotor shield bumped into the rotor shield of one of the other kids' copters, and the two bounced harmlessly off each other.

Zven aimed his copter to fly higher. He fell slightly behind the kid he had just bumped into, while the third kid flew forward, and was soon directly under him. The air sucked Zven down, and soon his feet bounced into the grid on top of the other copter's rotors.
Zven jumped off quickly, and he and the other kid both tumbled down a few meters before they stabilized and flew off in separate directions.
"The AI on these things is getting really good now", Gladias murmured.

The redball suddenly changed direction again, this time going upwards. Zven immediately set his rotor to full power and climbed upward. The kid he had just bumped into was still a few meters below him, and the other kid did not notice the redball's change of direction in time, and so Zven was ahead.
Zven saw the redball get closer, and then closer again. Now it was only one meter in front of him.

The redball suddenly turned off its rotors, and began to drop. Thinking quickly, Zven kicked the ball back up just as it dropped to the level of his feet, and moved his copter forward. He stretched out his hand, and caught the redball in his palm.

He then aimed the copter to fly toward the instructor. The rotor slowed down - though it did not stop completely. It sped back up when Zven's altitude was decreasing at the safe maximum of five meters per tick - the speed that you would hit the ground after a fall from a height of slightly under two meters. The instructor watched Zven land, and stretched out his hand to receive the redball that Zven handed over.
"First catch of the game by Zven, first point for team yellow!"
He let the redball fly once again. It quickly shot forward, in the opposite direction from where Zven was standing.
Zven flew back up, and continued his search for more redballs.
"How are Hreda, Lily and Febric doing?", Gladias asked Daia. Seila heard the question, and turned her head toward them slightly to hear the answer.
"Hreda is off in Northglade doing a math competition. We've been trying to get Lily more interested in art, though that hasn't been really successful so far."

"I also talked to Zven for a bit and he showed me his homework. I was surprised. I saw the questions they were giving him for arithmetic, and they seemed just slightly ... less advanced than what Febric got at his age?"
"Nice catch by Dommus!", the instructor shouted. "And nice catch for Gale! Two points for team purple"
Seila joined into the conversation.

"Well, Glad, you're a -" she stopped herself, briefly remembering that it would be improper even to specify Keeper - "an Order member now. Anything the Order can do to make Veridia's education better?"

"You know the schools aren't Order business, the public ones are run by the education committee, staffed by parliament. Though there have been people thinking about trying to support more private ones, support them out of Graph Funding, figure out some rubrics to give them the right incentives."

"Maybe you should try pushing for that in your Keeper meetings?", Seila replied, whispering into her watch as a substitute for a neck band. Better to just have this conversation privately than have to choose each word carefully to avoid giving out Gladias's position, she thought.
Delwart would be supportive, Gladias thought. Though he would be even more supportive of private schools with no rubric micro-nudging attached.
"Another nice catch by Zven! Second point for team yellow."

Gladias and Seila's attention went back to the game. There were three groups of three kids each in the sky, each group chasing what they assumed must be a different redball. Zven flew up alone, and did not try to join any of the groups. Instead, he seemed to simply wander the sky, his eyes constantly watching the horizon to try to find where the fourth redball might be.
One of the kids tumbled out of the sky, though the rotor's AI automatically broke his fall. He hit the ground, and then a few ticks later stood back up and went back into the sky.
A minute later, a kid landed beside the instructor, and handed him a redball.
"Another nice catch by Gale! Third point for team purple."
The redball flew back into the sky, and both Gale and the other two kids who were chasing the redball with him once again flew after it.
Two more minutes passed. Another kid landed beside the instructor.
"Nice catch by Dela! Third point for team yellow."
One more minute later, two more kids landed at around the same time:
"Nice catch by Plat! Fourth point for team yellow."
"And a nice catch by Meny! Fourth point for team purple."
Zven continued his solitary quest to search for the fourth redball, which all the other kids seemed to have completely forgotten the existence of.
"Nice catch by Egardo! Fifth point for team purple."
"Another nice catch by Dela! Fifth point for team yellow."
He began to fly closer to the ground.
Gladias and Seila saw Gale shooting ahead of his two competitors, getting ready to catch the redball. It was only one meter in front of him.
Gale's hand stretched out. He prepared to grab hold of it.

Then, suddenly, another kid bumped into him, and he veered several meters to the right. That kid attempted to grab the redball instead, but it quickly flipped direction and flew backwards, right in between the two of them. Gale and the other kid both attempted to grab it with their hands as it passed by, but both missed.
Gale regained sight of the redball first, and quickly flew towards it. His two competitors soon followed, though they were at least ten meters behind.
Gale and the redball both gained altitude, and Gale began to get closer to the redball. Five meters. Four meters. Three meters.
Meanwhile, out of nowhere, Zven seemed to fall to the ground, the fall broken as usual by the copter's AI.
High in the sky, far above the other players, Gale raised his hand triumphantly, holding the redball inside a clenched fist.
Many in the audience cheered. Gale maneuvered around the other two students who were following him, and began to drop back down at the maximum speed of five meters per tick.
Suddenly, Gladias and Seila's eyes shifted toward Zven. He had gotten out of his copter, and was running toward the instructor.
When Gale was still about thirty meters in the air, Zven opened up his hand and gave the instructor the fourth redball, with broken rotors, that he had found on the ground.
"And, nice catch by Zven. Sixth point for team yellow. Team yellow wins the game!"
Gladias sighed with relief.
Seila beamed with pride for Zven.
"He took the path less traveled", she quietly recited, quoting an old Veridian author, "and that blazed a trail for all."
Gladias slid the barrier open, entered the booth, and slid the barrier shut again.
Three other Keepers were already there. The other three, Gladias thought, must still be on their way.
This was the third circle of Keepers that Gladias was assigned to, and the topic was air quality. Here, his assigned number was two.
Gladias immediately took out his watch, and whispered into his neck band to check the air quality of the current room.
"How are we already at 906 with just four people here?", he asked. "Filters are working great, but I guess they haven't yet figured out how to give these secure booths any ventilation?"
"Yeah, pretty much everyone is really behind standards. We've been saying that we really have to increase the taxes on this bracket across the board."
The CO2 reading on Gladias's watch refreshed. It now showed 918.

"I think people will figure this out on their own", another Keeper replied. "It's just a matter of the technology being open and deployable enough. We've been making these filters twice as cheap every two years for the past decade."
"Well I feel like we have to push harder", Gladias replied.
"What do the indoor air quality tax rubrics say now?"

"It's a land tax component. Zero if your air quality is perfect, an extra third of a percent per year if the average occupied room reads worse than a thousand. The limits get adjusted up if you have filters or UVC."
"Only a third of a percent? For the difference between theoretically perfect and abysmally bad?"
"A third of a percent of the land value, per year. For many businesses, that's like a sixth of their revenue."

"There's so many things that go into land tax. Public aesthetics. Accessibility - both the kind that's about being friendly to disabled people, and the kind that's about letting people walk across your land freely and not fencing it off. What percent of the lot you're building on. Ground-floor active use, though that one is controversial and some people think it should just be folded into aesthetics. Emergency preparedness. Fire safety. There's just not enough space for everything."
"And come on, Veridians are not that sick. If you look at the broad listen report we ran a month ago, indoor airborne disease resistance is just not one of Veridians' top ten concerns."
"The ground-floor active use isn't just about aesthetics, it also contributes to walkability, reduces congestion-"
"Fine, though I think we should just target those things directly."
"Anyway, that's not our rubric to decide. Air quality is. You're missing the tail risk."
"What tail risk?", Gladias interjected.
"Super-pandemics. Like, deliberately released by the Arctics."
"Is there any evidence of them working on anything like that?"
"They're a super opaque society, the only evidence we have that the Arctics even know Veridia exists is that we have to listen to Lord Ephelion giving his sermons all the time."
"So what are the possible plans on the table?"
"Increase the maximum to two thirds of a percent. And then make the case to the funding organs - Graph Funding, Quadratic Funding, parliament allocations - that they should support more open-"
Another Keeper interjected:

"Quadratic funding? That round is a mess right now. Someone released a program you can download onto your device and prove that you donated to a particular project researching social media polarization - actually not a very good one - and get a reward. You donate ten zipcoins and get back twenty, they get a hundred including the bounded matching. Lots of people participated. And then yesterday some insider at Bluewhale blew the whistle, apparently that was all their doing."
"Bluewhale? But why would they do that? They don't even control the project that was getting that funding."

"It doesn't matter where it goes, if it was hiring people from Iptak to come dig holes and then fill them back up again they would still have done it. Their goal is to drain funding from anything that interfaces with open platforms. Starve the open ecosystem, the closed one wins by default."

"Fine, we'll stick to Graph Funding. Go through our channels to suggest to the Graph Funding people that they support more open source tech for air filtering, cleaning, wastewater scanning, all of it."

"Wastewater scanning too? You want to break everyone's privacy even more? What if the Arctics hack in and take all that data, and then they'll find out who lives where even if they move homes, and when each person is healthy or sick?"
"I thought you were the one who keeps saying there's no evidence the Arctics are actually doing those kinds of crazy things?"
"Isn't there some cryptographic way to get the data we want out of the scans, without ever collecting the data itself in cleartext in any one place?"
"Well, if you can find a genius who can figure out something like that, let us know."

Gladias got off the autobus, and pulled on the strap on his privacy robe's front face covering. His face was still covered, but the belt between the areas above and below his nose was now no longer tight. Less virus protection - outside the unusually crowded indoor space that was the autobus, he no longer needed it - but more comfortable and easier to breathe. He began to walk back home.

He passed by the same restaurant where he had bumped into Febric months earlier. On the restaurant's outer wall, he saw an advertisement. On the left side of the advertisement, there was a Hydrafill mascot, clothed in Hydrafill's classic yellow and green colors, hugging a small child, and using his back to shield the child from a jet of sludge-like green-colored water. On the right side of the advertisement, there was the text:
Heavy water, with its atoms of hydrogen replaced by the neutron-bearing isotope deuterium, is known to be toxic in large doses.
We studied our competitors' water, and found that on average, it contains 145 parts per million heavy water.
Our water comes from fresh Veridian NORTHERN ICE, bravely extracted only thirty kilometers away from the Arctic border, and it contains 132 parts per million heavy water.

Hence, our water is TEN PERCENT LESS TOXIC than our competitors. Only WE care about your health. Nobody else does. Hydrafill wants to heal and protect you. Our competitors think you deserve to drown in sludge and die.
Trust Hydrafill. Buy Hydrafill today.
Gladias smiled. He kept walking.
Suddenly, someone grabbed and hugged him from behind.
Gladias turned around.
"Seila!"
"Finally caught you on your way home."
"How was the rest of your day?"
"Finished up my post on urban economics in Freetown. It's online, you should go see it."
"Ooh, I'm excited."
"Jahn gave me some gossip recently, about how a lot of things are changing now that people there are getting more spooked about the Arctics."
"Do you have any theories about why people in Veridia seem so... nonchalant about the whole Arctic situation?"
"I guess the Arctics don't really affect people's lives here much? They just publish their stupid sermons from time to time and people watch and listen out of curiosity."
Gladias groaned.
"Even inside the Keepers, the situation is so strange. The older ones seem to understand there's a problem. But the newer ones ... not all, but many of them think we should just not care?"

"What's weird is that the corporates in Freetown seem more resistant to ... whatever is causing that stupidity. They're basically the only city taking the problem seriously - except for Redshire, and the cities partially run by Redshire's parliament through co-governance."
"I guess more than anything, the newer Keepers seem suspicious of Steering and Quadratic Funding and Graph Funding and government being able to do much of anything in general."
Seila sighed.
They continued walking. After a few minutes, they arrived at the door to their house. Gladias put his watch against the circle, and the door opened. They walked in.
Seila opened up her hand device.
"Dzego food truck in one minute. The usual I assume?"
"Yep, how did you know?"
Seila laughed.
Seila clicked a few buttons, and ordered.
The door to the house was not yet closed, and Seila could already see the food truck coming towards them from a few hundred meters away. They both waited for the food truck to arrive.
Seila went out, and picked up the food directly from the food truck. She walked back into the house, and closed the door behind her.
She put the food on the table, and immediately unpacked it.
They both sat down, opened their food boxes, and began to eat.

Sadzu Du, Dzego·3724 Grasstime 22
Zei looked out of the window of the train, as the train began to slow down.
At first, he saw trees. Then, he began to see buildings with greater and greater density. Finally, after a few minutes, he saw the station.
A sign slowly passed across the window.
"Main city", Dzego's helpfully-named capital city.
The train came to a stop, and Zei could hear the doors open. The other passengers stood up, and started to gather their belongings.
Zei decided he was not in a rush to leave first, and would maximize the quality of his time instead. For about two minutes, he finished his game of Minpentai against a bot.
Fin had never gotten around to writing the harness to fine-tune the AI to play well on custom rulesets, and so Zei was still playing against the stock AI.

At that moment, the other AIs resigned. Zei had beaten them one-on-three. To compensate for their lack of skill, he had adjusted the game to only give him one corner and three other AIs the other three corners, and put them all on the same team against him. Even despite this, Zei had won. He realized that the three-on-one did not even help the AIs that much - playing in that style was not in their training data, so they made basic mistakes and cannibalized each other's negentropy.
Zei put away his hand device and sighed.
By this point, the other passengers were almost all off the train. Zei grabbed his bag, and stood up and began to walk out of the train as well.
When he stepped out, there were six people wearing Minpentai priest robes waiting for him.
"Welcome to Sadzu Du, Zei", the lead priest, an older woman about the same age as Mu, said to him.
"Excited to be here", Zei quickly replied. "Only my second time to the capital."
"I'm Su by the way. I'm one of the organizers of the nationals."
"Well nice to meet you, Su."
"So what's on my itinerary these next few days?"
"Check in to the hotel, then orientation tomorrow morning. Thirty-two contestants, the brightest young minds in Minpentai across all of Dzego. You'll get to meet them all."

Su led Zei to a room that contained many doors. One of the doors slid open, and on the other side Zei could see the inside of a black car, identical to the one that Den had used to take him to the chip fab a few months earlier.
"Unfortunately, I'll have to leave you here, Zei. There's another contestant arriving here on a train in half a longhour. But have a good ride and have a good rest."
"Thank you so much."
Zei got into the car, and the door closed. The car started moving.

Zei stared outside the window of the car, marveling at the buildings and trees in the city. Parts of it looked not too different from Pafogai Du, though here there were fewer electronics stores, and instead a wider variety of venues. Some medicine stores.
On the window of one of the stores, Zei saw a sign:
"Get your longevity package here"
Soon the health stores gave way to some stores selling artistic furniture and other household items.
And after that a few traditional-looking restaurants and tea houses, in a style mimicking Dzego's own medieval era.

For a moment, the buildings on the right side stopped completely, and Zei could see a park. Behind the park, Zei could see several mountain pyramids, each about half as tall as the mountain pyramid south of Pafogai Du.
A minute later, the park ended, and the car crossed a bridge across a small river. Zei could see the buildings get denser further ahead.
The road slowly descended underground, and turned into a tunnel.

A few minutes and a few turns later, the car stopped. When the car's door opened, it was pressed tightly against another door, completely shielding Zei from being visible from outside the car and the building he was entering.
Zei stepped out. He was in a hotel.
He walked over to the nearest green circle, and tapped his watch against it.
Reputation above 150 verified. Payment not needed. Approved, room number is 304.
Zei's watch buzzed, confirming his room key.
Zei entered his room, and took a shower.
He promptly went to sleep.
An alarm buzzed.

Zei tapped on his watch to check what time it was. 30,003, the watch said. Only half a longhour before the commencement ceremony. He tapped a few buttons on the room service menu, and ordered a fruit and vegetable juice.
He put on his clothes.
Three minutes later, the juice arrived, and Zei quickly drank it. He immediately felt energized - or at least, energized enough to take the trip to the venue.
Without wasting any more time, he opened the door, and went downstairs.

A black car was already waiting for him. Zei walked through the lobby, and immediately stepped through the hotel door and car door that were already open and pressed tightly against each other. The door closed.
As the car began to move, Zei took out the cryptography textbook that Den had recommended to him in one of their meetings, and continued reading it where he had left off.
The section was on hash functions. In the middle of the page, there was a large diagram.
"Conception of a hash algorithm".
Zei read the accompanying text.

Hash algorithms, it said, were there to create a shrunken fingerprint of a large piece of information, that still uniquely identifies the original. The goal is for it to be infeasibly hard to find two different pieces of data that have the same hash.

Hashes inherently destroy information - representing a larger thing with a smaller thing is their entire goal. But there is a paradox: in the internal workings of all the best hash functions that we build, the largest component is an entropy-preserving transformation: a permutation.

The core building block maps inputs to outputs one-to-one. And not only that, it can be efficiently run both forwards and backwards. The shrinking, and the irreversibility, comes from a simple layer on top: a deletion, and an xor of part of the original input, added to the end.

Why do this? Why build irreversibility on top of reversibility? The reason is subtle. If you build irreversibility directly, then you cannot control when entropy is destroyed. If you apply an irreversible round function enough times, then about half the entropy collapses, bringing the protocol's security down along with it. And so even when destroying information is your final goal, it's best to cleanly separate out the piece that's going that - destroy information in one precise spot in the algorithm, on your own terms.
Zei put away his hand device, and leaned back.

"Welcome to the semi-finals", the announcer voice shouted.

"We have come far to get to where we are. We have had forty days of some of the most challenging matches we have seen. The top four players in the qualifiers were: Deluin from Redshire, who won six of six games, Zei Leimin from Pafogai Du who won five of six with an average win time of 5,047 turns, Gun Caibai from Dzundei who won five of six with an average win time of 5,699 turns, and Kau Seiza from Geijaken who won five of six with an average win time of 6,740 turns."

"Today, in this very special round, we will see Zei Leimin and Gun Caibai face off. And right after this, the other two players will have their own semi-final match. And in fifteen days, the two winners will face off in an epic best-two-out-of-three, and we will have our national champion!"

"And of course, today's rule change. The resources you can allocate in each intervention turn are reduced by eighty percent. But in addition, there will be five shrines, four arranged along the center of each edge of the board, and one in the center. Each thousand turns, any changes that had taken place to the contents of the shrine will be applied as an XOR to the regions near the four corners of the shrine, and the shrine will reset to being a default rock formation."
"FI LE GEI TAU FA."

Zei immediately understood the meaning of the new rules. The shrines are the only objects that violate mass conservation - though even still, with these new rules, nothing decreases entropy. XOR is not weight-preserving, but it is reversible. So the game board would get more and more full, and more and more messy, over time. The reduced resource allocation meant that the intervention turns were not for building - they were for steering.

Zei put down his usual walls, gliders and spaceships. This time though, he used some different designs - a steerable symbol-carrying spaceship he had developed months prior, that could change its direction if you intervene in only a few cells.
"MU GU GEI TAU FA."

Zei figured out one additional adjustment: he adjusted the positioning of his spaceships so that they could be located right past the shrines after exactly two intervention turns. This would let him send out a glider in exactly the right direction that it would turn a pair of shrines into an eternal glider factory: a glider would bounce back and forth, at each collision it would break off rock to spray even more gliders further north, and then every thousand turns, the rock would reset.
"PA GU..."
Zei put all of his effort into glider storms that would protect his spaceships as they went to the center, east and south; he decided to sacrifice the west.
Until the last moment, Zei kept optimizing his structures.
"TAU FA."
The spaceships and gliders started moving.
A thousand turns later, the first intervention turn came. Zei shot off a few gliders to turn more rock formations into symbols and glider factories.

He realized that he had one major weakness: while he could make symbols, it would take him four intervention turns to make a symbol-carrying spaceship or glider factory. That meant that his three symbol-carrying spaceships were all the fleet that he had, and he had to protect them.

Just before the second intervention turn, his spaceship and two of Gun's spaceships flew past each other in the center. Evidently, Gun was even more intent on doing something in the center than he was.
Zei realized that he had a choice to make: he could send gliders out to attack Gun's ship, he could put up walls to defend against Gun's ship, or he could set up the eternal glider factory.

The second intervention turn came. He decided on the last course of action, sending gliders out that would bounce between the center shrine and the south shrine, the center shrine and the east shrine, and the south shrine and the east shrine.

Right after the intervention turn finished, Zei noticed that Gun had done the exact same thing, using both his symbol-carrying spaceships in the center. He had also adjusted the heading of both of his ships, so that they would also head south.
Zei and Gun could not see the full view of what was going on, but the audience could.

A few hundred turns later, Zei realized that Gun's attack had been more effective. He had not only created eternal glider factories between the center and south shrines, and the center and west, but he had also unleashed a glider attack that destroyed Zei's symbol-carrying spaceship.
Meanwhile, Gun's two symbol-carrying spaceships were moving south, one of them on a collision course with Zei's own - a collision that would happen before the next intervention turn.
Zei would only have one symbol-carrying spaceship left, the one in the east.

Zei sighed. He realized that his last symbol-carrying spaceship was the last mobile structure he had that Gun knew nothing about. His best advantage might be keeping it that way. On his next intervention turn, he steered that spaceship to temporarily stop, just outside of visual range of Gun's northeastern base. He set the spaceship to fire off gliders to destroy the symbols that were undoubtedly in Gun's northeastern base. To avoid giving up his location, they would not fly north directly - instead, they would reflect off of the northern rock shrine.

Meanwhile, in the southeast, Zei's own symbols began to disappear one by one - first, from Gun's eternal glider factories, then from new gliders fired by his symbol-carrying spaceship now moving eastward from the south.
And just before the next intervention turn, Zei briefly saw Gun's symbol-carrying spaceship come into view near his southwest base - just before it sent out gliders that destroyed it.
Then the fourth intervention turn came.

Gun had a large advantage in material, Zei knew. Zei's only advantage was staying hidden. There were also gliders flying all over from the eternal glider factories, and the spot just south of the northeast corner was one of the more comfortable spots to be.
Zei decided he would continue to lay low. He stopped his symbol-carrying spaceship, and started on a five-intervention-turn-long quest to build another one.

Meanwhile, he remembered what he saw of the rock formations near the center just before his symbol-carrying spaceship there was destroyed, replicated the pattern in his sandbox, and figured out a strategy that would spawn an eternal glider factory between the center and north shrines to wreak havoc on Gun's northwest.

By the fifth intervention turn, his attack succeeded in heavily damaging Gun's bases in the northwest - though Zei had no way to know how much damage was done. Zei continued his quest to build another symbol-carrying ship.

Shortly after that, Zei's last symbol in the southeast got destroyed by a storm of gliders. The last thing he could see in the southeast was Gun's symbol-carrying spaceship starting to move northwards.
Zei sent gliders to create another eternal glider factory, this time flooding the space along the center of the west.
He did not move his own spaceship. He could not: for the next three thousand turns he was a sitting duck, as he was building his new spaceship.

The sixth intervention turn came, right when Gun's symbol-carrying ship was getting hit by a barrage of gliders. This gave Gun a lucky chance to protect it from gliders, allowing it to survive a little bit longer.
The spaceship finally did get destroyed, but only after it had gotten within visual range of Zei's own.
Zei calculated: Gun had been able to see Zei's ship, but not the new ship that Zei was building.

Zei decided to do the only thing that he could do: he kept building, while putting up extra walls along the west and the diagonal. He judiciously ignored his south: the existing glider storm, and the debris from Gun's ship, would itself be enough protection.
The seventh intervention turn came. Zei put all resources into building the new ship. Almost finished. The next turn would be just enough to finish it, and to give a steering instruction to both.
Then, a glider storm came toward Zei's ship from all directions.
At first, the walls handled it. But then, the gliders kept coming, and soon they began to breach the walls.

The eighth intervention turn came just in time. Zei's last ship was not quite yet destroyed, but it was almost there. He could now finish his new ship, and give his existing ship one last instruction.

Zei programmed both to head west. He figured that the existing ship's symbol would get destroyed within a hundred turns, but the wreck could still coast west, and crash into the northern shrine and release a large glider storm southward. Meanwhile, the new ship would also head west, but stop just north of the northern shrine. This would give it some protection from the glider storms that were getting more and more intense.

When the ninth intervention turn came, Zei used a nearby rock formation, which was almost destroyed by the gliders, to bounce a glider that would then head southward and re-adjust the eternal glider factories that were attacking to the south. He did not have time to calculate what the adjustment would look like, and he did not have any way to know what its exact consequences would be, but he hoped that it would make previously safe territory unsafe. He also launched one more glider attack westward.
The tenth intervention turn came. Nothing seemed to happen, except debris. More and more debris.
Zei reinforced the eastern and western walls beside his last symbol-carrying spaceship.

He launched a few gliders to try to create more eternal glider factories, that would hopefully create more chaos southward. One of the gliders was destroyed, hit by another stray glider before it even left Zei's visual field.

The eleventh intervention turn came. Zei figured out one last trick. He figured out how to bounce a glider southward off of one of his own walls so that it would hug the edge of the shrine. From his simulations in the sandbox, he saw that if it hit the corner of the middle shrine, it would bounce off back north. The glider would bounce back and forth between the center and the north. Each time it hit the center, it would simultaneously release another glider that would go west. And when that glider hit the western shrine, it would bounce off and go southeast, hopefully causing damage to whatever was in the south. He did this, and simultaneously set up a mirror image of the same strategy toward the east.

The twelfth intervention turn came. By this point, the debris and stray gliders in the game field were so intense that offense was impossible. Zei simply kept building walls. Hunker down, play defense, outlast.
The thirteenth intervention turn came. Zei had built four layers of walls around this ship, and finally the walls were beginning to crumble faster than he could create new ones.
Finally, a few hundred turns after that, an alarm buzzed.
"And ... Zei Leimin is the winner!"
Zei let out a sigh of relief.

Zei sat in the waiting room, watching the game between Deluin and Kau. From the beginning, Zei was surprised, and impressed, by Deluin's strategy. Deluin spent all his attention early on to use the resources in the rock formations near his north and northeast to build walls. Simultaneously, he sent out gliders to try to create eternal glider factories pointing southward.

Deluin did not build any mobile symbol-carrying spaceships. Instead, he simply fortified. Kau's eternal glider factories proved to be of limited use: though the gliders would keep coming forever, they would only have any effect for a short period of time. As soon as a storm of gliders came, Deluin would figure out how to reflect it.
Zei was impressed. Looks like Deluin had also managed to figure out that he needed to be more patient.

Seven thousand turns later, Kau was reduced to hiding behind the southern shrine. But Kau barely survived three thousand turns more: the number of stray gliders and debris kept increasing, and Deluin's walls made him far more protected than Kau was.
Ten thousand two hundred turns into the game, Deluin was announced the winner.
Deluin stepped out from the elevator.
"That was a really impressive job, Deluin."
"Thanks! I was impressed that the walls held out so well. Now I'm excited to see how you handled your game."
"Oh - my style was much uglier than yours. Though I also basically won by playing defense."
"Do you want to get tea later?"
"Sure!"
Deluin was sitting in the courtyard drinking a tea. As soon as Zei saw him, he started running to greet him.
"Deluin, good to see you!"
Deluin waved back. Zei ran the rest of the way to his table and sat down.
A robot immediately slid up to their table.
"jie mo kai tu jie hei ja ma?"
A menu appeared.
"Whoa", Zei gasped.
"What is it?", Deluin asked.
"I think these are some of the new symbols they're A/B testing for Dzegoban version nine."
He immediately realized he was talking to a foreigner, and followed up:
"Have you heard of Dzegoban version nine?"

"Oh yeah I had a couple people mention it to me. Making the language visual. Bringing back hieroglyphs for the individual roots, but pronunciation perfectly readable from the glyph. And also another layer where they're trying to make the grammar look more like math."

"Yeah, so I'm trying to parse this. The cup is water - 'ja'. I see two unusual things about the cup. More straight horizontal lines than usual, and the three diagonal lines on the right. Maybe those are the pronunciation markers? One for the consonant, one for the vowel?"

"Top right is 'kai'. The unusual things I see are ... the extra vertical vein on the left, and then the transition to veins being more and more squiggly on the right? Although ... I'm not sure if I would make the images so detailed, when they often have different meanings depending on context."
"Wait, you know Dzegoban?"

"Zei, the whole point of Dzegoban is that there's only 256 roots, you can learn it in less than a month, and you don't get all the nuances but you can make your way around just fine.", Deluin replied in a lecturing tone.
"I'm impressed, you're almost a local already."

"Well, wanna come to Redshire with me tomorrow? I have to fly back for my mom and dad's birthdays, they're only a few days apart, and get some last-minute tutoring from our top players. And if you come, I can tell them that it's okay to skip the tutoring if you're doing the same!"
"I'd love to see Redshire, though unfortunately I just don't have the money for that. Maybe in a few years."
"But I'm super curious to see what Redshire is like! Send me pictures."
"Oh I can show you a few now."

Deluin took out his hand device, and showed Zei some pictures of Redshire. He saw castles, pine forests, large pristine grasslands, red-colored mountains with their tops covered in snow, and one giant icy waterfall.
"Wow, that's beautiful."

"You know, when I was younger I thought it was a back-handed compliment, almost an insult, to praise someone's country by saying that the nature is beautiful. At the time I thought, if the nicest thing you can say about a country is something that the people did not even make themselves, rather something that the forces of orbital dynamics and biology and tectonics randomly handed them down for free, then that's actually pretty harsh on the people."

"But as I grew up I've come to realize, that's not true at all. Even beautiful nature takes so much human work to maintain. Human work to build the paths and roads so people can walk or drive there. Human work to maintain a political system that stops people from polluting it, cutting down the forests, putting their houses on the mountainsides and making them ugly, strip-mining the mountains - while still allowing housing to be built where people can enjoy the views, keeping that housing affordable, and maintaining industry. Human work to restore any damage that was done before we got wise enough, or maybe rich enough, to care about these things."
"I'll let you know as soon as I can afford to go."
"Hopefully that will be in fifteen days", he joked.
"Because I use my championship winnings to pay for you to go", Deluin playfully snapped back.

Jahn passed through the turnstile in the Freetown Economics Institute, and walked toward the restaurant.

It was still early morning, and Jahn had intentionally not yet looked at any of the news on that day - better to clear his mind, and enjoy whatever the lecture on the restaurant screen would end up being.
After a minute of walking, he arrived.
When he saw what was on the screen, his eyes froze with horror.
Special broadcast
ARCTIC EMPIRE INVADES AND ANNEXES REDSHIRE
Jahn began to listen intently to the reporter relaying the details of what happened.

At 15,500 this morning, a large number of Arctic drones and aircraft landed all across the major cities and military bases in Redshire, timed simultaneously with a massive land invasion from the north with thousands of vehicles coming out of never-before-seen underground tunnels.
The Redshire military was caught completely unprepared, and many suspect corruption at the highest ranks.
Major battles lasted less than two longhours, with very limited casualties. Almost all Redshire garrisons have by now surrendered.
He saw about ten people sitting in the restaurant, including Utaku, who seemed just as shocked as Jahn was.
Three government aeroplanes containing President Albor, Prime Minister Celedil and most of the parliament attempted to take off. All three were shot down. Current indications suggest no survivors.
The president's son, Tafindel, is believed to be in Arctic captivity.
The reporter paused briefly, and then began speaking again.
JUST IN:

The last Redshire garrison in the south has agreed on a conditional surrender. The garrison staff, plus thirty other personnel including two senators, will be allowed to fly to Devanvil, in exchange for the garrison discontinuing all attempts to defend itself.

The three aeroplanes will leave in five minutes, and will be the only aeroplanes allowed to leave. Arctic authorities are not allowing any other vehicles to enter or leave Redshire. They have cut off all communications and are already actively setting up jamming equipment.
"What do we do now?", Jahn, by this point standing beside the table with Utaku, mumbled.
"Take the threat seriously", Utaku replied.
Before Jahn could look away, Utaku had already begun typing frantically on her hand device.
Meldan, Veridia

Gladias and Seila stared at the screen with Febric and Hreda beside them. They had just woken up at sunrise, light coming in clean through the window, the trees on the footpath outside already throwing long morning shadows. The news was the first thing they saw.
Zven was still asleep, and Lily was still in her room.
Seila took out her hand device, and began frantically typing.
She clicked send.
A few ticks later:
Seila sighed with relief.
Gladias saw Seila messaging Jahn, and put his hand on her shoulder to comfort her. He did not respond further.
His mind soon shifted to the rubrics. Now we're definitely not adjusting the hardware openness rubric next month, he thought. Maybe we'll even be increasing the tax brackets.
A moment after that, he flashed with anger toward Delwart.
Seila left the room to wake up Zven and get Lily. Within twenty minutes, the four of them were on their way to school, and Gladias and Seila were alone in the house.
Gladias went down to the basement and closed the door.
"What do we do now, Mov?", he whispered through his neck band.
"Well clearly Delwart was wrong about a lot of things. And next time we talk to him, we really have a lot of questions to ask. We need a straight answer, not excuses."
"Remember, it's not just him turning out to be so wrong on the politics. It's about what I learned a month and a half ago - the sheer level of organization of whatever it is that he's doing."
"Did you manage to track him down any more after that time?"

"Only two more times after that. First was a meeting with someone in a privacy robe, not sure who, and they were talking a bunch about Silverchat. Second was a meeting with a Keeper, I made out some conversation about Dreadknot. Nothing more since about a month ago, he either changed his location or he got much better at hiding."
"So when is the vote?"
"First one is in about twenty days."
"Delwart might make a move to try to 'verify' that you voted in the correct way. So remember the machinery that the Order set up to make sure he can't do that."

"Only votes signed with a valid key count", Gladias recited. "You generate your voting key by meeting at least 3 of 5 people from your Key Allocation Group and registering each blinded share of the voting key with them. Once that's done, the information of which keys are and are not valid is only decryptable by the obfuscated circuit under the conditions that it specifies."

"So neither Delwart nor anyone else - technically, not even I - will know which key, how many keys or if any key actually got successfully registered. Only the result of the vote gets decrypted. So Delwart can't tell which votes I submit are real or fake. I don't have the ability to prove that to him, even if I wanted to. For Delwart to be able to take over my votes, he would have to take over my identity, which means going to the KAG and pretending to be me in person - difficult because the whole point of the KAG is that it includes people I've met in person."
"Humans - the ultimate trusted hardware."
"You've studied well."
"But I hope that this all won't be necessary, and Delwart is going to give me some sensible explanation for all this."
"Hope is not a strategy."
"Indeed it's not."
Pafogai Du, Dzego
Zei anxiously tapped buttons on his hand device, and sent off a message for a fifth time.

He sat crying at a table in the lobby restaurant of his hotel. There was a tea and a rice and vegetable dish on the table in front of him. He had drunk the tea quickly; the robot had already refilled it four times. The rice and vegetables were uneaten for almost a longhour.
Finally, he got a message in response.
It was not the outcome Zei wanted, but still much better than the outcome he feared. He breathed a sigh of relief.
Zei wiped off his tears, and started typing intently.
Zei thought for a moment, and realized that perhaps the time had arrived for him to become the instructor. He took out a keyboard and started typing furiously.
Zei sat back briefly, proud that he had managed to understand and explain not just a complicated concept, but the exact complicated concept that was needed for this exact job.
He decided to keep going, out of a feeling of personal pride in his understanding as much as out of a desire to let more people in Redshire sneak information past the Arctic censors.
He then realized that his last message might have come off too much as him trying to be a hotshot, so he sent a followup.
Zei felt more optimistic about how much of an improvement a better steganographic encoding would be, but decided not to press the point further.

Zei thought about saying "or that the Kungaupei could do", or even "or that advanced Dzegojan secret societies could do", instead. But he realized that first, it would be a breach of confidentiality to let an outsider, especially an outsider now in hostile occupied territory, know about the existence of those things, and second, he couldn't fully trust the connection - he hadn't even asked Deluin a security question yet. And so "smart people in my network" it was.

Zei put down his hand device, and breathed out. His eyes briefly wandered around the restaurant, and he saw that by this point there was no one else there. He finally began eating his rice and vegetable dish.
Zei felt someone put their hands on his shoulder.
Zei turned around. It was Su.
"So sorry to hear about Deluin."
"I assume the Kungaupei are figuring out how to get him out?"
Zei realized that technically he had just committed an error: he had not actually confirmed that Su knew or was supposed to know about the Kungaupei - so far that was just Den and Mu.

"That was the first thing I asked Den", Su began to reply. Zei gave out a barely audible sigh of relief. "So far they've acquired a bunch of internet links into Redshire, and they got a message from Deluin a minute ago, so at least he's safe for now. We'll let you know if there's any kind of rescue plan possible."
Zei nodded silently.
"The finals are cancelled", Su added.
"Cancelled? Not postponed? What if he comes back tomorrow?"
"Even if he does, at this point it's just not right to have more games. Also we don't want to give the audience false hope, and we don't want to distract people."
"You're the champion this year. And if Deluin does come back, we'll give him the same trophy and the same prize money that we're giving you."
"No...", Zei pleaded. "I don't want to win like this."

"I know it's already late today, but you should go talk to Den. He's in Sadzu Du, in the southern mountain pyramid right now. He might want you here, or maybe in Pafogai. He will know better than me."
Zei nodded. Of course this was all more important than the game, he understood. He hoped that Den would put him in Pafogai, so that he could see Fin and his mom again.

Zei's car arrived at an entrance to the mountain pyramid that he had not been at before. This was a series of doors on the side of the mountain pyramid, much nearer to ground level than the usual entrance, though further from the city. The car stopped, its door lined up perfectly with one of the mountain pyramid doors. The car door and the mountain pyramid door slid open simultaneously.
Zei stepped out, and walked down the hallway.
A hundred meters and a left and right turn later, he arrived at a door.
He put his watch against a green circle. The door opened.
Zei saw a long room, with a table at the end. Den was sitting on the other side, alone.
Zei sat down.
"Thank you for coming, Zei."
Zei nodded silently.
"I think you're one of the very few people who is in a position to help Dzego get through this next year."

Zei's eyes opened wide. He was now the national Minpentai champion, and he was getting far in his studies from Den's cryptography books, yes, but ... he still did not know how that made him valuable at this exact moment.
"In your last Minpentai game, you did two things that were crucial to winning. Do you remember what they are?"
"I can think of a few answers, but I'm not sure if any of them are what you had in mind."
"First, you hunkered down and played defense, and outlasted your opponent."

"Second, you made the most out of a very limited-bandwidth information channel, by pre-publishing most of the data - the symbol-carrying spaceship - and then using only a few bits of manipulation at the end to deploy the most important parts of your strategy."

"Actually a very similar tactic to what you used in your other game months earlier, when you sent out a spaceship that encoded basically every possible glider attack strategy, and then another glider to choose which specific one you wanted to use."
"How is this related?"
"We have contact with Deluin. Do you know how we accomplished that?"
"Actually, he got in touch with me and he told me. Some Arctic soldier is charging people zipcoins to hide their messages in his health data."

"Correct. And so everyone is dropping down to the most efficient, lowest-bandwidth form of communication they can use - raw text - and pushing all that through him. One soldier's health data, communications for thousands of people."

"A quarter longhour ago the rates he was charging suddenly dropped by two thirds - we suspect he found some more efficient way to encode data. Interestingly enough neither he nor anyone else has found any better channel than health data so far."

"Okay, now I wonder if that was me. I told Deluin to tell the soldier to train an LLM on his own health data and then modify the health data that he is sending out in-flight by flipping the bits that the LLM says are safest to flip, and using XOR over buckets to encode the message so he has a lot of freedom in choosing which bit to flip. Much better for reducing the 'suspiciousness' per bit of hidden data encoded, so he could afford to hide more data inside the same cover traffic."
Den's eyes opened up.
"Well we have no way to know if he used that specific trick-"
Zei remembered to check his watch.
"Looks like he did."
"See, you've helped the anti-Arctic resistance already."
"Look, Zei. What's happening now is, our hand has been forced. We can't just keep improving our capabilities secretly anymore. Dzegojan society has to come out of hiding."

"The shadow society has to become the society. The shadow government has to become the government. We have to sprint to deploy everything that we have figured out across all of Dzego - before the Arctics can make any moves on us."

"The part of this most relevant to you - the cryptographic infrastructure we need so that our coordination can keep functioning and we what needs to be secret can stay secret - is run out of Pafogai Du. So I want you to take the train back - Su can reschedule your ticket for tomorrow - and I'll message you about whom you should reach out to next."
"For now, maybe see if you can come up with any more ideas for that soldier to sell more packets. That seems to be even better cryptography training for you than my textbooks."
