Gladias pulled open the barrier on the booth, walked in, and slid the barrier shut behind him. He sat down angrily on the bench across from Delwart.
"You have a lot of explaining to do."
Delwart looked downwards toward the table, with a sorry expression on his face.

"Look, Gladias, you were right, I was wrong. I let my hate for all this interventionism in Veridia's government and culture blind me to the fact that there are things government has always been for, and defense is one of them."
"That's not why I'm angry."
Delwart looked up, startled.
"I mean, it's one of the reasons, but far from the primary."
"What is the primary then?"
"What the hell is going on? Who are you? Who are you working with?"
Delwart sighed. For a few moments he was silent. Then he leaned forward.
"Fine, I will explain."
"I'm not just one ideologue who is doing this alone. I, and a group of others - I don't know them - are working for Silverchat."

"We were frustrated by these rubrics that were increasing our taxes just because a bunch of people were putting crude jokes on our platform. We wanted Silverchat to be a refuge from the blandness that's taking over so much of the rest of Veridia. We wanted to be a place where Hydrafill and even Dreadknot could be welcome."
"And so we decided to take matters into our own hands. Make an organized effort to try to pull the politics in a better direction. Appeal to the Keepers directly."

"And now I realize just how naive this all was. If we manage to ward off blandness, but at the price of the Arctic Empire being able to take over and inflict things far worse - first on Redshire and later on the whole world - then this whole thing was not just not worth it - it was ruinous."
Gladias sighed. He was still extremely angry at Delwart, but the anger was now mixed with a dose of sympathy.
A robot slid up to them, carrying a salad, a rectangular nutrition bar and water for the two of them to eat and drink.
Gladias and Delwart both first picked up their plates of food, and put them down on the table. Gladias then picked up his cup and drank about half the water in one gulp. Delwart did the same.
They began eating, silently. After a few minutes, the conversation resumed.
"What do you want me to do now?", Gladias asked.

"Obviously don't make the rubric exclude military now. You could even increase the tax brackets, though you doing that would only help a tiny bit - the most important levers there are on the Graph Funding side."
"But I also have another idea for what you could do."
"What is it?"
"I think you should go to Dzego."
"Me? Dzego? Why?"
"They clearly have this whole Arctic question figured out much better than we do in Veridia. Study them. Learn from them. See what you can bring back to Veridia."
"And why should I listen to you when you've been so untrustworthy?"
"Well definitely don't just listen to me. Ask your closest friends and advisors. See what they think."

Gladias walked along the same path through Kalimar that he would usually pass through. As usual, it was covered with trees and surrounded by stone houses on both sides. But on that day, it was unusually hot, and Gladias sweated slightly as some of the sunlight managed to shine through the tree cover and warm up his entire body inside of his privacy robe.

He passed by one of the houses that he remembered for selling traditional Veridian food products. This time, an additional note was hastily taped on to the poster, advertising packages that offered tasty, nutritionally complete and long-lasting preserved food that was sufficient for thirty days of survival.
He tapped his watch, and called Mov.
"So I had my chat with Delwart."
"How did it go?"
"You're right. There was an organized effort. Turns out - at least he now says - he's been working for Silverchat this whole time."
"Silverchat? And here I was expecting some more evil company, like Bluewhale."
"I guess it makes sense, probably that conversation I overheard a month and a half ago was with a Silverchat guy."
"So he wants me to go to Dzego now."
"Dzego? What for?"
"He says we in Veridia have a lot to learn from them. Do you think that's true?"
"You know, one of my friends mentioned something like that to me the day Redshire got taken over. He thought I should go, and see how their secret societies work or something."

"Well you know, Seila has a friend from there now, and the last thing she told me was that he's been climbing up the Minpentai ranks really well, gotten into the nationals. So if I go, maybe I will actually be able to learn a few things."
"Yeah I can certainly see the appeal. Veridians really need to know the outside world better. Especially the people in the institutions - the Order, the Courts, the parliament, all of them."
"Give me a few days to think through this."
"Well, the votes on the rubrics are in eight, twelve and sixteen days, so you have that time to think through it no matter what happens."
Gladias paused for a moment.
At that moment, he was walking past the restaurant near his home where he would often stop for food and drinks. Through the window, he could see Febric eating.
"I'll think about it too", he finally said, and ended the call.

Gladias entered the restaurant, and almost immediately took off the face cover from his privacy robe, and partially unzipped the front. He could not be that private while eating anyway, and he had been sweating in the hot sun. He sat down beside Febric.
"Oh uncle Glad, happy to see you here again!"
"And I'm happy to see you!"
Gladias noticed that Febric had been watching the screen. A game of Helisport was actively broadcasting.
Gladias let himself watch the action for a minute. The screen was following the lead player wearing a yellow shirt chasing a redball.

Suddenly, out of nowhere, a player from the other team, wearing a purple shirt, whacked him off to the side. The player in the yellow shirt tumbled, and then automatically regained his bearings about five meters further down.

The screen shifted view to the player wearing the purple shirt. He caught a blueball in midair. Two other players wearing yellow shirts started flying towards him. Before they could get to him, he threw the blueball toward a teammate. That teammate successfully caught it, and began flying forward.

The screen shifted view toward ten yellow standing pins arranged in a triangle on a circular board mounted on a pole high above the ground. The player wearing the purple shirt holding the blueball came into view. A player wearing a yellow shirt zoomed into position between him and the pins.
The player wearing the purple shirt suddenly threw the blueball up high into the air, just as a different player wearing a yellow shirt crashed into him.
The blueball passed about five meters over the player wearing the yellow shirt protecting the pins, and then landed on the board. It knocked three of the pins down.
A scoreboard onscreen adjusted.
Purple's blueball score had just increased from 20 to 23, and their combined score from 1540 to 1771 - enough to push them ahead of their opponents.
Suddenly, while the player who had just taken down those pins was celebrating, a greenball hit him in the back and splatted its paint over him.
The score adjusted again.
"You have to admit, the scoring system is really good now", Febric exclaimed.

"I remember when I was much younger, they kept adjusting the ratios between what a redball gives you, versus a pin knockdown or a player hit. And they just couldn't get out of having a situation where the rational thing is to just focus all your attention on one."
"Even when they got it right, within a year the strategies adjusted, and it became lopsided again."
"I think making the score multiplicative was the only way out. That way you pretty much have to care about all three of the point types."
"Or try really hard to make sure your opponent can't get any of one type", Gladias interjected.

"Ah yeah that was the first thing a few people tried", Febric replied. "Holding onto redballs for more than thirty ticks had already been banned for ages, that had been a good cheat for whichever side was worse at redballs even back when the scores were additive. But what one team did try, is knock down a bunch of pins very early in the game, and then use most of their players to protect their pins for the rest of the game."

"Turns out it doesn't actually work. People on copters can only pack together so tightly, no matter what you do, the other team always manages to sneak a few blueballs through. And then if you do pack tightly in one place around the pins, you're a sitting duck for the greenballs."
"Are you thinking of playing?", Gladias asked.
"No, but I just had a bunch of conversations with Zven about this. The math is almost as fun as the actual game!"
Gladias and Febric both turned their attention to the food.
"How's Lily doing by the way?", Gladias asked.

"She actually started getting a little better over the last couple of months. She mentioned to me a few days ago that she got seventy on her latest civics test. She seems happier. And she's even more engaged playing that game on her hand device."
"Do you know what game?", Gladias asked.
"She doesn't show me either."
Gladias and Febric both returned to eating. A few minutes later, they were both finished.
"Did you remember to take out your zipcoins this time?", Febric asked playfully.
"Hey, I may make lots of mistakes, but I don't make the same mistake twice", Gladias snapped back.
"By the way, Febric, thanks for reminding me - I need to test my recovery procedure for my coins", he whispered through his neck band.
"Want me to help you sign a test operation?"
"Sure! What do you want the test to be?"
"I dunno, buy a Hydrafill bottle?"
"Buy a Hydrafill bottle? Straight out of a life savings wallet?", Gladias asked incredulously. "Those ads really have been getting to you too, haven't they?"
"Hey, you're the one who asked me!"
"Okay fine ... let me start the operation."
Gladias began whispering into his neck band. Out of the corner of his eye, he saw Febric run off somewhere, though he was too busy to wonder where.
A few ticks later, Febric's watch buzzed.

Febric opened up his hand device, and a more detailed view of the transaction appeared. He asked Emerald to search for the receiving address online. A few ticks later, Emerald replied with a confirmation that it was, in fact, the Hydrafill purchase address. He then checked the amount - 5.5 zipcoins. It seemed reasonable for a water bottle plus shipping, though the bulk of the cost was definitely the shipping. He checked the transaction data field. Yep, looked like an encoding of Gladias's home address, in the correct format according to the standard online shopping protocol.
In the cryptographic network that processed these transactions, all of this data was, of course, encrypted.
Febric clicked "Confirm".
Gladias's watch immediately buzzed.
Less than a minute later, Gladias's watch buzzed again.
Gladias immediately whispered into his neck band a reply.

A few moments later, Gladias's watch buzzed again. Three signatures done, including his own. One to go. Either Mov or Pelow - or, of course, if he really had to, himself running to the vault and picking up his second key.
"I'm obviously not gonna ask who that was, or who else you need to confirm it", Febric added. "But good luck!"
"Seila, I'm home!"
"Glad!"
"So I have interesting news."
"What is it?"
"There's some chance I'll be going to Dzego soon."
Seila stared.
"Why?"
"I talked to Mov about this. He thinks that Veridians, especially Keepers, the Order, the institutions generally, have a lot to learn from what's going on over there."

"I'm not sure about this ... it's a difficult time. You're not really the best person to make good use of a Dzego trip. And the Keepers would benefit from having a strong hand guide them these next few months."
"Arctic stuff is really much more of a military and parliament responsibility, maybe Graph Funding too. And ... maybe I can make good use of a trip if you introduce me to Zei?"
Seila retreated into her thoughts for a few moments.

"If Mov thinks it's a good idea, then fine. But please do your homework first. Find someone, anyone, in Graph Funding or in parliament to talk to, so you get some idea of whether this trip will be useful, and if you do go, how to make it as useful as possible."
"But really, think hard about this."
"If you go, then yes, of course I'll introduce you to Zei. And Bai too."

Chapter 17
Meldan, Veridia·3724 Fruitmoon 11
Gladias walked forward along a path covered with trees on both sides, toward the large circular parliament building in front.
When he arrived at a side door of the building, he tapped his watch on the green circle.
The circle buzzed.
The door opened. Gladias walked in, and followed the instructions that were being relayed by his watch. Forward, then right turn, then forward, then third door on the left.
Gladias got to the door, and tapped his watch again.
The door opened.
Inside, he saw a man wearing a Veridian parliament robe.
"Gladias, thank you for coming!", the senator exclaimed.
"And thank you for seeing me, Senator Verdow!"
"Please sit down."
A robot slid into the room.
"jie mo kai tu jie hei ja ma?", the robot asked.
Gladias briefly stared in surprise.
Verdow laughed.
"I adjusted the settings to make it do that a few months ago. Just a little something as a reminder that other countries exist and that they matter."
Verdow tapped a few buttons on the robot's screen, and turned the screen toward Gladias.
The screen was in Dzegoban. Gladias's eyes wandered around with confusion.
"Oh, if you want water, that's 'ja'. And if you want tea, that's 'kai ja'. Literally 'plant water'."

Gladias clicked on 'kai ja'. If he's going to be in Dzego for a few months, might as well get acclimated and start drinking some tea - and knowing the local word for it. The robot beeped, signaling acceptance of the order, and began to quietly glide away from them. The room door briefly opened, and the robot exited the room.
"So you think I should go to Dzego?"

"You're obviously smart. Of course I have no idea what you say in your secret meetings, but judging from everything you said in the hearing, and from your original application to the Order years ago, I think you're a good and smart person. We need people like you to be more active in serving our country. Being a Keeper is nice, but come on, you're only one of over a thousand. I think getting and bringing back some first-hand experience from Dzego could be even more meaningful."
"If you think it's a good idea, I'm happy to. But who should I talk to there? That's what I wanted to get your input on."
Gladias intentionally omitted any mention of Zei - not out of any desire to hide that indirect connection, but because he wanted to get a fully independent answer from Verdow first.

"Well my strongest connections are with some of their authors and musicians", he said, gently laughing. "Though I also know a few people in the government there, especially the security and health ministry. I'll send you their contacts, and give them a heads up. I wouldn't stop with them, but I think they can help get you started."
"Thanks, that would help a lot!"
"I only know two people from there, indirectly; my wife met them at a chance meeting in the Economics Institute in Freetown. Zei and Bai, they were in Minpentai."

Verdow's eyes opened. "Honestly, you might have a better lead than I do. When you see the Minpentai games in Dzego, the players and the people who train them are clearly top-notch. If I had to find someone to defend me against the Arctics, I'd almost trust them over the actual Dzego army."
"How advanced are Zei and Bai? Did they get into any of the championships?"
"Last thing Seila told me, Zei won the semi-finals, and then they cancelled the finals when Redshire was invaded."
"The semi-finals, like municipal level?"
"National."
Verdow stared with a mix of surprise and joy.
"Your connections are definitely better than mine then. When you come back, you'll have to tell me more about Dzego!"
"Anyway, I'll introduce you to the other folks I mentioned so you can see them when you come. It's always good to get more than one perspective."
Gladias nodded appreciatively.
"Oh, by the way, speaking of getting more perspectives, one of the Graph Funding stewards is here about to visit me. You want to talk to him too?"
"About what?"
"Oh, his work, how he's feeling about Graph Funding, and of course Dzego."
"Sure, why not?"
A few minutes later, the door opened, and another man, wearing a Veridian privacy robe but without the face cover and hood, walked in.
"Belgor, good to see you again!"
"Good to see you too, Verdow!"
"And meet Gladias, he's a Keeper."
"Nice to meet you, Belgor."
"And nice to meet you, Gladias!"
"So Gladias is thinking of going to Dzego soon. We thought that maybe you should tell him more about Graph Funding, and any advice on what he should do or learn in Dzego."
"Sure, happy to. How familiar are you with how Graph Funding works?"
"Honestly, not very."
"Great."
He took out his hand device, and pressed some buttons. A diagram opened up on the screen, and he showed it to Gladias.

"This is the subgraph for airborne disease resistance. For each node on the graph, the cryptographic network randomly selects a committee, that makes the decision of what weights the edges right below that node get."

"So it's secure in the same way the Courts and the Order of Steering are. Having something like that for funding is especially important now, given that the Arctics just did the same attack on Quadratic Funding that Bluewhale did but at ten times the scale - and of course any more traditional style of allocation, they would try to interfere with as well."
"Oh you're definitely right. Even the Keepers are getting attacked lately, though with all the secrecy and internal communication barriers, at least for now the system is holding."

"Oh is that so? Good to hear. Though I am sad that we don't have a good way to make both of these things more democratic. Listening to citizens' assemblies is good and Heralds are good, but they're not a substitute for actual public accountability."

"Anyway, one difference between the Graph Funding design and how the Courts and the Order work is that Graph Funding allows even more specialization. After all, funding allocation is a pretty technical task."

"The goal is to try to split up each decision of funding allocation into more manageable pieces. Don't ask 'what percent of all Veridian public funding should go to this study on UVC lamps'. Ask, what percent should go to health, then within health, what percent should go to airborne diseases, and so on."

"And if one project benefits two areas: say, some lamp that's somehow useful both for UVC lamps and for defense, then the graph stops being a tree, it becomes a proper directed acyclic graph. One node can have multiple parents, and the funding you get along all paths adds up."
"So a committee is responsible for allocating the funding going to each node among its direct children?"
"Yes."
"Can they remove children or make new ones?"
"Yes, of course. That's how the graph gets made in the first place."
"This is fascinating."

"I mean, this all hinges completely on how effective these committees are, right? The more you can specialize, the more it might get captured by special interests, and the more you randomize, the more you get decisions made by people who know nothing about what they're deciding?"
"Of course, that's always the tradeoff."

"There's also another tradeoff. It turns out that it's fairly easy to get committees up to the point where they can tell bad projects from good ones, but very hard for them to tell good projects from great ones. So for the lower levels of the graph, there's been a movement lately to just randomize at the top end. If the committee says you're in the top ten percent, you have the same chance of getting in, no matter if you're at ninety one or ninety nine."
"So the further someone is above ninety, the more they basically don't have to worry about optimizing for the committee at all, they can just do what feels right."

"Exactly. Sometimes you don't actually want accountability, you want to give space for people's intrinsic motivation. The people at the very top may even be smarter than the committee. That's what randomize-above-cutoff does: accountability for those who won't succeed without it, and freedom from incentives for the best - they can convince the committee that their work is good enough with barely any effort at all."
"Anyway, here's what it looks like zoomed in at the level of individual projects."
"Is it wise to have these randomly-selected Graph Funding committees making decisions at that level of granularity?"

"I'm not sure myself. The nice thing about this design is that it can always evolve without changing the structure. Committees could just decide to give the VNU Materials Science Lab 'ownership' of an entire category, and let them allocate internally. Actually, for the open source social media analysis, we basically did just that, eighty percent is just going to Silverchat."
"Bluewhale is unhappy, but, hey, their choice to be so closed and proprietary with everything."
"So how does this all connect to Dzego?"

"Ah, well a lot of this tech does actually make its way over to Dzego, they're starting to take the air filters and ultraviolet lights more seriously - a few of them are getting paranoid that the Arctics might hit them with a deliberately-released pandemic at some point."
"Is there any chance that the Arctics could hit them with a pandemic that won't eventually bounce right back to them?"

"Well, if Arctic anti-pandemic technology shoots far enough ahead of the rest of the world, then yeah, they could release a pandemic that only they can effectively protect only their own people from. That's a big part of why it's so valuable to open-source all this stuff - at least the defensive things. Put the whole world on a more level playing field, so no one is in a position to light a fire and be the only ones with fireproof suits."
"Anyway, if you end up going to Dzego, do tell me what you learn about their public health when you get back - I am curious!"
Gladias opened the door to his house, and entered.
Seila and the kids were already eating dinner.
"Today is your first vote, isn't it?", Seila asked.
"It is, glad you remembered!"
"So are you leaving again this evening?", Zven asked.
"Oh no, the in-person part was the discussions months ago, and the key registration, I did that right after my meetings at the Parliament."

"There were also some discussions happening more recently in our Keeper discussion group online, though that chat automatically cut off seven days before the vote - have a quiet period to make more space for independent thought, the argument goes."
"Oof, so the cutoff was after Redshire got annexed. What was that like?"

"I think everyone who said we should cut military hardware out of the best tiers in the rubric went quiet. Eighteen then proposed a new amendment that increases the tax brackets, pushing up the incentives to open things up even more. I'll probably vote for that."
"Glad to hear."
"How did your Parliament meetings go?"

"Very well. The Senator and the Graph Funding person both seemed quite supportive of me going. Though they said that Zei might be an even better contact to help me with my visit than anyone they knew!"
"That actually makes sense, everyone knows the official Dzego government is not where any of the interesting action is happening."
"I guess I'll talk to Zei and put you two in touch then!"
Gladias, Seila and the kids took a few bites of their food. Soon, the dinner conversation resumed.
"Febric, Hreda, want to share your news?"
"We're going on an exchange trip to Northglade for the winter term!", Hreda exclaimed proudly.
"Ooh, that's pretty far northeast, almost at the Arctic border", Gladias replied.

"It's fun, we'll get to ski off mountains wearing a copter and then glide back down!", Hreda exclaimed. "And it's not like it's right at the border, Northglade is over two hundred kilometers inland. It will be my first time there!"
"So what are you guys doing there?", Gladias asked.
"Veridia's best math university is there," Hreda replied. "I'm in the top five percent in math in my class, so I got accepted to attend some special education there."
"Same for me," Febric added. "Though I'm in computer science."
"Didn't Lily also want to go to Northglade?"
Lily was in the washroom, so she could not answer.
"Vil said that he will take her in the summer if she gets to seventy-five percent in her exams."
"She prefers summer, she doesn't like the cold as much."
Gladias's hand device buzzed.
"Well, voting on the hardware openness rubric started."

This felt anti-climactic, Gladias thought. So much ceremony, in-person meetings, debate and work in the months leading up to the vote. And then the vote itself was just ... tapping buttons on a screen.

It was reasonable, Gladias supposed. The way that the cryptography worked, as long as key registration was secure, this part could just be done on his own hardware at home. And even if Delwart did come knocking and demand to stare at him from behind his shoulder for the entire fifteen-longhour voting window, he had no way to prove to him that the key on his device even was the one registered - as opposed to being a distraction while the real voting was done by Mov, Seila or even Zven.
Gladias took one last look at the screen, and nonchalantly pressed: No, Yes, Yes.

Pafogai Du, Dzego·3724 Fruitmoon 18
Gladias exited the air harbor, stepping through a sealed opening that opened immediately into a large black car.
Zei and Bai were both already sitting inside, Zei on a backward-facing seat and Bai facing him on a forward-facing seat.
"You must be Zei and Bai."
"We are indeed!", Bai replied.
"Well, I'm glad to finally meet."
"As are we."
Gladias sat down to the left of Zei.
The door closed, and the car began to accelerate.
Gladias stared to the right, looking past Zei to the right-side window of the car.
The car exited the air harbor, and soon began passing by a series of stores.
Gladias immediately noticed that something was off: the view on the window shifted as the car moved, but it did not respond to Gladias himself shifting his body position.
"Is that a real window?", Gladias asked.

"It can be", Zei replied. "But we have heightened security protocols now, and the black cars changed their settings. Can't let light pass through windows directly, because that would be bi-directional even if it was dimmed - a good camera could see that we're inside. So it's a simulated window now, picking up the view with cameras."
"It actually works well when there's one person, because it tracks your eyes too so it adjusts to look more natural. But now there's two of us, and it's picking me."
"Huh."

Gladias looked through the left window instead. He adjusted his body a few times to test it. The colors and the depth seemed somewhat unnatural, but otherwise it looked surprisingly normal. He continued looking, paying close attention to everything that he saw outside.
Many of the stores had cartoon animals on the sides, with speech bubbles saying various things in Dzegoban that Gladias could not understand at all.
Gladias could briefly see the products inside each of the stores: hand devices, compute boxes, lamps, drones, sensors.
"MIN KUI", a sign on a store selling compute boxes read.
"GUI SAU", a sign on a store selling lamps, most of them in the shapes of long cylinders, read.
But to his surprise, only a few of the stores seemed to be open.
The buildings were all one or two storeys tall, with many stairways leading underground.
There were people outside, though fewer than Gladias was used to seeing in Veridia - despite the visibly greater density of Pafogai Du compared to his own hometown.
"hun fe bin jin zo de jan li gi", Zei wondered aloud.
"Huh?", Gladias replied.
"Ah, sorry. So many people wearing neck bands, I was just saying."
Gladias also noticed a large number of identical black cars on the roads.
"Does everyone in Pafogai Du use this kind of black car? Is this a privacy thing?", he asked.
"Now that I think about it, no. We've had them for a while, but having this many people use them is quite new. Just a few days ago, there were barely half as many."
They continued riding silently.

A few minutes later, the car descended into a tunnel. Midway through, it slowed and then came to a stop. Gladias could feel a gentle bump, some mechanical noises, and what seemed to be the car shifting in all directions: up, sideways and then down. He looked out through the window, but could see nothing. And about half a minute later, the procedure ended, and the car appeared to be accelerating forward again.
"Did we just ... swap cars?"

"Swapped cabins. The system waits for ten cars to come, swaps the cabins around randomly, and then everyone drives back out. No one watching the exits knows which one we're in. Like a mixnet, but for people."
Less than a minute later, they exited the tunnel. Soon, the mountain pyramid in the south of Pafogai Du came into view.
"That ... is an impressive structure", Gladias said.
"Heh, everyone says that. Actually we carved it out of a pre-existing mountain."
"Still impressive! Probably more secure that way too, if ninety or ninety-nine percent of the inside is solid rock."
"It's ninety-six point seven."
"So one over thirty open space? If a normal building is ten percent solid, that makes it equivalent in capacity to a normal building three times smaller in each dimension?"
"You got it!"
"Maybe you're right we should be impressed. It is the largest one of these in all of Dzego."
The car began to slow down, and soon it came to a stop. The car door opened, directly into the hotel.
"This is your hotel, Gladias!"
Gladias stood up, and stepped out of the car with his bag.
"So what's the plan?"
"Take a longhour to rest, we'll meet you back here and chat more."
Gladias walked into the hotel, and tapped his watch onto the nearest green circle.
His watch buzzed. He had his room key.
Gladias looked around. Zei was right, he realized. Almost everyone was already wearing neck bands here.
Gladias walked into the elevator. The elevator door closed. When it opened again, Gladias stepped out, and walked into his room.

Gladias stepped out of the front door of the hotel, and looked outside. He had only taken forty minutes to rest; he had another sixty left before Zei and Bai would be expecting him. He figured that he would go on a walk, and take a look around at least this one piece of Pafogai Du himself.
He turned around. He saw the hotel address: 1565 Tan Kai.
He turned right, and began walking.

Almost immediately, his watch began flashing warnings at him, "unknown" counts in the double digits. Figuring that this was just his Veridian watch not being up to date on Dzego electronics, he decided to ignore the warnings, and continued his walk.

He crossed the street. He saw a black car pass by him, and then almost immediately slow to a stop. A man walked out from a nearby shop, holding a large box. He put the large box down on the ground beside the car.
The door of the car opened, and the driver stepped outside, putting her own large box down on the ground, identical in size. She proceeded to open the top of the box.
Looking at the box from a few meters away, Gladias could see about thirty much smaller white boxes on the top row inside.

The driver took out a tray containing the top row, and put it on the ground, on a staircase. The man from the store took out a hand device, and seemed to scan the two-dimensional codes on all the white boxes simultaneously.
The driver then took out a tray containing the second topmost row, and put it on top of the first tray. The man from the store scanned again.
This repeated five more times. Then, the driver opened up the man's large box, and scanned it row by row as well.
After scanning each row, she put the tray into her own box. And finally, she took the box back into her car and drove away.
"What's going on?", Gladias asked.
"Shipping", the man replied. "High security."
The man finished putting the trays on the staircase into his own box, picked up the box, hurried back inside his shop and locked the door.

A mixnet for physical objects, Gladias realized - Zei had told him about it once. Each object would pass through several carriers, and no single person knew both the source and the destination. There was no way to sabotage one person's device without sabotaging everyone's device - and if you did that, you would quickly get caught.
Gladias kept walking. He turned right on 17th street, and could see Pafogai Du's giant mountain pyramid in front of him, and the pathway leading up to it starting after only two more streets.

On this street, Gladias could see far more shops that were open. Almost every shop had a sign above the window advertising it, about half the time polished and professional and the other half the time improvised and hand-made from neon lights. He saw a flower shop, still bustling with customers. About twenty meters after that, a clothing shop. The posters on the outside still advertised jackets, but looking through the window inside, he could see that about half the space was now taken up by hastily-added privacy robes. About twenty meters after that, an unmarked staircase leading to a basement, with two teenage boys and one girl climbing down.

At the top of the staircase, Gladias saw a sign. There were pictures of cute cartoon animals playing with electronic gadgets and chemistry lab equipment, with a backdrop of green trees and blue skies. In the middle of the sign, he saw a motto in Dzegoban:
He wondered what the words meant.
He made a mental note to himself: gotta actually learn those 256 Dzegoban roots now that I'm here.

About twenty meters after that, he saw another staircase, leading down to what seemed like an underground tea shop. The entrance and the staircase were decorated in a style that reminded Gladias of depictions he had seen as a child of Dzego's medieval era.

And soon after that, Gladias arrived at the next street: Zin Go. The sidewalk had had good tree cover, enough so that he had lost sight of the giant pyramid towering in front of him. Here, the street intersection temporarily interrupted the trees, and he could see the pyramid once again. He saw many people going up and down the inclined walkway leading up to the entrance. The majority of them were wearing privacy robes. He wondered what they were up to.
He crossed the street, and continued walking until he got to the next street: Dzai Gun. This was the last street before the hill began. He crossed the street again, and began to walk up the incline.

About five minutes later, Gladias was high enough that he was now towering over Pafogai Du, and could see the roofs of nearly all of the buildings. From the top, the city was a mix of concrete roofs and green trees - much more green than Freetown, but still much less green than Veridia.
He noticed a large rock nearby. He sat down on it, and enjoyed the view.
A few minutes later, he began to walk back down.

He got to Dzai Gun street, and turned left, walking along the edge of the city until the westernmost point. He was pleased by the beautiful path covered with trees that seemed to surrounding the whole perimeter of the city. He saw many people walking and running along it. When he reached 0th street, on the west edge of the city, the path turned north.
He continued following the path, walking north two streets back to Tan Kai, and then crossed back into the city, heading east until he got back to his hotel.

Gladias entered the hotel, and immediately turned left to enter the lobby restaurant. Even though he was ten minutes early, he saw Zei and Bai already sitting down at a table, looking at a hand device. Bai looked up, and waved at him.
Gladias headed over to their table, and sat down.
"What are you looking at?", he asked.
Bai showed him the screen.
"Do you know what it means?"
"Well, that first line is from a Veridian."
"Indeed. And the rest?"
"Not yet. I only know like five Dzegoban roots", Gladias laughed.
"Two percent of the language already", Bai replied.
"People should dream. If one person dreams, they will not fear pain. If a hundred thousand people dream a hundred thousand dreams, pain will fear them."
"It's an old poem."
"Not too different a message from ours."
"Indeed. Although you're blazing trails, and we're fighting here to survive."
Immediately after she finished speaking, Zei and Bai both turned to wave at someone else who was running up to the table.
Zei immediately recognized him, and slid out the remaining chair for him to sit down.
"Gladias, meet Fin."
"Nice to meet you, Fin. Seila mentioned all the good things that Zei had said about you."
"And nice to meet you too, Gladias. Anyone Zei brings is a friend to me."
"Well I'm just happy to finally get to see Dzego with my own eyes."
"So what's been up in your world, Fin?", Bai interjected. "I think this is the first time we've seen you in almost half a month."
"I'm really sorry I've been ignoring you guys for so long. But thank you for asking the question - because finally, I think I can give a worthy answer."
Gladias, Zei and Bai all turned to stare at Fin.

"You might have been wondering", Fin began, "why we spend so much effort on the Bansunpei. What's the point of optimizing Dzegoban, optimizing the measurement units, all of this, when there's so much else that Dzego desperately needs - education, defense, economic development, all of it."
"And for quite a few years, I've been wondering this myself. And it's not until my Bansunpei meeting the day Redshire was attacked that I finally got the answer."
"What is the answer?", Zei asked.
"Dzegoban is coordination training."
Zei and Bai both opened their mouths.
"Think about what we're doing each time we release a new iteration of Dzegoban."
"First, we A/B test many different versions of it. We motivate different people to try different things, and report back on their experiences."

"This ensures two things. First, it ensures that there's public feedback into the process, so the final product is informed by what behaviors actually work when you get real human beings to try to start doing them."

"Second, the public feedback, and the fact that the final outcome is a result of many people choosing between many different options across different dimensions, helps people accept the outcome. It takes no one by surprise. Anyone who disagrees with some part of it almost always knows someone who likes it more, and can at least hear their perspective."
"The Bansunpei intentionally seeks out members from all walks of life - you actually get bonuses for recruiting someone whom no one else in the organization knows."

"And so on the day Redshire was attacked, the Bansunpei digitally convened, and made an unprecedented decision. At least for the time being, they were putting Dzegoban version nine on hold. Releasing a few basic highlighting changes that had been agreed upon for over a year, but that's it."
Zei audibly sighed with relief.
Gladias could understand. The last month had been intense for everyone - hardly a good time to get everyone across the country to learn a whole new version of their language.

"Instead, they decided to use the exact same machinery, though with less public participation and more secrecy because of the unique circumstances and the time constraint, to coordinate a totally different set of changes across Dzego."

"Have you seen how many more people are wearing and having conversations through neck bands now? Or wearing privacy robes? Or going between places in black cars? Or buying products online, through the physical-delivery mixnets, instead of going to stores. And ten times more meaningful than any of that is what you don't see - more of the sensitive meetings are just going online, and everyone doing things on the internet is using much more secure tools too. Bluewhale Messenger has almost disappeared from Dzego overnight."

"None of that was happening three days ago. Instead, the Bansunpei just released its new privacy and security recommendations, through the channel where all the people who follow them were expecting news about Dzegoban version nine. About five percent of the population saw the recommendations at the same time. They were surprised, but they read and understood the reasoning, and respected the people who made the decisions. The majority of those people have already changed their behavior in at least one major way, and even that two and a half percent was already enough to start a trend that's now sweeping across all of Dzego."
Fin grew even more excited, and he continued.

"The Arctics talk a lot about a person's Intelligence Score, and how society should be run by those whose score is the highest. A few Veridian academics say that we should take Emotional Intelligence Scores seriously as well - though they always have a hard time getting people to actually do anything beyond just nodding along to that statement."

"But there's a third category that they are completely missing. The Coordination Score. A Coordination Score is not a property of a person - it's a property of an entire community. It's a community's ability to make collective decisions, to choose positive-sum, even if personally risky, cooperation over zero-sum competition, and to jump out of bad equilibria into better ones."

"This is what the Arctics think can only be done with a strong leader that everyone bows down to. But we Dzegojan say NO. We say 'gie fe kiu kai ci bin hu' - grow roots, no head. And now we've grown our roots, and we Dzegojan, who have improved and perfected our language eight times with no top-down coercion and no head, are going to take on the Arctics with no head. And we are going to WIN."

Chapter 19
Pafogai Du, Dzego·3724 Grapetime 15

Gladias and Zei were sitting at a table in a cafeteria, deep inside the mountain pryamid. Attached to one of the walls, they could see two large screens, doing the best job that they could to pretend to be windows showing a view of Pafogai Du as though the cafeteria was sitting on top of the mountain, rather than thirty meters below ground.
"So who is this that you wanted me to meet again?", Gladias asked.

"Den. He is a High Council member of the Kungaupei. You wanted to better understand Dzego's institutions, he helps run the one that's already been protecting us from the Arctic shadow campaign for the last decade. You want Veridia to learn from him, not from our official government."

At that point, they heard a faint buzz that began to rapidly get louder. Almost immediately, a few small drones, similar to those that would check Zei for cheating equipment in the Minpentai championships, flew into view.
Gladias's watch buzzed.
"What's going on?", Zei asked.
"Ah, I think my watch is detecting those drones as a threat. It's been doing this for many days now, I'm assuming it's just not been updated yet."
"Ah, let me check mine", Zei replied.
Zei took out his watch.
He clicked on the green, and scrolled through.
"Err... let me try this", Gladias said, staring intently at the watch.
"'mo fan' is eating room, so something to do with the cafeteria."
"Yep!"
"'min' is machine, 'jan' is person, so I guess the two together mean ... robot?"
"Yep!"
"'kun gau' is ... wait, is that connected to the Kungaupei? So these are Kungaupei robots?"
"Yes, but what does 'kun gau' mean?"
"I'll guess security?"
"Exactly."
"Security robots. Phew, that wasn't hard at all!"

"Just be glad I'm not Fin, he would start taking half a longhour to go through this whole interface and explain the history of each and every word and why they decided to keep it as they were shrinking the vocabulary."
One of the robots buzzed closer to Gladias, and stopped to hover about half a meter to the right of his ear.
"But anyway, why have I been detecting so many hostile devices? Is my watch just not up to date on something?"

"Ah yeah, it's just every lamp and drone and camera announcing itself; the protocols stepped up a lot these past few days. Your watch just doesn't speak the language yet. Here, let me help you with that."
Zei then spoke in a softer voice:
"jo sun fe zin ten lai de cau tie dai"
About one tick later, his watch buzzed, indicating that the data was received.
Zei moved his watch beside Gladias's.
"be"
The two watches buzzed at the same time, indicating a connection, and a file transferred from one to the other. Gladias pressed a button on his watch to accept.
He then checked his watch again.
"Looks good!"
"Huh, you're measuring CO2 and PM2.5 on there as well?"

"Yep! Pretty standard in Veridia. We really care about having a clean environment. We breathe twelve kilograms of air every day, more than what we eat and drink combined. So we're really all under-rating how important the air is."
"Why is CO2 on there? We have air sensors on our watches too, but that's more for smoke detection and poisons."

"The average concentration of carbon dioxide in our atmosphere is 300 parts per million. Air that we breathe out is 40,000 parts per million. So if the air you're breathing has 700 parts per million, then either there's some other source bringing that extra CO2 in, or, more likely, one percent of the air you're breathing in is air that someone else breathed out. And aerosol particles carrying all kinds of things stick around in the air for a long time - especially airborne viruses."
"Ah, I see, so it's not even about industrial pollution."
"Actually I'm surprised you're not caught up on this, and that the CO2 numbers are so poor here. I would have thought you would care a lot from the defense side, for pandemic prevention."
"Ah well you can ask Den when he comes!"
A robot arrived, bringing a salad and tea for Gladias, and a vegetable and rice dish covered with mushrooms and a tea for Zei.
"Wait, that dish you're eating. I think that's exactly what we call Number Ten in our Dzego food trucks!", Gladias exclaimed.
"Do you want to try it? I'm happy to take your salad. Tell me how it compares to the version you're used to."
"Sure!"
They switched plates, and began eating.
"Okay, this is much better than what we get in Veridia", Gladias excitedly remarked.
They continued eating silently for a few minutes, and after finishing their food switched to drinking tea.
Zei's watch buzzed again. Zei checked his watch, and his eyes opened wide.
"What is it?", Gladias asked.
"A message from a courtyard where I ate in Sadzu Du once. This is really weird."
"It seems to be addressed directly to me."
"How does the courtyard know you ate there? Payment is done in zipcoins, that's fully anonymized."
"Exactly. The courtyard seems to have sent it to all their guests from the past half year, and it has some kind of tag that my local AI accepted, almost everyone else's filtered out."
"What does it say?", Gladias asked.

"It's from the Beautiful Plants food court, on 2415 Len Su street, in Sadzu Du. An anonymous person burned four hundred zipcoins to send this message. The message envelope says that the recipient 'is successful' and is 18 years old. I know nothing else."
"That's a ... well-calibrated description."

"Indeed. They're trying to make the set wide enough to make sure it contains me, they burned four hundred zipcoins to signal to the courtyard, and to our local AIs, and to us, that the message is worth putting an effort into understanding, but also they made the set narrow enough that they could make this broadcast for only four hundred zipcoins."
"And narrow enough that not too many people find out about this message."
"Okay, let me open it up..."
Zei stared in shock again.
"What is it?"
"The message is a series of links to some files, in total over sixty gigabytes. I need to download eighty percent of them apparently."
"Will that take a while to download?"
"About a day wirelessly. But it looks like the digital archive node inside this mountain pyramid already has enough of the files."
"Shall we just walk there?"
"Exactly what I'm thinking."
Zei put his watch against a green circle on the corner of the desk. A moment later it buzzed. He stood up, and Gladias stood up immediately after him.
They exited the cafeteria, and started walking through the network of tunnels.
A few minutes later, they arrived at a large ornamented door.

To the left of the door, there was a drawing of a river horse reading a book, with a backdrop of a marsh with green trees and a blue sky in the background. To the right of the door, there was a drawing of a hamster sitting at a computer. Both drawings were a careful balance of cartoon-like playfulness, and a serious aura of mystery.
At the top of the door, Zei could read a slogan:
"Outside of a dog, a book is man's best friend", Zei translated for Gladias. "Inside of a dog, it's too dark to read."
Zei and Gladias stepped through the door, and entered.

To their left, the entire wall was a large shelf, about five meters tall, filled with physical paper books. The upper half of the shelf was set back about a meter, allowing the roof of the lower half to serve as a walkway to look at and take books from the upper half.

The shelf had openings in two places on the upper floor, leading to two miniature tunnels lined with more books. The shelf also had an opening in one place on the lower floor, also lined with books. All three openings seemed to go inwards for three to six meters; after that, one of the book-lined hallways turned ninety degrees rightward, another ninety degrees leftward, and the third, the one on the lower floor, turned into a T-shaped intersection.
It looked like the book section was deliberately constructed to be a maze, Gladias thought.
To their right, there was an open space with tables, and along the wall, there were many computer terminals.
Near the front of the space with tables, Zei saw a woman wearing a robe. He immediately ran toward her.
She turned around.
"Welcome to the Pafogai Du grand library. What is it that you seek?", she asked.
"There are very large files in the archive that I would like to load."
The librarian laughed.
"Glad you're being honest", she replied.
"Most people tell me they're looking to learn some high-minded thing about history or culture or mathematics, and then go and download their movies as soon as I'm not looking."
"Well I'm not downloading a movie, it's more ... a mysterious message."
"Ah, a quest! Even if that ends up just being an excuse, even that is something new and interesting in my day. Well, just follow me."
Zei and Gladias followed.
"So you got a mysterious message telling you to download some big files? Any idea what kinds?"
"Well so far I just saw some hashes..."
They arrived at a computer terminal. The librarian took out a data cable, and put one end of the cable into the terminal.
"Here, put the other end into your hand device."
Zei followed the librarian's instructions. The download started almost immediately.
"Wow, only eight minutes!"
"So now might you be more open-minded to the things we stodgy librarians say about how physical spaces are still relevant to the pursuit of knowledge after all?"
A robot slid up to them.
"jie hei ja ma?"
A menu appeared onscreen; there was no food, but a selection of drinks was available.
Gladias immediately clicked a button asking for a tea. Following along, Zei did the same.
"This space is beautiful, I am glad you have it."

Gladias stood up and walked over to the shelf with the books. He opened a few one by one. At that moment, not in the mood for straining his brain at reading and interpreting Dzegoban - especially not the earlier-version Dzegoban that the older books were in that he could understand nothing of at all - he focused his attention on the diagrams and pictures.

Two minutes later, the robot slid up to him, and gave him his tea. The tea was in a sealed cup, from which he could only drink through a straw. Surprised, Gladias turned to Zei, and saw that Zei, sitting at a table far away from any books, already had his tea. The cup that Zei received was open-faced, without much protection against the tea spilling.

Gladias found a book about Dzego architecture, titled "zui fia pai dan". He flipped through it. It contained pictures of many designs of basement rooms, shelters and underground rooms inside of mountain pyramids. The book showed them in roughly chronological order starting shortly after the war against the Arctic Empire a hundred years ago.

The earlier designs were very practical in construction, with not much thought put to comfort, or even safety against non-human threats. The designs in the middle started resembling ordinary rooms, with the main glaring exception being lack of windows. And finally, the designs near the end of the book were very well-decorated and comfortable, even more so than above-ground construction. About half had imitation windows, pretending to be outside. The other half did not have windows, and instead had plants, well-decorated walls, and other objects that seemed carefully chosen to make the inhabitant not see any space that they might think is supposed to have a window.
"Gladias!", Zei shouted. "Come back, it's almost done!"

Gladias turned around, and walked back. Just as he arrived, the last progress bar reached 100%. Another window automatically opened. A script began running. "Reconstructing data... estimated time remaining 175", it said onscreen - not in Dzegoban.
Gladias and Zei sipped their tea, and stared at the timer counting down. The librarian, curious, hovered quietly about two meters behind them.
Right on schedule, a little under two minutes later, the script finished, and a screen appeared.
Zei stared.
"Let's reschedule the meeting with Den for tomorrow. I have a feeling this is not going to be a simple task."
Gladias nodded.
"Are you going to answer?"

Zei pressed a few buttons on his hand device. "I put this program into a sandbox using a journaling file system, so it can't access the internet, and I can always revert it back to start. So there's no privacy leak risk, and if I'm not happy with the outcome I can just revert it back to start and try again. So why not?"
"Now ... to remember what I did on the 10th of Firemoon ... or rather I'll just ask my hand device."

A record of Zei's life events on that day popped up. That day was his last Minpentai game, the semifinal against Gun - the last day when things in his life were at least somewhat normal. Before that game, he woke up and had a meeting with Bai. After that game, he met up in the courtyard with Deluin.
Wait, Zei thought, the courtyard ... what was the address again? He looked it up.
The exact same cafeteria that the original message was from.
This was, as his local AI liked to say, the punchline. Zei started typing, recalling that day of his life from a combination of the AI records and his own memories which were rapidly coming back.
Waking up.
The meeting with Bai.
Going to the game.
Waiting for the game.
The game itself.
Watching Deluin's game.
A brief conversation with Deluin after the game. What was it I had said ... "my style was uglier than yours. Though I also won by playing defense"
And then the meeting with Deluin at the courtyard itself. Zei spent as much time detailing this event as the rest of the day put together.
The robot. A/B testing the new proposed hieroglyphs for Dzegoban.
Deluin invited him to Redshire. He refused. Deluin showed pictures of Redshire.
Deluin talking about how the nature of a place being beautiful actually does say something about the civilization there.
And then Deluin's gently trolling line: "I'll use my championship winnings to pay for you to go."
After typing everything in, Zei clicked "send".
"Okay, so this is a language model. But how large was that file? After the data reconstruction."

"10.7 gigabytes. The overhead was exactly a factor of six. I had a background thread check where the files were from, they were all recently uploaded. One sixth was a few recent movies - public data, though of course the selection of which movies they chose is a secret key of sorts. Another half was a big pile of someone's health data. The last third was also video, though it seemed to be AI-generated. It was all Arctic sermons talking about how fundamentally flawed the Veridian and Dzego civilizations are."

"The recombination algorithm was a five-of-six erasure code of five pieces of 10.7 gigabytes each. Each of those pieces, in turn, was a steganographic encoding: they used language models to find bits to flip so that the data still looked plausible, while encoding the actual underlying message, at a very ambitious rate of one bit of plaintext per four bits of ciphertext. And then the movies were a sort of cryptographic pad: if you don't know the exact set of movies that were used, even if you could fully uncover the plaintext, it would just look like random data."
"Wait, if they wanted a pad, couldn't they just pseudorandomly generate one by repeatedly hashing some data?"
"Ah actually you're right. Maybe I was overthinking it, maybe they just did it this way to throw people off."
"Okay, so 10.7 gigabytes, what is it?"

"It's not a plaintext language model. It's an obfuscated language model. Level two obfuscation, much weaker parameters than the full cryptographic-grade parameters that are used in the cryptographic networks for voting in DU or Bansunpei or for that matter the Order of Steering, but it's still the same algorithm."

"Level two obfuscation is actually the right tradeoff for language models, because language models themselves are big and compute-intensive, so they can't handle the high overhead of going level four, and on the other hand, language models are at least partially obfuscated and resistant to bit flips all on their own. If you uncover the value of a few weights, or get the ability to reliably flip a few values in a few tensors, it's not like you can get anything useful out of that."

"Overhead factor of level two obfuscation is in the tens to low hundreds on size, and high hundreds to low thousands on compute. So this model is pretty tiny; I suspect whoever sent this fine-tuned it to only do this one task. I also think this language model's wrapper program, the full package that's being obfuscated, is doing the thinking all at once, to verify whether or not my answer is satisfactory. If it is, it will just give us its message at the end."
As though on cue, Zei's hand device buzzed. The program finished executing. A new message appeared onscreen:
