Meldan, Veridia·3724 Mistime 10
Seila woke up, as the alarm in her watch buzzed. Her watch was flashing bright red - a message from Emerald of a type that she had never before seen.
She immediately sat up, and opened up her hand device to take a look at the news in more detail.
When she saw the top line, her heart almost stopped.
ARCTIC EMPIRE INVADES NORTHGLADE
Northglade. Febric and Hreda were there. No.....
She kept reading.
At 5,250 this morning, Arctic soldiers, flying vehicles and drones descended on the province of Northshore from all sides.
The Veridian military offered almost no resistance, and within two longhours their soldiers and drones were stationed in Northglade.

The entire area is now fully under Arctic control, with only one exception. The Greater Plum Harbor inside Northglade has remained untouched by the Arctics, and seems to be at present respected as some kind of neutral zone. Hundreds of refugees streamed into the Greater Plum Harbor, before the Arctics set up barricades to stem any further entrances. More refugees attempted to enter on personal copters. About half succeeded, especially in the first longhour, and others were shot down.

Internet communications between Northglade and the rest of Veridia have been cut, except for the Greater Plum Harbor. Long-distance transmissions between the Greater Plum Harbor and the rest of Northglade, which are evading the jamming mechanisms, are now the main channel of two-way communication with the province of Northshore.

Neither local Northshore politicians nor Arctic officials have yet made any public comment. As of our last knowledge, Lord Ephelion, Arctic consul to Veridia, was in Northglade at the time of the invasion. We await further information.
She scrolled down in her hand device, and saw that Emerald was highlighting five other messages that it deemed very important to her.

Seila started typing back a message, confirming to Febric and Hreda that she received their message and she and Vil and Daia would do everything she could to bring them home. Before she finished typing, she began to cry.
A longhour later, she heard a knock on her door. She walked up to the door, and saw through a screen that there was a man wearing a privacy robe outside.
"Who are you?", she asked.
"I'm Mov. Gladias knows me well."
"Why should I believe you?"
The man whispered a few words into his neck band, and put up his hand device against the green circle beside the door of the house. Seila's watch buzzed.
Seila cautiously opened the door, and let the man in.
Mov took off his shoes, and immediately proceeded to the basement room, knowing exactly where within the house it was located. Seila followed him.
They both sat down.
"I'm getting really concerned about what's happening to Veridia."
Seila looked at him with a blank stare, suprised that it was even possible to say something so uselessly obvious.
"I don't mean the invasion of Northglade. That was really shocking, it's terrible. And I'm really sorry Febric and Hreda are there. I hope they're safe."
"They are. The Arctics are leaving the Greater Plum Harbor there alone somehow, and Febric and Hreda managed to get there in time."
"So what do you mean?"
"I mean the things that made that invasion possible, and succeed with so little resistance. All of those factors are true in the rest of Veridia too."

"Gladias would be the person I would normally speak about this with, but he has been very busy in meetings with some Dzego secret government people the past few days, and he's been asleep the past few longhours. So I wanted to talk to you."

"What do you think I know? Our politicians are clearly bought out, or blackmailed, or apathetic, or some of all of those things. Gladias doesn't talk to me much about the Order, after all he's not supposed to."

"Maybe I'll tell you what I know. I was following Delwart, the mysterious gentleman who has been having meetings with Gladias for the past months. He was not just talking to Gladias, he was talking to various other Keepers, he seemed to have a pretty wide network."

"At one point, before I lost track of him, I caught him in a meeting with someone from Silverchat. And then Gladias told me that he confronted Delwart, and Delwart admitted that he had been working for Silverchat the whole time."

"Silverchat? They're doing some kind of big operation to corrupt the Order? But why? I would have expected Bluewhale to do things like that, but Silverchat were always the good ones! And what does this have to do with the Arctics?"

"I think our society has just gotten really complacent. Everyone is focused on maintaining their happy life, getting some advantage that they can, and people don't value actually maintaining the things that keep Veridia running. Even Silverchat. And what's worse, the Keepers just don't seem to be watching out for this."

"The Order seems to be performing better than any other part of our institutions. The military has failed completely at setting up defenses for Northshore. From what I can tell, the Keepers have done what they could, the tax rubric even changed to be even more supportive of open-sourcing defense hardware, Gladias told me that much. He was really proud of it, as was I."
"Indeed, though that was a close call. Whoever split up the Keepers into three groups that could not talk to each other was a genius - otherwise Delwart might have gotten to all of them."
"Something about this doesn't sit right. Silverchat... they just don't seem like the people who would do this."

"I know you've loved them since you were a child, for the same reasons Gladias did. And I did too. But sometimes ... your heroes turn out not to be heroes. Or maybe Silverchat doesn't care about that particular rubric, and that was just Delwart himself being an extreme peace dove."
"Do you know any of the other Keepers that Delwart talked to. Can we talk to any of them?"

"I did put trackers on two of them. I could have totally ratted them out to the cryptographic network and gotten a big bounty, but ... I thought it would be better to keep the option to track them more."
"Can we talk to them?"
"I suppose."
"Let's go visit them. Like, right now."
"You don't want to focus on seeing what you can do for Febric and Hreda today?"

"I may be a worried mom - or, well, aunt - but I know there's not much I can do. I had a call with them already, they're sitting tight, I'm sitting tight, I don't think we and they are any better at pulling off some kind of grand escape from Northglade than any of the hundred people trying to fly in to the Greater Plum Harbor who got shot down. So, sit and tight is the plan, nothing more to do today. But figuring out what on earth is going on with the Order, that's something I can do today."
She sighed.
"I guess I feel like I have to be doing something, and this is something that I can do."
Mov nodded.
"Just don't take a copter. You might think it's faster and this time the crazy high noise taxes are worth it, but you would just be inviting attention to yourself."
"Don't worry, I wasn't planning to."

A taxi arrived. Seila put on one of Gladias's privacy robes. She and Mov, who was already wearing his privacy robe, rushed toward the taxi. Seila reached the door first, and she tapped her watch against a green circle beside the taxi door, simultaneously opening the door and cryptographically approving the payment. They got in the taxi.
The taxi began moving, headed to a location a short autobus ride away from the home of one of the other Keepers.

Twenty minutes later, they arrived at an apartment building. It was a new construction. The outer wall was wrapped with some kind of imitation stone material. On the ground floor, they could see restaurants and shops selling various kinds of goods. On the higher floors, from the outside all they could see were regularly-spaced but well-decorated windows of people's apartments.
They saw another man walking towards the door, about to enter. They immediately slowed down their walk so that they would appear to naturally reach the door right after the man.
The man walked to the door, put his watch against the green circle beside the door, and the door opened. He walked through. Before the door closed, Seila and Mov walked in too.
"He's in room 515", Mov said. "Let's just go up the stairs."
"How do you know that?"
"The tracker I put on him."
They walked up the stairs, and eventually got to the door of room 515. They knocked.

On the inside, they heard footsteps. Mov removed the hood on his privacy robe, a gesture to appear less threatening. He was not supposed to know this man, so he had no way to prove that he was someone to talk to - except perhaps for burning a hundred zipcoins at his doorstep. Seila removed her hood too.
The man simply opened the door.
"Hello?"
"Hi, I'm Seila. I know this is awkward, but we wanted to talk about the Order and Delwart."
The man's eyes opened wide.
"Nice to meet you Seila."
"And I'm Mov."
"I'm Telroy. Though ... if you know I'm in the Order and you know about Delwart, maybe you already know that too."

At that moment, Mov realized that in a certain sense, he already had burned much more than a hundred zipcoins at Telroy's doorstep - by clearly having enough information to claim a large bounty by ratting out his role to the Order's cryptographic network, and choosing not to do that.
Mov and Seila walked in. Telroy directed them to sit down on the couch, and he began preparing tea for the three of them.
"So what do you know about me and Delwart?"

"You're a Keeper, you're in the rubric group on cybersecurity. One of the rubrics being debated has to do with data retention in environmental sensors. You met Delwart at least once, though I was not able to hear the content of your conversation."

"Okay, you do know a lot. Delwart has been insistent during our conversations that the recent push for trying to minimize data collection did not actually make sense, it was some kind of paranoid threat against an enemy that was not really present - though maybe now, he will have changed his tune. He argued to me that the more important information threat is protecting against insider trading."

"He also said that the local environmental and public safety agencies need broad access to be able to adapt to changing circumstances quickly without asking for permission every time - and that the main privacy defense we really need is delaying their access to non-disease-related data by five or ten days so that they can't trade with it."
"That ... does not sound at all like the Delwart that Gladias told me about."
"Did he say anything else?"

"He was generally anti-war, as I mentioned - that's how he described himself. Otherwise not too much - his main opinion was that he thought people were getting overcomplicated trying to throw in all the cryptography, and we should just trust people more."
"Okay, now I'm curious - what is the Delwart you know?"

"He was anti-war. He valued people's freedom to live their own lives, he wanted the Order to do much less - even the tax nudges were too much for him. In particular, though, he was really against this change to a tax rubric -"

Mov paused. He realized that Seila had already volunteered Gladias's name, and if he continued, he might be giving Telroy information through which Telroy might be able to figure out Gladias's rubric, and collect the bounty by ratting him out.
But then he thought - Telroy was trusting him and Seila, the least they could do was reciprocate back with some trust of their own.

"The rubric for open source hardware. He believed that anything military-relevant should be exempt from tax breaks, because military is a zero-sum game, we're not doing anything good for the world by participating in that."
Telroy nodded. "I guess he really is anti-war then."
"But then I followed him around more, and Gladias confronted him after Redshire was invaded, and ... it turns out he has been working for Silverchat."
Telroy stared in surprise. "Silverchat?"
"That is ... surprising."

Seila and Mov got out of the taxi, and walked along the forested path through Kalimar. A gentle cool breeze blew against their backs, subconsciously driving them to walk faster. A few hundred meters later, they walked off the path and turned right. Thirty meters after that, they saw a stone house that was mostly underground, with the above-ground part sticking up only a meter above ground. The whole structure was barely visible from beyond a few meters away.
That was one way to score high on aesthetics, public access and emergency shelter functionality at the same time, she thought. That house was probably paying close to no land taxes.
Seila and Mov walked down a staircase, and knocked on the door. They took off the hoods of their privacy robes.
They heard footsteps.
"Who is this?", they heard a female voice ask.
Seila quietly stepped on Mov's toe, urging him to stay silent. Mov picked up the cue, and stepped back.
"Hi, I'm Seila. I know this is awkward, but we wanted to talk about the Order and Delwart."
The door immediately opened.
"Hi, I'm Balme. Please, come in."
"Is it okay if my friend Mov comes in too?"

Seila felt slight discomfort from Balme - the interaction was now two on one, and Mov had a larger and more imposing physique - but at that point she had already opened the door, and it would have been very awkward at best to shut it on them.
"Sure", she replied softly.
Seila and Mov both entered.
"I apologize for intruding so rudely, and for spying on you to know where to come. But I hope you'll forgive me; our country is in a pretty dire situation as you can tell."
Balme nodded.
"What do you know about Delwart?"

"I met him a few times. The first time we talked was when he sent me an anonymous message about a longhour after a Keeper meeting. Somehow he had been able to track me down. I'm in a rubric group for private schools. He talked a lot about his own views about education, and how he thought we should not be putting our thumbs on the scale, using the tax rubrics to encourage what he considered biased civics education talking about how beautiful Veridia is and encouraging the students to cherish and love it - he thought that schools should just teach people knowledge, and they should learn to love Veridia by seeing how great it is on their own."
"Did he have any other perspectives?"

"He seemed generally pro-freedom, he believed that people should be left to evolve on their own, generally things work out best when they happen spontaneously and naturally, the Order should not be putting its thumb on the scale so much."
"Anything about international politics?"
"Not really, he never brought that up. He seemed not to care."
"He did once ask me what I thought about Dreadknot. I responded that I did not like them much. He didn't answer, and changed the subject."
Seila nodded.

"The Delwart that I know is also concerned about freedom, also thinks the Order should do much less. But... he also does have strong opinions on international politics. He basically thinks anything military is a zero-sum game, you can't know what will lead to a good or bad outcome, and Veridia should stay out entirely."

"Although ... he's apparently more mixed on the freedom thing. He seems okay with the public security agencies collecting more information, and not using cryptography to try to limit the data collection and get guarantees about what purpose the data is being used for."
Balme's eyes opened wider in surprise.
"Wait, I'm curious, how could you use cryptography for that?"

"I have a friend from Dzego, Zei, who told me about it once. Basically you have a language model inside the camera, that detects whether or not, say, an act of violence is going on. And only if that's happening, it passes the information along. Every time it does, it also uploads a hash onto a cryptographic network, so we get a public trace of how many times the check was triggered."

"And then they have a whole infrastructure to verify that the hardware is actually running that code. Signatures from keys that were randomly generated inside the chip by chemical imperfections in the manufacturing process at the time the chip was created. There's apparently a rule that anyone has a right to randomly take down a camera and micro-inspect it, and many people are doing that as a hobby, so no manufacturer can get away with making cameras that cheat the rules."

"That ... sounds amazing. Cryptography is not my area at all, but ... cameras that you can actually trust, that makes total sense! Wait, but Delwart was so pro-freedom, how could he not already know about that kind of thing and be enthusiastic about it?"
"I'm confused too."
Seila paused for a few moments.
"Okay, I know this is a random question, but - do you know any Keepers who are in any rubric groups related to social media?"

"I know a few Keepers as friends, but I don't dare ask them what they're working on. It's our tradition, you only talk openly about things you did when you already finished your three years and moved on to a different rubric group."
"Could you ... forward a message to them from me? I'll write it up for you right now. And tell them that it's worth responding to."
Balme thought for a moment, checking with herself whether or not she thought Seila, and her friend who had so far said nothing at all, could be trusted. An instinct told her that they can.
"Of course."

Seila walked up to the door of a house, similar to the one that she and Gladias lived in. This time, Mov stayed back entirely. Seila seemed more effective at winning trust alone, he thought, so he might as well let her do the questioning on her own. If he needed to, he could suggest questions by earpiece.
Seila knocked on the door.
No response.
A minute later, she knocked again.
Still no response.
She heard footsteps inside, but they did not seem to be getting closer to the door.
Her watch buzzed. She got a notification:
Mov ... she thought. She knew that whoever was in the house would see the same message, and know that she was serious.
Seila knocked on the door for a third time.
She heard footsteps again, this time coming toward the door.
"What do you want?"
"Hi, I'm Seila. I'm the one that asked Balme and Telroy to send the message about the social media rubrics. I want to talk."
The man opened the door.
"I'm Lectoby. I'm in the social media openness rubric."
"I'm sorry I didn't open the door. My wife is stuck in Northglade. I've been really upset today, I just don't want to talk to people."
Seila nodded.
"I'm Seila. I understand. My kids are stuck in Northglade too."
"Why did you burn those zipcoins? You could have just asked Balme to tell me you're coming."
Mov ... Seila thought to herself furiously. Why did he have to be so impatient?
"I'm sorry, I'm just really desperate."
Lectoby motioned for Seila to come in, and she followed. They both sat down.
"So what is this about?"
"Has there been any strange man who attempted to contact you, or anyone else you know in your rubric group? In the past year or so."
"Huh ... nope, never heard of that happening."
"Could you maybe ... directly ask in your rubric group chat? I want to confirm."
"Have you had that happen?"

"My husband has. Balme too. Quite a few others. He has strong opinions that seem to differ depending on whom he talks to. Sometimes he's anti-war, sometimes he isn't. Sometimes he's against the Order intervening in anything, sometimes he isn't."
Lectoby whispered a few sentences through his neck band.
"Let's wait for my Keeper group to see what they say."
He stood up.
"Would you like some tea?"
"Sure."
Lectoby walked over to the kitchen, and started to boil water for himself and for Seila.

"I'm sorry about your kids. This whole Arctic thing is just ... so crazy. Redshire, now this. It feels like they're shifting gears, and within a year or two they'll just launch a big war to take over the whole world."

"Or worse, less than a year. They took Northglade, seems like no one is lifting a finger again. I checked the senate hearing on my way here, a lot of performative outrage, no action, no introspection about how we got here."
Lectoby sighed.
He brought a cup of tea for himself, and a cup for Seila, and they sat down. They drank it silently.
Twenty minutes later, Lectoby leaned forward, and Seila's attention turned to him.
"They all replied", he said.
"And?"
"None of them had that happen. One did reply that a friend in a different rubric group had that happen to him. But none in this rubric group."
"That is ... so strange."
"It could be a coincidence, but..."
"What's the matter?"
"Your rubric group is on social media openness and interoperability, right?"
"It is."
"Delwart was supposed to be from Silverchat. But this is the one topic that Silverchat should care about the most, and ... zero inroads into this rubric?"
"Again, this could be a coincidence, but..."
She stood up.
"Wait, what's going on?"
She knew Mov would want her to leave, so she could sync up with Mov privately. But Lectoby had trusted her, and she thought it was fair to trust him too.

"Why would someone from Silverchat care about whether or not Veridian schools are teaching people civics well? Why would someone from Silverchat be so anti-war? How could someone from Silverchat be so effective at tracking down keepers? And ... why would someone from Silverchat, in that position, not make any effort at all on the rubric that Silverchat cared the most about, getting properly rewarded for being so effective at openness and interoperability?"

But by this point Seila had long since known the answer, and this was simply a final confirmatory straw. She figured there was no harm in blurting out her conclusion, as she stood up, and picked up her hand device, getting ready to leave.
"Delwart is not from Silverchat."

Meldan, Veridia·3724 Mistime 20
Seila, Vil, Daia, Lily and Zven were all seated around the table in Seila's house, waiting for dinner to arrive.
"Thank you guys for coming and keeping us company", Seila said softly. "It really means a lot to me."
"Any more news from Febric and Hreda?"

"I just sent them some more zipcoins for their personal expenses a few days ago. They're just living the life they can inside Greater Plum Harbor. The schools are full, but one of the other refugees was a math teacher, and we're hiring her to informally give them and a few other kids some lessons."
"No word on when there will be any way for them to get back here?"
"Still none. At this point I'm starting to suspect that the Arctics' plan to reunify everyone is to just invade the rest of Veridia too."
"Well at least they're safe."
Seila sighed.
"How is your lawsuit against Divergent going?"
This time Vil sighed.

"We won in the original trial a few months ago. But then they appealed. So a whole different group of judges got selected to hear the case, and a month ago they ruled in our favor too. But only a few days ago, we learned that they're appealing a second time."

"Can they just keep on doing that forever? Do another appeal, another five judges get sortitioned in, you have to convince them all over again, and keep doing that until you're too tired to keep going and then you give up and settle for like a quarter of the money?"

"Fortunately no, there are Veridian common law rules where judges can rule a case to be in bad faith, and require the submitter to give the other side a bunch of extra money as a penalty. That often happens to frivolous appeals."

"Here, their latest appeal document has some new footage from Jump's internal monitoring systems. Of course it was all encrypted, but some former employee had access and handed it over. They found some video and messages that make some of us look bad. So they're arguing it's a genuine appeal because of that. But really the video says nothing that's actually relevant to the case. I'm hoping these judges can see through what Divergent is doing more quickly than the previous round's judges did. We're accusing them of making a bad-faith appeal in our defense statement, with luck that should close things quickly."
"These hedge funds really are mean, aren't they."
"If judging wasn't anonymized, randomly selected and split into two and a half groups each round, I'm sure they would find a way to threaten or bribe the judges too."
At that point, Lily rushed into the room.
"Uncle Vil, Aunt Daia, Mom! I got eighty one percent on my latest civics test!"
"Congratulations, Lily!", Daia replied.
"Normally I would say, now you've earned your trip to Northglade.", Vil added. "But, well..."
"If it's safe in a few months and Gladias doesn't need me, I'll take you somewhere in the United Cities instead. Maybe Mabuli", Seila offered.
The doorbell rang. Before anyone else could react, Zven ran to the door to get the food.

Zven opened the door, picked up two bags from a robot, and closed the door. Zven brought the food back to the table, and immediately began unpacking. He, Seila, Daia, Vil and Lily each found the boxes with their own meals, and the five of them began eating.
"How was your time in school been, Zven?", Daia asked.
"My team won another Helisport game yesterday!", Zven replied excitedly.
"I also got ninety five on a physics exam a month ago. My teacher is really impressed."
"That's amazing", Seila replied.
"So a few days ago he took me out privately to a garage, and showed me a mini rocket. He let me take a look inside, and then press the button to let it blast off. It was so fun!"
"I want to build a rocket when I grow up! And then I want to fly in it. Maybe I'll even be able to go to the moon one day!"
"Sounds like you won't need me to take you on any adventures!", Vil added.
Daia continued asking the family table for status updates.
"So what else is new for you, Seila?"
"Well aside from Febric and Hreda, I've basically been thinking nonstop about those meetings with the other Order members I had recently."
"Are you able to say more?"

"Not the specifics. But in general, it feels like there's a really coordinated effort to try to manipulate the Order, they're saying different things to different people to manipulate each person based on their exact position, they have amazing spying powers, and their objectives don't even seem to be anything commercial."
"Is it the Arctics?", Zven blurted out, with the excitement of a hero in a detective novel solving a mystery.
The table went silent.
Seila was sitting in the chair in her basement, and was staring at her hand device.
Come on, she thought. Gladias should be awake any minute now.

She hit her palm against her face for a fifth time, ashamed at how blind she had been. Gladias had been having these secret meetings for half a year, and she had not asked anything, assuming that he had things under control - and that anything Gladias could not figure out himself, his shadowy friend Mov could.

But as it turned out, Gladias and Mov had been successfully hoodwinked by this man the whole time. And when his original pretense - that he was just a kindly man who cared about peace and freedom - fell through, they then got hoodwinked again by his mask, his pretense that he was from Silverchat.

Seila herself had seen through the Silverchat ruse within a day - really, she had felt doubts within minutes. But she had not gone further quickly enough. She had entertained the thought that it might be the Arctics, but she had dismissed it - none of Delwart's lines seemed anything like anything she had ever heard from Lord Ephelion. Why would an Arctic say anything nice about peace and freedom? But now the picture had all come together. When you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, how improbable, must be the truth.
Her watch buzzed. It was Gladias.
She immediately called.
"Seila! I miss you so much. How are you?"
At first, she wanted to scream.
"Gladias, you idiot! Do you know what you've done?!!!!"
At first, silence.
"What's wrong, Seila?"
"Delwart."
Silence again.
"I see. Did Mov catch you up?"

"Mov was an idiot too. And you're a double idiot for trusting him. Yes, he did catch me up, Gladias. But I saw through Delwart's lies almost immediately, and I dragged Mov out to do some sleuthing myself."
"What did you find?"
"He's not working for Silverchat, you incredibly naive idiot!"
"What?"
Silence again, this time from Seila's side, as she figured out the next thing she would say.
"What do you know?"

"We tracked down two of the other Keepers that Delwart talked to. One of them was on a rubric for data retention in environmental sensors. Delwart tracked him down, the same way he tracked you down. And he was telling him to not bother pushing for more privacy preservation in any of the security or environmental the data collection."
"We then tracked down another. She was on a rubric for education. Delwart was telling her to remove the incentives for private schools to have proper Veridian civics education."

"And then finally, just to confirm, we found a Keeper who was on the rubric that Silverchat should care the most about - social media openness and interoperability - and neither Delwart nor anyone else had tracked down any of them at all."

"But ... Mov overheard Delwart talking to a Silverchat person, how did that happen? Is this someone else trying to corrupt Silverchat too? Convince them to up-boost some content favoring whatever their position is?"

"No, you idiot. Delwart faked that. Come on, his spying ability is much better than Mov's, at some point he must have caught on to the fact that Mov was following him, and one day he planted that seed on purpose, to make his cover story more believable."

"Think about what we now know about Delwart's goals. You thought he cares about freedom - but not when he's pushing for unrestricted surveillance. You thought he is anti-war, but he never mentioned that to the second Keeper at all. And then eventually you thought he cares about Silverchat - but he never found his way at all into the Keeper group that was working on the rubric that Silverchat would care about the most!"
"There's three Keeper groups, they don't talk to each other. He could always have gotten into the other two."

"IT'S ABOUT THE PREPONDERANCE OF EVIDENCE", Seila snapped. "Remember the probability update formula, Hreda has shouted it at us many times. Each individual unit of evidence might only shift the odds ratio by a factor of two or three. But when there's three independent factors that all point in the same direction, that multiplies up to shifting the odds ratio a factor of eight to twenty seven."
"Okay, so what do you think Delwart's real motives are?"
"He's an Arctic."
"WHAT?"
"That's really hard to believe. Nothing he has ever said to me sounds anything like Lord Ephelion."
"Gladias... how can you be so naive?"

"Ephelion and Delwart are not intellectuals, they are propagandists. Their goal is not to seek and share what they think is the truth. Their goal is to adjust the discourse environment, either of one person or of a whole country, so suit their interests. To turn bystanders into friends, and enemies into bystanders."

"Ephelion's goal is to inspire people inside Veridia to join the Arctic cause. So he's openly saying a version of the Arctic cause that some smart, but sick and twisted, people in Veridia will find appealing."

"Delwart's goal is to break down the Order. He knows he can't make the Order pro-Arctic, but what he can do is make it ineffective. And so it's a better message for him to be sometimes pro-freedom, sometimes pro-peace, sometimes whatever else, depending on the rubric and the person he's talking to."
"Why are you so certain?"
"PREPONDERANCE OF EVIDENCE. Let's list it all."
"What are Delwart's goals? Not the goals he says he has, but the goals that are visible from his actions?"
"One: reduce support for open source defense hardware. One point for freedom, one point for peace, one point for Arctics, zero points for Silverchat."
"Two: push for unrestricted surveillance. One point against freedom, zero points for peace, one point for Arctics, zero points for Silverchat."

"Three: push for Veridian schools to not teach people Veridian civics. Delwart specifically said: 'people should learn to love Veridia by seeing how great it is on their own'. One point for freedom, zero points for peace, one point for Arctics, zero points for Silverchat."

"Four: not participate in the social media openness and interoperability rubric. Fine, there's three Keeper groups, we can multiply this one by half. Zero points for freedom, zero points for peace, zero points for Arctics, minus half a point for Silverchat."

"Five: once he blew his cover, he sent you off to Dzego. You might say, that's a good suggestion, Veridia should learn from Dzego more. But that's not the only interpretation. The other interpretation is that he wanted you out of the way, halfway across the world so that once you got suspicious, you would not interfere with any of his plans! Both are possible. So one point for every possibility."

"Six: his spying capabilities, beyond any corporation, far beyond some nonprofit group of idealists. Minus one point for an idealistic freedom lover or a peace lover, zero points for Silverchat, one point for Arctics."

"Sum it up. Arctics five, freedom two, peace two, Silverchat one half. And if you say it's a Silverchat person who also cares about freedom, then, well, we're at plus one half. I'd even multiply the last point, about spying capabilities by two, then you get six points for Arctics and zero or a half for any of the other explanations."

"And notice what it took, Gladias. He got to you, and through you he got to one third of one discussion group. The military, the parliament, media platforms - he and his friends walked straight through all of them. The only doors that he couldn't break were the ones whose keys he couldn't find: the Order, the Courts, the graph funding. Privacy isn't a luxury, it's why we're still here."
Seila stopped talking. For a few moments, Gladias stayed silent.
"I'm sorry, Seila."
"I'm sorry I didn't trust you enough to involve you in this. I love you. I should have trusted and respected not just your heart, but also your mind."
Silence again.
"So what do we do?"

"I hope that Delwart was wrong that you would be useless in Dzego, and you have something amazing to show from all the adventures you've been having there while I've been crying because our kids are stuck in an enclave surrounded by Arctics and trying to clean up your mess."

"I think I understand their military well now. Or rather, their shadow military. The official Dzego military is as compromised as ours, and the same situation for the rest of the government. But they've basically built up their Minpentai championship as a sort of secret army training ground, making the bet this whole time that the war that will matter will be a drone war - more similar to Minpentai than to anything like Helisport."

"I've been doing my best to convince them that the next battle will be in Veridia, not Dzego - we're ahead on technology and industry that might be a threat to them, but behind on thinking at all about defense - and that if they want to save themselves, they need to come help us over here first."
"Good. I hope for the kids' sake, and for Veridia's, and for yours, that you're actually going to have a plan to make that happen."

"Convincing the Dzegojan is only half the battle. We also have to convince the Veridians to accept them. And not the Keepers, the parliament. The same parliament whose subcommittee just barely accepted you as a Keeper, eleven to ten, despite having no valid reason to think anything negatively of you - unless they had some magic foresight about how naive you are, which I doubt."
"I know."
"Do you have any idea how we can do that?"
"I do not."
"I can try to figure this out. But you will have to trust me."
"I will, I promise."
"No more secrets, okay?"
"Okay."
"I promise."

Jahn, sitting in a taxi, looked out through the window. He saw Freetown's usual chaotic mixture of buildings: some glass and steel, some concrete, some stone, some tall, some short, some beautiful, some ugly.

The taxi passed under a highway, and he could see piles of uncollected garbage on the sides of the road. Almost immediately after the highway, the taxi passed by a small park to the left, and a tall industrial building on the right. A movie with subtitles was playing, projected onto the industrial building's wall. Jahn looked again to the left, to see where the movie was projected from. Just before the taxi moved too far away for Jahn to be able to see, he found the projector, hidden under a bench in the park. Even without Graph Funding or rubrics, he thought, some people will always provide public goods.
On the whole, everything seemed normal - though Jahn could just barely notice that the amount of activity on the streets seemed to be lower than usual.
The taxi passed under another highway. On the other side, on the side of one of the buildings, Jahn noticed a large advertisement.
Buy a luxurious room in a shelter, right on the northern edge of central Freetown.
10 meters underground, maximum-grade physical, bio and info filtration and insulation.
Only 325,000 zipcoins!
A minute later, another advertisement:
Shelters for the common man, in all shapes and sizes.
Prices start at only 50,000 zipcoins, mortgage plans available!

As the taxi continued west, it entered the region that the advertisement was talking about. Here, Jahn saw a type of activity that, to him, seemed to have been steadily increasing for the past six months: construction of roads. Jahn had also seen many shelters being constructed, but roads were a close second - particularly on the northern side of the town.
Jahn's hand device buzzed in his lap.
"Hey, Chief?", Jahn asked the driver.
"What is it?", the driver replied.
"Do you know why there's so many congestion charges this time? The road seems quite a bit less congested than usual, why would the tolls be going that high?"
"Ah yeah, they're bumping up every tax and toll they can. Funding defense, they say."
"Huh, the roads too?"
"Are they bumping up any other fees on you?", the driver asked.
"Actually not the government", Jahn replied. "At least, not directly. But, the shelters. I heard some interesting gossip there."
"And what is that?"

"The best shelters were originally owned by a few defense companies. Soon after Redshire got annexed, they got together and formed a cartel. Sold off a lot of the shelter space for money, and used that to modernize their armor and weapons a bunch."

"Huh, all private companies? I guess that's their property, their rules. Less shelter space left for us poor folks than if they just rationed it, but hey, they are trying. And if they use that money to defend us well, less chance we'll end up needing any shelters in the first place. And with fewer cars on the road, I'm enjoying the roads more too."

"Well, yes that's the polite story. Freetown's economic philosophy at its finest. But I'm getting the feeling it's not quite that clean. The government seems to be making a special effort to build roads in exactly those places that make it easier to get to and from the shelters. There's no evidence of any collusion between them and the companies - that would get knocked down hard by the courts - but my theory is that it's a sort of retroactive reward. Create the expectation that if you use your private property for the public good, then the government will twist the public work that it does in order to make life easier for you. It's a trick to work around the maximum budget rule - pay people without actually directly paying them."

"And if you refuse to use your private property in public-spirited ways, well... if things get really bad the next step might be that they'll start closing some roads for 'maintenance'. Though I guess people can always fly."

"The Greater Plum Harbor has been refusing to fund anything that could be seen as going against the Arctics, they're scared that their node in Northglade might get shut down. I guess that's where we'll find out how good Freetown is at staying 'free'."
"And at defending itself."
The driver and Jahn stayed silent for a minute. Soon, the taxi slowed to a halt. Jahn looked outside the window. He had arrived at the Freetown Economics Institute.
"Thank you Chief, and have a good day!"
"You too, boss", the driver replied.
Jahn opened the door, and got out of the taxi.
Jahn passed through the turnstile in the Freetown Economics Institute, and walked toward the restaurant.
After a minute of walking, he arrived. He saw a familiar face: Utaku.
"Utaku! Surprised to see you still here."
"My parents told me to come back. They think Freetown is taking defense more seriously than the other United Cities, so it's safer than Belpaki here."
"Do you think that?"

"There have been some moves recently to create a unified defense grid between the aks. I'll be more optimistic if that goes through. But even then, I worry it's more theater than anything substantive."
"Has Freetown been doing anything substantive?"

"Well the big corps are paying insurance on all their property, the rates tripled when Redshire was annexed, and doubled again after Northglade. And then apparently the rates dropped back down by a quarter when the corps announced their recent defense packages."
"So ... somehow the market incentives seem to be working."

"You know, I've been talking to Zei from Dzego lately, and learning how quickly they've gotten everyone to start caring about privacy, now about bio safety, average indoor CO2 levels dropped by over a hundred points within a month. All coordinated by machinery that they originally created, supposedly, to upgrade their language - and to give us a much more sensible distance and time system."
"I've been getting this feeling that maybe almost any system can work well if people accept it and believe in it."
"Do people in Freetown believe strongly in economic freedom? Everyone in the Economics Institute does, obviously, but what about regular people?"
"Are you familiar with the early history of the United Cities, a hundred years ago?"
"Vaguely. I know there were some wars, both between some of the cities and against the Arctics."
"But do you know how those wars got resolved?"
"Eventually the armies of this continent came together and cooperated more, and that was a big part of why the Arctic offensive against Dzego was finally stopped."

"Coming together in a crisis is easy. What's hard is keeping that spirit together through the easy times, the boring times, the times when the founding generation dies out and the kids and the grandkids need someone to fight against and have a hard time resisting the urge to start turning on each other."
"So what happened? The co-governance system, I'm guessing?"

"That's one part of it. Each city gave a percent of the votes in its parliament to its neighbors - not enough to threaten the cities' independence and their unique cultures, but enough that future politicians would not have an incentive to ignore their surrounding continent completely."

"But also, they did another thing to preserve unique cultures. They had a period during which they subsidized people swapping homes and citizenships. People who felt more at home in another city were able to move easily and change their allegiance to their new home."

"The government of Freetown made a decision. They passed a new constitution, the one we still have today, which limited the government's power to regulate and tax anything down to a bare minimum. And then they said: this is what we are about. If you are scared of it, go to another city, but if you like it, no matter which city you're from, we welcome you. They even did a personality test without telling people what it's for, and then gave bigger subsidies to people who got what the government thought was a compatible result."
"Wow, I did not know that."

"Actually Arturia did a similar thing, in a somewhat opposite direction. They described their values as being about peace and quiet, research and learning, and they filtered by conscientiousness and test scores. Today, their whole society is sort of like a big university. If you go against the system too much, you get pushed harder and harder to leave and go to Freetown. But if you're fine with the system, you can learn a lot and have a lot of fun inside it. They actually do quite a lot of good science and have reliable infrastructure."
"The strongest legitimacy comes from people buying in to an idea voluntarily - signing the form, knowing exactly what they are getting themselves into and what they are giving up."
"That sounds like selection matters too. Different styles work for different people. Maybe a Freetown made out of people from Arturia would be a disaster, and same with the reverse."
"Of course, now we're several generations into people being just born here, like people get born anywhere else. But for now, Freetown has held."
"Do you think some people are ... genetically more freedom-loving than others? And Freetown got a lot of those people back then, and those genes got passed down?"

"People here bring that idea up from time to time. To me it feels unlikely. All the congestion tolls that I paid to get here, all the turnstiles, I somehow doubt that there can exist a gene that would register all that as being "free". You need to have a pretty deep education to understand how it's free - how it's all part of a market, each person and institution allocating their private property as they see fit, and how all these payments give people the ability to honestly self-report whether or not they truly value something more than the resources that it costs to make it available for them, and how that's better and more civilized than the government just deciding what things it thinks are wasteful and banning them."

"I think there might be a core that even someone from the medieval era would understand. I don't bother you, you don't bother me. We're all each just trying to live our own lives, if we can help each other that's great, but not at the expense of leaving each other space to be in peace. You don't get the forager freedom of the great outdoors, especially not in the city, but within your own box you are the master."
"At least, that's what Freetown always feels like to me."

"Although ... I do love the economists here. Well, the intellectual culture in general. I like that you can honestly bring up the genetics stuff, and even if people disagree, it's not like Belpaki where they just immediately think you must be an Arctic or something."

"Changing the subject a bit, of course I know why they would never tell either of us, but I am curious what these defense companies are up to. What do they think the threat model is? Same type of invasion as Redshire and Northglade? But what happens if we resist harder? And how are they going to fight back?"
"Well, funny you ask. I actually do know some gossip, although ... this is military, I don't think I'm allowed to tell you."
"Huh, I'm surprised you got into those circles at all. Were they interested in your thoughts as an economist on how to raise more funding for defense?"
Jahn sighed. "Unfortunately, I really can't tell you. Freedom of speech is great for many things, but ... not for military secrets."

Jahn ordered a dish with vegetables and a tea, and stayed in the restaurant area studying the internet to better understand exactly the question Utaku had asked: what options Freetown still had to raise more funding for defense. He took out a computer, and made a table, scoring different options in three columns: how much money it could raise, how much economic collateral damage it would cause, and how much it risked making Freetown less ... free.
A longhour later, Jahn's watch buzzed. It was Zei, asking for a call.
Jahn picked up his computer and his glass of water, and moved over to a nearby calling booth.
"What's up, Zei?"
"Thank you again for that connection you made with the defense companies last month. I actually have some interesting updates there!"
"Hey, I only connected you to the Economics Institute director, the connection to the companies was his doing."
"But what is it?"
"Well, first let me give you a status update. Do you know what the Dzego folks have been doing with the defense companies' help?"
"I do not."
"They've been hunting down Arctic drones in Redshire."
"If you're allowed to ... tell me more?"
"How about I show you more?"

Jahn's computer buzzed, and he saw a file download. It was a view-once file. If Jahn wanted, he could of course save it clandestinely through the operating system, or just take a picture of the screen with another device. But by default, once opened, the file would stay viewable for five minutes, cannot be copied, and would self-delete at the end. Politeness dictated not interfering with these defaults.
Jahn clicked on the file, and a view opened up.
"What am I looking at here?"
"This is happening right now as we speak. It's our clandestine kill chain on an Arctic ground drone in Redshire."

"The red square is the enemy. The blue circles are seven of our own drones, that we arranged in a hexagon. Their role is to jam communications. Right now, they are dormant, waiting for the Arctic drone to get fully inside."
"So what happens next?"
"Ah, well let's find out together."
About ten ticks later, another view-once file appeared on Jahn's screen.
"Just waiting a little bit longer."
"I'm excited."
"And ... action."
"Do you see it?"
"Yep."

"The jammer drones are jamming. The red X signifies that there was a hit on the target. It's supposed to be two hits: one on its main antenna, and the other on its legs, to prevent it from leaving the jamming area. And the blue triangles are our two attack drones."
The conversation paused for about twenty ticks.
"Still not dead? What's taking so long?"
"Our drones, the triangles, are not actually trying to make a kill - if we wanted to do that, we could have just done that with a bigger first strike."
"So what are they doing?"
"They are dancing."
"Dancing?"

"Their goal is to survive as long as possible, trying any kind of trick to avoid getting killed, ideally get mistaken for an Arctic drone or even an animal, and eventually only kill when the target is too close to escaping the trap."

"That's our goal. Using Arctic drones as target practice to improve our ability to kill them is expensive. But using Arctic drones as practice to improve our ability to survive them, that we can do, for basically as long as either of the triangles is still alive. Then the seven drones in the hexagon can finish the kill, and make sure to fry the target's circuits so the Arctics don't get any training data themselves."
"Wait ..."
"What's the matter?"
"We have a problem."
"Arctic reinforcements? Are you going to take over and pilot your drones to victory now?"
"Yep, that's exactly what I'm doing. Temporarily have the two damaged-but-alive jammers play dead, lure the attackers to center, jammers reactivate, reform a circle, and then make a kill."
"Do your thing, no need to give me a play by play."
"I'm talking to the AI and letting you listen."
"Circles, finish the northwest square now. Goal: all comms and memory dead."
"Deactivate all jamming except left and top left."
"When it makes sense, reform the circle, reactivate jamming and strike. Maximize surprise."
"No-"
"Wha-"
Jahn stopped mid-word, remembering that he was not supposed to distract Zei.
"They started jamming, I got disconnected."
"Nothing for me to do now. It's just our AI against the Arctics, AI plus human. And if our jamming works, our AI against theirs."
They both waited silently.
Ten ticks.
Twenty ticks.
Thirty ticks.
Finally, the download icon turned on again on Jahn's computer.
"That was really close."
"Wow."

"Only one undamaged drone on our side. Last step is that it will walk around and chip and memory-kill all the drones, first the Arctics and then the rest of our own just in case. It needs to do that before more Arctic drones come."
"Can the damaged ones help?"
"They can't move. They can still attack, but proper chip and memory-killing is best done from ten centimeters away."
"Even then we can't actually be certain that the Arctics won't be able to salvage training data. We can just hope for the best."
"Okay... I gave it the instructions, now I'm just watching."
"I am curious. How does your internet link into Redshire work?"

"Ah, that's one of our other big projects. The problem now is that the Arctics have confiscated all the un-backdoored electronics. There's still many watches, hand devices and compute boxes left hidden in various places, but the Arctics will be able to tell if any device tries to transmit things. So what we do is steganography."

"Two people pretend to have a voice or video call. While the call is happening, the un-backdoored device is sitting nearby, and it's softly playing audio. That audio stream sounds random - it's representing encrypted data wrapped in an erasure code that's highly noise-tolerant - but we use the same tricks I told you before with the health data to maximize how much data we can hide, so that it appears to anyone or any bot spying on the call that there's nothing abnormal."
"One of ... do you have more big projects?"
"Well, the next step is that we want to actually kidnap an Arctic drone and bring it back to Dzego for analysis."
"Wow."
"Actually, that's what I'll ask for your help one more time for."
"So what do you need?"
"I want you to introduce me to another defense corp. Preferably not through the Institute director, find a different path."
"Why?"
"The company the Institute director introduced does seaborne well, I want to find one of the others, that are better at airborne."
"Also, come on, it's Freetown, this is a market. You gotta talk to multiple people and compare them against each other, to make sure they're not screwing you over."

Pafogai Du, Dzego·3724 Mistime 22
Gladias, Bai and Fin were sitting at a table in a cafeteria, deep underground inside the mountain pyramid.

Between the tables and the wall of the cafeteria, there were green trees on all sides. Two of the walls were covered with vines. The other two walls were covered with large mirrors, making the whole room seem like it was part of some kind of endlessly-repeating infinitely large space. There was a single entrance, with two thick shrubs on both sides blocking the view to the entrance tunnel, in one of the corners.

In one of the other corners, and in the middle of the cafeteria a few meters away from them, a few air filters stood on the ground - clearly recently added, with not yet much thought put in to how to make them fit into the room aesthetically. Downward-pointed fans and violet lights hung on the ceiling.

The three of them were in a private area, with shrubs blocking most of the rest of the cafeteria from view. Two speakers were simulating the sound of cicadas buzzing in a forest in the morning, drowning out the conversations from the other tables - and thus, they knew, protecting their own conversation as well.
Zei walked in, visibly exhausted, and sat down with them.

"That was close. We got ambushed by some Arctic drones, we just barely managed to beat them. Fortunately, we had a full five minutes before the next swarm came to finish ours off, so I think we were able to destroy any chips that the Arctics could extract to get training data from the battle."
"How are the Freetown folks feeling?"
"They're very excited."
"See, I told you that working with Freetown first is going to be a good way to warm the Kungaupei up to cooperating more internationally."
"You have to give people some quick wins that they can show their superiors or their friends, get legitimacy by performance as soon as possible so people trust you to take the next step."

"Yep, your advice was good. But ... I suspect the next step will be harder than this one. The Freetown defense corps want to cooperate. In Veridia, we'll have to find a way to work around their institutions, that's much harder."

"You can do small projects by working around people. But if you want to win the big battle, you need scale. And if you want scale, you have to do the hard thing, and actually bring some of the bigger institutions onto your side."
"Do you have any ideas on how?"
"Seila says she's going to try to figure something out. I gave her Verdow's contact, so far he's the only senator I really trust. So we'll see."
A robot arrived, putting food for the four of them onto the table. They began to quietly eat the food.
Fin and Gladias finished their food first, and rested for a few minutes, drinking their tea.
Fin took out a book from his bag, and handed it to Gladias.
"Here, let's see how good your Dzegoban is. Open up a page and read."
Gladias grabbed the book and flipped to a random page. He took a look.
"You think I can do this?", Gladias asked incredulously.
"Come on, try."
"Okay, here goes..."
"From material world small thinking, to internet small thinking."
"Small thinking is minimalism."
"Ah, I see, this is one of those cases where knowing the roots on its own really doesn't get you there."
"Indeed. And the whole project of shrinking the roots down only succeeded once we accepted that that's inevitable."
"Containing inside the green, forty years ago, a big pattern change in beautiful thinking in the whole world was minimalism."
"That first bit is a set phrase, it means 'including Dzego and Veridia'. Beautiful thinking is aesthetics."
"Many people recognized that having many physical things is not only line-heartedness but also a locked room."
"Line-heartedness is a feeling of simplicity, or convenience, a locked room in this context is more like a prison."
"A complicated room implies a complicated heart."
"Good!"
"Living with the warm-heartedness - happiness? - of having few things is freedom."
"Great!"
"That this happened forty years ago has a logic - a reason?"
"Yep."
"Electric machines and the internet began to exist."
"This implied that many people gathered physical things ... wait, physical things gathered by many people, began to be unwanted."
"I would say unnecessary here."
"Hand devices caused to be unnecessary aggregate-and-group devices, music devices, sound conversation devices and ten other devices that one would previously have."
"Aggregate-and-group devices should be add and multiply devices - calculators. Sound conversation devices are phones."
"It can contain books without an upper lid."
"Unlimited."
"Many parts of that we all live are moving to the electric world."
"Many parts of all our lives."
"As a result, the complexity of the physical world stopped behind."
"Was left behind."
"In the nearby few years, we are seeking a different change in pattern."
Gladias paused for a few moments.
"Okay, I'm tired. But I am curious. Can you just tell me what the rest means?"
Zei picked up the book.

"Social media is not always good for people's mental health. Much of the interest in privacy is driven not just by fear of the Arctics, but rather the sheer volume of everyone talking about everyone else, and the unpredictability with which random events from people's private lives become public discourse."

"People are afraid of many parts of the internet, especially in other countries where privacy technology is not as strong and well-understood. Location tracking, behavior profiling, all of it. And it's not just privacy - people are recognizing that the internet can be as addictive as drugs."

"And so now we're slowly seeing the emergence of a different kind of minimalism: internet minimalism. Disconnect. Do things on your own device. And like physical minimalism was made possible by the growing capabilities of the digital world, internet minimalism is made possible by the growing capabilities of AI and local software - you can have your whole world on your own device."
"Fascinating."
"Gladias, you're doing very well."
"Thank you. Now your turn. How well do you understand the Order of Steering's governance rules?"

"There is a collection of tax rubrics. For each rubric, twenty one Keepers are randomly chosen - seven added in each year, for a three year term. The job of the group is to propose and vote on changes to the rubric. The twenty one are split into three sub-groups of seven, all mixing first, second and third years. Any Keeper can make a proposal for a change to the rubric. Each sub-group discusses every proposal independently, they don't know who the other sub-groups are. After a few rounds of discussion, all twenty one Keepers vote on each of the proposals, and the ones that pass, with at least thirteen out of twenty one votes approving them, get accepted."

"There is a separate mechanism, the Sentinels, who are randomly selected and put into groups that audit individual businesses. There, it's three groups of three. They have a very specific task: determine what tier on each rubric a business gets. And then smaller businesses have audits done by Acolytes, Order members in training. For an Acolyte to get accepted, they have to both pass Senate committee approval, and be in the top ten percent by prediction score - by how well their votes on the small portion of their audits that get randomly sampled and re-done by Sentinels agree with the Sentinels' results."
"Now, what about the Courts?"

"Same mechanism as the Sentinels, though with five judges instead of nine. Also, in civil cases either side, in criminal cases only the defense, can appeal a ruling. There's no hierarchy, it just selects another random sample. There's a common law rule that if you submit a case - either an appeal, or even a first-time lawsuit - that has no merit to the point of being bad-faith, then that case can end not just with you losing, but even with a penalty judgement against you. That's the protection against what we call denial of service attacks."

"Actually, good that you mention that last part. My co-father, Vil, was in a long lawsuit against, well, basically his former employer, for doing some financial trickery to fire him and get away without paying the pre-agreed severance. He won the first round. The company appealed and lost. Then they appealed again. And just yesterday, the court struck down their second appeal, declared it bad faith, and tripled the amount that they have to pay Vil and the other workers."
"Glad to hear the system works!"

"That's always the most important question: whether or not it actually works. The Parliament hearings approving new Keepers and Sentinels, for example, barely work at all at this point - at least in my view."
Bai spoke up.

"This is all really good info, Gladias, and thank you Zei for getting up to speed on it so quickly. If we want to affect Veridia, understanding how these institutions all work today is just as important as the military side."
"Anyway, I think Den is waiting for me and Zei in his private room. We should start heading over."
"Sounds good", Zei replied.

Zei and Gladias simultaneously raced to put their watches against the small green circle on the corner of the table. They ended up both pushing each other's wrists too far away to make the connection. Fin joined in, and slapped his watch against the circle. A moment later, his watch buzzed.
The four of them all stood up, and began to walk to leave the cafeteria.
Gladias was in bed, getting ready to go to sleep. Suddenly, his watch buzzed.
He had only seen messages in this shade of red twice before: once when Seila had messaged him when Northglade was attacked, and once when she had called him about Delwart.
Emerald was letting Gladias know the level of importance and Seila's mood and, Gladias knew, this was already a large part of the message.
Gladias's heart raced, as he answered the call.
"DO YOU KNOW WHAT HAPPENED TO LILY?", Seila screamed.
"I ... do not. I just remember hearing that she got eighty-one percent on her latest exam. What happened?!"
"I entered her room. She was talking, typing on her hand device. And I could see what she was reading and saying in the mirror."
"For a few minutes, I just stared. I could not believe it."
"What was it?"
"She was in some kind of chat group, and they were sharing Arctic propaganda. Cheering on Lord Ephelion's messages. Hoping that the Arctics would come to the rest of Veridia soon."
"WHAT?"
"I snapped. I called her out on it, and asked how she could possibly be betraying us like this, when Febric and Hreda were stuck a thousand kilometers away because of them."
"What did she reply?"

"That the Arctics were right. Their philosophy, their idea that some people are worse and other people are better, and that the better people should rule everyone else, and the most important thing in life is to strive to be one of the better people, was the thing that had motivated her, and given her a reason to study and work hard. That our unconditional love was poison. That the Arctics' philosophy - appreciation and love only as reward for success - actually brought her out of her hole, when nothing we did helped even a little bit."
"That's ... horrible."
"I screamed at her for ten minutes, and shut the door."
"I cried for a longhour. And then, when I opened the door again, the window was open, and she was gone."
"Can you ... track her? Through her watch?"
"Already got Mov to do that. It was a waste of time, she threw her watch onto some random autobus."
"Wow. Now I feel so bad. We really haven't been doing anything to actually motivate or encourage her."
"GLADIAS, SHE GOT BRAINWASHED BY THE ARCTICS. DON'T YOU DARE GET IN YOUR PHILOSOPHER MOOD AND TELL ME THEY HAVE A POINT."
"HOW COULD YOU HAVE BEEN SO NEGLIGENT?"

"Okay, hold on. Not seeing through Delwart, that one is on me. I was dumb. Mov was dumb. I admit it. This, this is on both of us. You're Lily's mom. You saw her many times - before she went to Vil and Daia's, when we visited them during her time with them, and after she came back. You had many chances to make things better, just like I did. And you didn't succeed, just like I didn't succeed. So let's solve this problem together."
"YOU DON'T UNDERSTAND AT ALL, DO YOU?"
Seila hung up the call.

Gladias checked his watch. The time just hit 20,000. He had been awake all night after his call with Seila. He had tried to go to sleep twice, but gave up after twenty minutes each time.
He could not go to sleep knowing that three of the four children he loved dearly were now, in one way or another, in the hands of the Arctics.
He could not go to sleep after Seila gave him that kind of vote of non-confidence, and then cut off communication without giving him any chance to even apologize.
And he definitely could not go to sleep when both of those things were happening to him at the same time, and anyone he could hug for emotional support was thousands of kilometers away.
Finally, thinking as much about redeeming himself in Seila's eyes as about his daughter's safety, he decided to do something unorthodox: he called Zven.
Zven picked up immediately.
"Dad?"
"Are you still in contact with Lily?"
"Her icon went green about forty minutes ago. I think she logged in from a new device."
"Good."
"Zven, are you willing to help us save Lily?"
"Of course! Anything for my sister."

"Then here's what I want you to do. Stay in touch with her. Reach out, ask her what's up. Don't give any indication that you disapprove of her decision. Even show sympathy for her. Just stay in contact, and try to learn where she is."
"What is it?"
"That's like ... exactly what Mom told me to do a longhour ago. She gave me a lot of good advice for things I should and shouldn't say."
Gladias opened the door, walked through the hallways until he left the hotel area, and then turned left and kept going through the tunnel.

This was now his eighth day living entirely underground, inside the mountain pyramid at the south end of Pafogai Du. Soon after he first arrived in Dzego, he had been relocated there from his original hotel. The new recommendations were for all "important business" to move to underground locations, and as a de-facto Kungaupei advisor, Gladias certainly qualified.

For over two months, he would take daily twenty minute walks every day along the trees around the perimeter halfway up the mountain pyramid, and sometimes a longer walk down and into the nearby forest. For the past few days, he had been spending each day in the library, learning about different aspects of Dzego and having almost daily calls with Verdow to think through how to convince the Veridian military to cooperate with the Kungaupei.
And today, after what happened last night, and after only getting one longhour of sleep after it, he did not have the will to go outside at all.
Gladias walked slowly, taking many breaks to stare at the wall and at any side rooms that he walked past on his way to the library.

"Who got first place?"
"Zei. And he had a motivation to succeed that was even more pure, even more beautiful, than my desire to succeed in order to prove to the world that I deserve love because I am strong."
"And what motivation was that?"
"Curiosity."
The conversation paused for a moment. Then Gladias spoke up again.
"When you hugged me a few minutes ago, were you not offering exactly the thing that Ephelion says is poison? Love as a reward for weakness?"
"I would not have done that a year ago."

"I would love to say that I did that because I gave up the false god of greed and converted to the true religion, that of valuing curiosity. But even that is false. "It definitely would have."

I'm not going to say I'm fully unopinionated between all the different motivations that human beings might have - I'm very comfortable saying, today, that curiosity is almost always a better motivation than greed. And resentment might be the worst of all. But I don't think there's a one size fits all for everyone."
"So how do I save Lily? And, for that matter, Febric and Hreda? And how do I get Seila to stop hating me?"

The only way she can be happy, is if she can hug Febric, Hreda and Lily again. And there is no way to use emotional support and love alone to bring the three of them back. The only thing that will bring them back, is if you win - by helping Veridia win against the Arctics. So let that motivate you to try harder, so that in this next battle you can be a winner."
